topics.title: How the web works: client, server, request, response
topics.summary: Every app you manage is a conversation between a client (browser or phone app) that asks and a server that answers. The client sends a request over the internet, the server does some work (often reading a database) and sends back a response.
topics.why: This is the mental model behind almost every engineering conversation: where a bug lives, why a page is slow, which team owns a failure. If you can trace one request end to end, you can follow any architecture discussion.
concepts: Packets and the network in between
What happens when you press Enter in the address bar
topics.do_it: Open any website, press F12, go to the Network tab and reload. Pick 3 requests and ask Claude to explain each one (who asked, who answered, what came back).
topics.prove: Talk for 2 minutes on "What happens when a user logs in?" without notes. Record yourself on your phone.
topics.interview: Walk me through what happens when a user types our URL and presses Enter.
covers: Frontend: how frontend talks to backend

topics.title: Frontend basics: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript
topics.summary: HTML is the structure of a page, CSS is how it looks, JavaScript makes it interactive. TypeScript is JavaScript with types added, so many mistakes are caught before the code runs.
topics.why: When a designer, a frontend developer and QA argue about a defect, you need to know whether it is a markup, styling or logic problem, and why teams choose TypeScript for larger codebases.
concepts: DOM: the page as a tree the browser can change
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to build a one-page 'project status card' in plain HTML/CSS/JS. Then ask it to change only the CSS, then only the JS, so you see the three layers separately.
topics.prove: Explain to a non-technical stakeholder why changing a button colour is a 10-minute job but changing what the button does may take days.
topics.interview: Why would a team move from JavaScript to TypeScript, and what does it cost?

topics.title: Frontend frameworks: React, Angular, Vue, Next.js
topics.summary: Frameworks are toolkits for building complex interfaces from reusable components. React is the most common; Angular is an all-in-one framework popular in enterprises; Vue is lighter; Next.js adds server rendering and routing on top of React.
topics.why: Framework choice affects hiring, speed of delivery and performance. You will be asked to weigh in on rewrites and migrations, and you need to know what 'components', 'props' and 'state' mean when developers estimate.
concepts: Hooks (React's way to use state and side effects)
topics.do_it: Ask Claude: 'Build a tiny React task list with add and complete'. Then ask it to label which parts are components, props and state.
topics.prove: Explain props vs state using a project-plan analogy in under 60 seconds.
topics.interview: Our team wants to rewrite an Angular app in React. What questions would you ask before agreeing?

topics.title: Rendering strategies: SPA, MPA, CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR
topics.summary: Rendering is where and when the HTML is produced. In the browser (CSR/SPA), on the server for every request (SSR), once at build time (SSG), or rebuilt on a schedule (ISR). An MPA reloads a full page per click.
topics.why: This choice drives SEO, page speed, hosting cost and complexity. Marketing pages, dashboards and product catalogues usually need different strategies, and the trade-off often shows up in your roadmap discussions.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to make a table: for an e-commerce site, which rendering strategy for home page, product page, cart and account dashboard, and why.
topics.prove: Explain why an SEO team might push back on a pure single-page app.
topics.interview: Product wants the catalogue to be fast and searchable on Google, but prices change hourly. What rendering approach would you discuss with engineering?
covers: SPA, MPA, SSR, CSR, SSG, ISR

topics.title: Web quality: responsive design, accessibility, performance, build tools
topics.summary: Responsive design adapts layouts to screen size. Accessibility (a11y) makes products usable by people with disabilities, measured against WCAG. Performance techniques include lazy loading, compression and minification. Build tools (Webpack, Vite, Babel) and package managers (npm, pnpm, Yarn) bundle and manage the code.
topics.why: Accessibility is often a legal and contractual requirement, and performance directly affects conversion. These are non-functional requirements you must put into acceptance criteria and release checklists.
topics.do_it: Run Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools > Lighthouse) on your company website. Paste the report summary into Claude and ask for the top 5 fixes ranked by user impact.
topics.prove: Write 3 accessibility acceptance criteria for a login form.
topics.interview: How do you make sure accessibility doesn't get dropped at the end of a release?
covers: Webpack, Vite, Babel, npm, pnpm, Yarn

topics.title: Backend basics: what the server side actually does
topics.summary: The backend receives requests, checks who is asking, applies business rules, reads or writes the database and returns a response. Code is usually split into controllers (handle the request), services (business logic) and data access.
topics.why: Most estimates, outages and data issues live in the backend. Knowing the layers lets you ask precise questions: is this a validation rule, a business rule or a data problem?
concepts: Synchronous vs asynchronous work (queues, background jobs)
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to draw (in text) the layers for 'user places an order' and to list which layer each failure would come from: card declined, out of stock, server timeout.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why 'just add a field' can touch three layers and a database migration.
topics.interview: A feature looks small in the UI but engineering says 3 sprints. How do you find out why?

topics.title: Backend stacks: Node.js, Python, PHP and their frameworks
topics.summary: Common backend languages and frameworks: Node.js (Express, NestJS), Python (Django, Flask, FastAPI) and PHP (Laravel). They differ in speed, ecosystem, hiring pool and fit for AI work (Python dominates AI).
topics.why: You don't need to code them, but you will hear them in architecture reviews and staffing plans, and AI integrations often add a Python service alongside an existing stack.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude for a one-page comparison of Node/NestJS, Python/FastAPI and PHP/Laravel for a team adding an AI feature to an existing app.
topics.prove: Explain why AI teams often pick Python even when the main product is in another language.
topics.interview: How would the existing tech stack influence your plan to add an LLM feature?

topics.title: APIs and HTTP: methods, status codes, REST
topics.summary: An API is the contract one system uses to talk to another. REST APIs use HTTP methods (GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove) and return status codes (2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error).
topics.why: APIs are how every integration, mobile app and AI tool connects. Reading an API doc, understanding an error code and spotting a breaking change are core TPM skills.
concepts: HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
topics.do_it: Install Postman (or use your browser) and call a free public API such as a weather or country API. Ask Claude to explain each part of the request and response.
topics.prove: Explain an API to a business stakeholder using a restaurant-waiter analogy, then explain what a 401 vs a 500 means for who must fix it.
topics.interview: A partner says our API is 'broken'. How do you triage it in the first 15 minutes?

topics.title: JSON and data formats
topics.summary: JSON is the text format almost all modern APIs and AI tools use to send structured data: keys and values, lists and nested objects. A schema describes what shape the JSON must have.
topics.why: You will read JSON in API docs, logs, AI structured outputs and automation tools (Zapier, n8n). Validating that data matches the agreed schema prevents many integration bugs.
concepts: Objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to design the JSON for a 'project risk' record (id, title, owner, severity, mitigations list). Then deliberately break it and ask Claude to validate it.
topics.prove: Read an unfamiliar JSON API response and explain what each field means.
topics.interview: How would you make sure two teams agree on the data contract before they build?

topics.title: API styles: REST vs GraphQL vs WebSockets vs gRPC
topics.summary: REST: resources over HTTP. GraphQL: one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. WebSockets: a two-way live connection for chat and live updates. gRPC: fast binary calls, mostly between internal services.
topics.why: Teams argue about these choices. You should understand the trade-offs in complexity, performance, caching and tooling so you can help the team decide and document why.
concepts: When each is a good fit
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to recommend an API style for: a public partner API, a live chat feature, internal microservice calls, and a mobile app with slow networks. Challenge each answer.
topics.prove: Explain in one minute why a chat feature can't just use normal REST polling.
topics.interview: Engineering wants to introduce GraphQL. What benefits and risks would you put in the decision record?

topics.title: Webhooks, events and idempotency
topics.summary: A webhook is an automatic message one system sends to another when something happens (payment succeeded, form submitted). Because messages can be retried, receiving systems must be idempotent: handling the same message twice must not, for example, charge a customer twice.
topics.why: Payments, CRMs, automations and AI agents all rely on webhooks. Duplicate or lost events are a classic source of production incidents.
topics.do_it: Create a free Zapier or Make account and build a webhook trigger that posts a message when a Google Form is submitted. Then ask Claude what would happen if the webhook fired twice.
topics.prove: Explain idempotency using a 'pressing the lift button twice' analogy, then a real payment example.
topics.interview: Customers were double-charged after a gateway timeout. What questions do you ask engineering?

topics.title: Authentication vs authorization, sessions and JWT
topics.summary: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are; authorization (AuthZ) decides what you may do. After login, apps keep you signed in with a session or a token such as a JWT, which carries signed claims about the user.
topics.why: Security reviews, enterprise sales and AI agent permissions all hinge on these concepts. Many breaches come from authorization mistakes, not broken logins.
topics.do_it: Paste a sample JWT from jwt.io into its debugger. Ask Claude what each claim means and what would happen if the token never expired.
topics.prove: Explain the difference between AuthN and AuthZ with an office building analogy (badge vs which floors you can enter).
topics.interview: An enterprise client asks how our product controls who can see which records. What do you need to confirm with engineering?

topics.title: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SSO
topics.summary: OAuth 2.0 lets one app get limited access to another on a user's behalf ("Allow this app to read your calendar"). OpenID Connect adds login on top of OAuth. SSO lets employees use one company login for many apps, usually through an identity provider like Okta or Azure AD.
topics.why: Enterprise deals often require SSO. AI agents and MCP connectors use OAuth to act on a user's behalf, so you'll be scoping these flows.
concepts: OAuth roles: user, client app, authorization server, resource
SSO and identity providers (SAML vs OIDC)
topics.do_it: Use 'Sign in with Google' on any site, then ask Claude to map each screen you saw to the OAuth step happening behind it.
topics.prove: Draw the OAuth flow on paper from memory and explain it in 90 seconds.
topics.interview: A large customer requires SSO before signing. How would you scope and plan it?

topics.title: Databases: SQL vs NoSQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis)
topics.summary: Relational (SQL) databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL store data in tables with fixed schemas and strong consistency. NoSQL databases like MongoDB (documents) and Redis (key-value, in memory) trade some structure for flexibility and scale.
topics.why: Database choice affects data integrity, reporting, scale and migration effort. You need to follow these discussions and spot when a choice creates delivery risk.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to model the same 'project with tasks and owners' data as SQL tables and as MongoDB documents, then list pros and cons of each for your use case.
topics.prove: Explain to a finance stakeholder why their reporting team prefers SQL.
topics.interview: When would you push back on a team choosing NoSQL for transactional data?

topics.title: Data modelling: keys, relationships and ER diagrams
topics.summary: An ER diagram (ERD) shows the entities in a system (Customer, Order, Product), their attributes and how they relate: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many. Primary keys identify a row; foreign keys link rows across tables.
topics.why: Reading an ERD lets you check that requirements are actually supported by the data model, find hidden dependencies and estimate the impact of changes.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to generate an ERD (as a Mermaid diagram) for a simple project-management tool. Paste it into mermaid.live to see it, then ask it to add 'task dependencies' and note what changed.
topics.prove: Upload an ERD from your own project (anonymised) to Claude, ask for an explanation, then explain it back to Claude and ask it to grade you.
topics.interview: Here's an ERD. What would break if we allowed a task to have multiple owners?
covers: Semantic Search: upload ERD to AI and ask for explanation

topics.title: Queries, joins, indexes, transactions and ACID
topics.summary: Joins combine data from related tables. Indexes are like a book index: they make lookups fast but slow down writes and use storage. Transactions group changes so they all succeed or all fail; ACID describes those guarantees.
topics.why: 'The page is slow' is very often a missing index or a heavy query. Knowing this lets you ask the right questions instead of asking for 'more servers'.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a slow query scenario: 'Find all overdue tasks for a user' on a table with 10 million rows. Ask what index would help and what the trade-off is.
topics.prove: Explain ACID using a bank transfer example.
topics.interview: Users report the dashboard takes 12 seconds to load. Engineering suggests a bigger database server. What do you ask first?
covers: Database Query Optimization (TPM level: ask the right questions)

topics.title: ORMs, migrations, backups and why DB changes affect the app
topics.summary: An ORM lets developers work with database rows as code objects. Schema changes are shipped as migrations. Connection pooling reuses database connections. Backups and point-in-time restore protect against data loss.
topics.why: Database migrations are one of the riskiest parts of a release. Rollback plans, downtime windows and data-loss risk land on your desk.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to write a release plan for 'rename a column used by 3 services' with zero downtime. Note each step and why order matters.
topics.prove: Explain to a non-technical stakeholder why a 'small database change' needs a release window and a rollback plan.
topics.interview: A migration failed halfway in production. What should already have been in the plan?
covers: Explain why DB changes affect app

topics.title: Scaling databases: replication, sharding, partitioning
topics.summary: Replication copies data to other servers (read replicas, failover). Partitioning splits a big table into parts. Sharding spreads data across many databases by a key such as customer region.
topics.why: These come up when a product grows fast. They are expensive, slow to change and affect every team, so they belong on the roadmap early.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude: 'Our SaaS has 5x'd customers in a year and the database is at 80% CPU. Give me options from cheapest to most complex.' Turn the answer into a one-slide decision summary.
topics.prove: Explain replication lag with a real symptom a user would see.
topics.interview: How would you plan a sharding project so it doesn't freeze feature delivery for six months?

topics.title: DNS, domains and nameservers
topics.summary: DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns names like example.com into IP addresses. Domains are bought from registrars, nameservers hold the records, and record types (A, CNAME, MX, TXT, SOA) point traffic and email to the right place. TTL controls how long answers are cached, which is why changes 'propagate' slowly.
topics.why: Launches, migrations and outages regularly involve DNS. Knowing TTL lets you plan cut-overs instead of waiting and hoping.
concepts: Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SOA
topics.do_it: Use a free DNS lookup site on your company domain. Paste the records into Claude and ask what each does.
topics.prove: Explain why you lower the TTL a day before a migration.
topics.interview: We're moving our website to a new host on Saturday. What DNS steps go into the plan?

topics.title: Email deliverability: SPF, DKIM, DMARC
topics.summary: SPF, DKIM and DMARC are DNS records that prove your emails really come from your domain, stopping spoofing and keeping your mail out of spam folders.
topics.why: Product emails (password resets, invoices, notifications) failing to arrive is a common launch blocker, and the fix sits across marketing, IT and engineering.
concepts: SPF: who may send for your domain
topics.do_it: Open any email in Gmail > Show original. Paste the authentication results into Claude and ask what passed and why it matters.
topics.prove: Explain in 60 seconds why password-reset emails might land in spam after moving to a new email provider.
topics.interview: Customers say they never get our onboarding emails. Who do you involve and what do you check?

topics.title: IP addresses: IPv4, IPv6, public, private, static
topics.summary: Every device on a network has an IP address. Public addresses are reachable from the internet; private ones are used inside networks. IPv6 exists because IPv4 addresses ran out. Static IPs don't change, which matters for allow-lists.
topics.why: Client firewalls, allow-listing, VPNs and cloud networking all depend on this. It often comes up when integrating with enterprise or banking clients.
topics.do_it: Search 'what is my IP' and compare with the private IP in your computer's network settings. Ask Claude to explain why they differ.
topics.prove: Explain why a bank client asks for our static IPs before integration.
topics.interview: An enterprise client's firewall blocks our webhooks. What information do you gather?
covers: Public IP, Private IP, Static IP

topics.title: Network protocols: TCP, UDP, HTTP(S), ports, sockets, SSH
topics.summary: TCP delivers data reliably and in order; UDP is faster but may drop data (used for video and gaming). HTTP and HTTPS run on top. Ports route traffic to the right program (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH). SSH is a secure way to log in to servers.
topics.why: Firewall changes, connectivity tickets and security audits use this vocabulary. You'll understand 'port 443 is blocked' or 'we need SSH access' immediately.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to make a cheat sheet of 10 common ports and what breaks if each is blocked.
topics.prove: Explain why video calls often use UDP.
topics.interview: A client's network team says 'only 443 outbound is allowed'. What does that mean for our product?

topics.title: HTTPS, TLS and certificates
topics.summary: HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS (the successor of SSL). A certificate proves a site's identity and is issued by a certificate authority. Certificates expire and must be renewed.
topics.why: Expired certificates cause embarrassing, avoidable outages. Security questionnaires also ask about TLS versions and certificate management.
topics.do_it: Click the padlock on your company site and view the certificate. Ask Claude what each field means and when it expires.
topics.prove: Explain what users would see if our certificate expired tonight and who should own renewal.
topics.interview: How would you prevent certificate-expiry outages across 40 services?

topics.title: CORS, proxies and reverse proxies
topics.summary: CORS is a browser rule that controls which websites may call your API from JavaScript. A forward proxy sits in front of users; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers (for routing, caching, SSL and security).
topics.why: 'CORS error' is one of the most common blockers when frontend and backend teams integrate. Reverse proxies like Nginx appear in most architectures.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a real CORS error message and which team (frontend or backend) must fix it.
topics.prove: Explain why a CORS error can't be fixed from frontend code alone.
topics.interview: The frontend team is blocked by CORS errors two days before launch. How do you unblock it?

topics.title: CDN, load balancers and firewalls (WAF)
topics.summary: A CDN caches content on servers close to users for speed. A load balancer spreads traffic across servers and removes unhealthy ones. A firewall, and especially a web application firewall (WAF), blocks malicious traffic.
topics.why: These three sit in front of almost every production system. They affect performance, availability and security, and they often feature in incident timelines.
concepts: Load balancing algorithms and health checks
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to draw a request path: user > DNS > CDN > WAF > load balancer > app servers > database, and list what each layer protects against.
topics.prove: Explain why a CDN makes a site faster for users in India when servers are in the US.
topics.interview: Traffic will triple during a sale. Which layers do you check with the team?

topics.title: Private networks: subnets, NAT, gateways, VPN
topics.summary: Cloud networks are split into public subnets (reachable from the internet) and private subnets (for databases and internal services). NAT gateways let private servers reach out without being reachable. VPNs create encrypted tunnels into private networks.
topics.why: Security reviews and cloud cost discussions mention these constantly. Understanding them lets you follow infrastructure designs and client connectivity requirements.
concepts: Zero Trust as the modern alternative
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a three-tier network: load balancer in public subnet, app servers and database in private subnets. Ask why the database should never be public.
topics.prove: Explain why 'the database is in a private subnet' is a good answer in a security questionnaire.
topics.interview: A client wants a private connection to our platform instead of the public internet. What options would you explore?

topics.title: What an LLM is, and your first API call
topics.summary: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. That simple objective, at scale, produces models that can write, reason, summarise and use tools. You can use them through chat apps or through an API.
topics.why: Every AI product decision you make rests on this mental model: what the model really is, what it can't know, and why answers vary.
topics.do_it: Create a free Gemini API key in Google AI Studio and keep it private. Use AI Studio's prompt screen, then click 'Get code' and ask Claude to explain every line of that code.
topics.prove: Explain to a sceptical executive what an LLM is and isn't in 2 minutes, without jargon.
topics.interview: What's the difference between using ChatGPT and building on an LLM API?
covers: REST API, SDK, API Key (first use)

topics.title: How LLMs are built: pre-training, fine-tuning, RLHF
topics.summary: LLMs are first pre-trained on internet-scale text (expensive, months, many GPUs), producing a base model. They are then post-trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to become helpful assistants.
topics.why: This explains why models have knowledge cut-offs, why they sound confident when wrong, and why training your own model is rarely the right project.
topics.do_it: Watch the first hour of Karpathy's deep dive. Ask Claude to quiz you with 10 questions on the training pipeline.
topics.prove: Explain why a model doesn't know about last week's news, and the two ways to fix that (search/RAG or retraining).
topics.interview: A stakeholder wants us to 'train our own ChatGPT'. How do you respond?

topics.title: Transformers and attention (concept level)
topics.summary: The transformer is the neural network design behind modern LLMs. Its key idea, attention, lets every word look at every other word to work out context, and it processes text in parallel, which made huge training runs possible.
topics.why: You don't need the maths, but you'll understand why context length is expensive, why models are fast on GPUs, and what people mean by 'attention' and 'KV cache'.
concepts: Why attention cost grows with context length
topics.do_it: Read The Illustrated Transformer with Claude open. After each section, explain it back to Claude in your own words and ask for corrections.
topics.prove: Explain attention using a meeting analogy: everyone listens to the people most relevant to their point.
topics.interview: Why do longer prompts cost more and run slower?

topics.title: Tokens and tokenization
topics.summary: Models read and write tokens, small chunks of text (roughly 3–4 English characters each). Prices, limits and speed are all measured in tokens. Different models split text differently, and non-English text often uses more tokens.
topics.why: Every AI budget, rate limit and context limit is in tokens. You'll estimate costs and explain why the same feature costs more in Hindi than in English.
concepts: Rough rule: 1 token ≈ ¾ word in English
Rate limits in tokens per minute
topics.do_it: Paste the same paragraph in English and in Hindi into the tokenizer tool. Compare counts and ask Claude why they differ.
topics.prove: Estimate how many tokens a 10-page requirements document is, and show your working.
topics.interview: Our AI feature's costs are double the estimate. What token-related causes would you check?

topics.title: Context window
topics.summary: The context window is the model's working memory: everything it can see at once, including instructions, conversation history, documents and its own answer. Anything outside the window is invisible to the model.
topics.why: It decides whether a model can read a whole contract, how long a chat stays coherent, and why agents need memory strategies. Bigger windows also cost more per request.
topics.do_it: Give Claude a long document and ask a question about a detail near the start, then near the end. Ask Claude to explain how context windows affect what it 'remembers'.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why the chatbot 'forgot' something the user said an hour ago.
topics.interview: When would you load a whole document into context versus using retrieval?

topics.title: Prompting fundamentals
topics.summary: Prompting is how you specify the task to a model: clear goal, context, constraints, examples and the output format you want. Good prompts read like a good brief to a capable new colleague.
topics.why: This is the skill you'll use daily to write PRDs, user stories, analysis and code with AI. It's also how you'll review prompts your team ships into products.
concepts: Be clear and direct; give the why
topics.do_it: Take one recurring task (weekly status report). Write a prompt, run it 3 times, score the outputs against 5 criteria, improve the prompt, and save the before/after in a document.
topics.prove: Show a before and after prompt and explain each change.
topics.interview: How would you make prompt quality measurable rather than a matter of opinion?

topics.title: Advanced prompting techniques
topics.summary: Beyond basics: role or system prompts, structured prompts with XML tags, asking the model to think step by step, chaining prompts into a pipeline, and asking for structured output such as JSON.
topics.why: These techniques turn one-off chats into reliable workflows, and they're what product prompts and agents are built from.
topics.do_it: Build a 3-step prompt chain: (1) extract requirements from meeting notes, (2) turn them into user stories, (3) write acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then. Save it as a reusable template.
topics.prove: Demonstrate the chain on a new set of notes and explain why chaining beats one giant prompt.
topics.interview: How would you version and test prompts that run inside our product?
covers: AI Coding Assistants (AI for stories and ACs)

topics.title: Hallucinations and how to reduce them
topics.summary: A hallucination is a confident but false or unsupported output. It happens because models generate plausible text rather than look up facts. You reduce it by allowing 'I don't know', grounding answers in provided sources, asking for quotes and citations, and verifying.
topics.why: Hallucination risk is the first question executives, legal and customers ask about AI features. You need a clear, honest mitigation plan.
topics.do_it: Ask a model 5 questions about an obscure topic with and without a source document attached. Log which answers were wrong and which mitigation fixed them.
topics.prove: Present a one-slide 'Hallucination mitigation plan' for a customer-facing chatbot.
topics.interview: Legal is worried our AI will make things up. What controls do you propose?

topics.title: Grounding
topics.summary: Grounding means tying the model's answer to trusted sources (your documents, a database, search results) instead of its general training memory, ideally with citations so people can check.
topics.why: Grounded answers are what make enterprise AI trustworthy and auditable. It's the bridge between hallucination risk and RAG.
topics.do_it: Upload 3 project documents to NotebookLM and ask 10 questions. Check every citation it gives against the source.
topics.prove: Explain grounding to a stakeholder using an 'open-book exam' analogy.
topics.interview: How would you prove to an auditor that our assistant's answers come from approved documents?

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.summary: An embedding turns text (or images) into a list of numbers that captures meaning. Texts with similar meaning end up close together, so 'cheap flights' and 'low-cost airfare' match even with no shared words.
topics.why: Embeddings power semantic search, RAG, recommendations and duplicate detection. Choosing an embedding model affects quality, cost and language support.
concepts: Re-embedding cost when you switch models
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain, with a toy 2D example, how 'king', 'queen', 'apple' and 'banana' would sit in embedding space. Then read the Gemini embeddings docs and ask Claude to explain the sample code.
topics.prove: Explain why semantic search finds results that keyword search misses.
topics.interview: We want to switch embedding models. What's the migration cost and risk?

topics.title: Vector databases
topics.summary: A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly. Examples include Pinecone, Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, FAISS (a library) and pgvector (a PostgreSQL extension).
topics.why: Every RAG project needs one. The build-vs-buy choice (managed service vs extension to an existing database) is a classic TPM decision.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to build a comparison table of Pinecone, Chroma, Qdrant and pgvector on cost, hosting, scale and ease for a team without ML engineers.
topics.prove: Recommend one option for a 10,000-document internal knowledge base and justify it in 3 bullets.
topics.interview: Do we need a separate vector database, or can our existing Postgres do it?

topics.title: Semantic search and hybrid search
topics.summary: Keyword search (such as BM25) matches exact words; semantic search matches meaning using embeddings. Hybrid search runs both and merges the results, which works best for real-world queries that mix concepts with exact codes or names.
topics.why: Search quality is the biggest driver of RAG quality. Knowing hybrid search helps you diagnose 'it can't find the right document' complaints.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude for 5 example queries where keyword search wins and 5 where semantic search wins, using your own domain.
topics.prove: Explain why a product code like 'SKU-4471' might not be found by pure semantic search.
topics.interview: Users say the assistant can't find documents they know exist. How do you investigate?

topics.title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
topics.summary: RAG retrieves the most relevant passages from your documents and adds them to the prompt so the model answers from your content. The pipeline: split documents into chunks, embed them, store them, retrieve the best matches for a question, generate an answer with citations.
topics.why: Most enterprise AI assistants are RAG under the hood. You'll scope these projects, estimate them and explain their failure modes.
concepts: Failure modes: wrong chunk, missing context, stale data
topics.do_it: Load 3 project documents into NotebookLM, ask 10 questions, and log where it answers wrongly and why (wrong passage, missing information, misread).
topics.prove: Explain RAG to an executive in 60 seconds and name 3 ways it fails.
topics.interview: Walk me through how you'd scope a RAG assistant for our HR policies.
covers: Executive communication: explain RAG in business language

topics.title: RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompting
topics.summary: Three ways to adapt a model: prompting (change the instructions), RAG (give it the right knowledge at question time) and fine-tuning (further train the model on examples, including cheaper methods like LoRA). They solve different problems and can be combined.
topics.why: Choosing the wrong approach wastes months. Most business needs are solved with prompting plus RAG; fine-tuning is for behaviour, format or style, not for adding facts.
concepts: RAG for changing or private knowledge
Fine-tuning (full, LoRA, QLoRA) for behaviour and format
Cost, time and maintenance of each
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to build a decision flowchart (as a Mermaid diagram) for 'prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune' and test it against 4 scenarios from your work.
topics.prove: Write a half-page decision record recommending one approach for a support-ticket classifier.
topics.interview: An engineer proposes fine-tuning a model on our wiki. What do you say?

topics.title: Machine learning basics: supervised, unsupervised, classification, regression, clustering
topics.summary: Classical machine learning learns patterns from data. Supervised learning uses labelled examples to predict (classification: spam or not; regression: a number such as price). Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering customers into segments).
topics.why: Not every AI problem needs an LLM. A classifier can be cheaper, faster and more accurate for narrow tasks, and you'll be asked to choose.
concepts: When a classic model beats an LLM
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to propose both an LLM approach and a classic ML approach for 'route support tickets to the right team', comparing cost, accuracy and data needed.
topics.prove: Give one real example each of classification, regression and clustering from your industry.
topics.interview: When would you not use an LLM?

topics.title: Neural networks and deep learning (intuition)
topics.summary: Neural networks are layers of simple units with adjustable weights. Training repeatedly nudges the weights to reduce errors (gradient descent, backpropagation). Deep learning just means many layers.
topics.why: This intuition helps you understand model size, training cost and why models are 'black boxes'. Concept level only; no maths needed.
concepts: Why more layers and data help
topics.do_it: Watch the first two 3Blue1Brown videos. Ask Claude to quiz you on the intuition only, with no maths.
topics.prove: Explain 'training' to a non-technical person using a 'tuning many dials' analogy.
topics.interview: Why are large models expensive to train and to run?

topics.title: AI cost, latency and why AI gets expensive at scale
topics.summary: AI APIs charge per input and output token, with different prices per model. Costs grow with users, conversation length, documents in context and agent loops. Latency depends on model size, output length and network. Prompt caching and batch processing can cut costs significantly.
topics.why: You will own the business case. Token cost modelling is now part of project estimation, and surprises here can kill an AI feature after launch.
concepts: Price per million tokens (input vs output)
Cost per request, per user, per month
Model choice: big vs small models
Latency and time to first token
topics.do_it: Build a simple cost model in a spreadsheet: users × requests/day × tokens/request × price. Ask Claude to check the formulas and add a 'switch to smaller model' scenario.
topics.prove: Present monthly cost for 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 users, plus three ways to reduce it.
topics.interview: Our AI feature works but costs too much. What levers do you pull?

topics.title: How AI is hosted and served: API-based AI systems
topics.summary: Most AI products call a hosted model through an API (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) instead of running their own. The model runs on GPU clusters in the provider's cloud; your app sends a request and receives tokens back, often streamed. Alternatives are cloud platforms (Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure) or self-hosted open models.
topics.why: Hosting choice affects data privacy, cost, latency, vendor lock-in and compliance. It's a standard architecture decision you'll facilitate.
concepts: Hosted API vs cloud platform vs self-hosted
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to compare calling Claude directly, via AWS Bedrock, and running an open model yourself, on privacy, cost and effort, for a regulated industry client.
topics.prove: Draw a simple architecture: your app > your backend > model API, and mark where customer data travels.
topics.interview: A bank client asks where their data goes when our AI feature runs. How do you answer?
covers: AI Infrastructure (how OpenAI/Gemini APIs are hosted)

topics.title: Claude for builders: Projects, artifacts, Claude Code
topics.summary: Claude comes in several working modes. Chat is for thinking and drafting. Projects keep your files and instructions together so every chat starts with the right context. Artifacts turn an answer into a page, document or small app you can share. Claude Code works directly inside a codebase: it reads files, runs commands and makes changes.
topics.why: Picking the right mode is most of the skill. A PM who drafts specs in a Project, prototypes in an artifact and hands real code changes to Claude Code can ship working software without writing code by hand. That is how this learning hub was built.
concepts: Chat vs Project vs artifact vs Claude Code
Claude Code: the agentic loop (read, plan, act, check)
topics.do_it: Create a Project called 'TPM Learning' with your study PDF as knowledge and an instruction such as 'Explain like I'm a PM, give one real example'. Then open this repo in Claude Code and ask it, in plan mode, how the progress tracker saves data. Don't approve changes; just read the plan.
topics.prove: Write a one-page 'which Claude mode for which job' guide for your team with three real examples from your own work.
topics.interview: How do you personally use AI tools to deliver faster, and where do you not trust them?

topics.title: Building safely with AI when you don't write code
topics.summary: A set of habits that let you build real software with AI without being able to judge every line yourself: small steps, save points in Git, automatic checks (tests and CI), secrets kept out of code, and independent review before anything reaches users.
topics.why: AI writes plausible code quickly, including plausible mistakes. Your safety net is process, not reading skill. These are the same controls good engineering teams use, so learning them also makes you a better TPM.
concepts: Plan first, then build in small steps
Commits as save points; branches for experiments
Tests and CI as the automatic reviewer
Secrets in .env, never in code or chat
Second-opinion review and asking 'what could go wrong'
topics.do_it: In this repo, ask Claude to explain the last commit in plain English, list what could break, and say which test covers it. Then check the GitHub Actions run for that commit is green.
topics.prove: Write your personal 'AI build checklist' (10 items max) and use it on your next change.
topics.interview: You don't code. How do you make sure what you ship with AI is safe?
covers: Added: reviewing AI-written code as a non-coder

topics.title: Cursor and AI code editors
topics.summary: Cursor is a code editor (based on VS Code) with AI built in: autocomplete as you type, a chat that can see your project, and an Agent that can edit many files and run commands. Other editors such as VS Code with Copilot and Windsurf offer similar features.
topics.why: Your engineers probably use one of these daily. Knowing what they can and cannot do helps you estimate work, set team norms and understand why some tasks now take hours instead of days.
concepts: Tab autocomplete vs chat vs Agent
Ignore files for privacy and speed
topics.do_it: Install Cursor, open this repo and ask the chat: 'Where is login handled, front end and back end?' Check its answer by opening the files it names.
topics.prove: Compare Cursor and Claude Code on the same small task (for example, change a button label) and write five lines on the difference.
topics.interview: How would you roll out an AI code editor to a 30-person engineering team?

topics.title: GitHub Copilot concepts
topics.summary: GitHub Copilot is GitHub's AI assistant. It suggests code in the editor, answers questions about a codebase in chat, reviews pull requests, and has a coding agent that can take an issue and open a pull request on its own.
topics.why: Many companies standardise on Copilot because it lives inside GitHub, where their code, issues and permissions already are. As a TPM you'll be asked about licences, policies and how assigned-to-AI issues fit into sprint planning.
concepts: Copilot coding agent (issue to pull request)
topics.do_it: Read the Copilot docs home page and list which features your company could use today with the tools it already has.
topics.prove: Draft a one-paragraph team policy: which tasks may be assigned to an AI coding agent and who must review the result.
topics.interview: An engineer wants to assign half the backlog to Copilot's agent. What do you ask before agreeing?

topics.title: How AI reads a codebase: repo indexing and context
topics.summary: An AI model can only consider what fits in its context window, and a real codebase is far bigger. Tools solve this by searching: some build an index of the code (chunks turned into embeddings, like RAG for code), others search on demand with tools such as grep and file listing. Either way, the AI only 'knows' the parts it found.
topics.why: This explains most AI coding failures: it edited the wrong file, missed a second place that needed changing, or invented a function. Good context (clear file names, a README, rules files, pointing at the right files) fixes more problems than better prompts.
concepts: Agentic search: grep, glob, reading files
Context fills up; start fresh sessions
topics.do_it: Ask Claude Code or Cursor 'Which files would you change to add a new field to topics?' and compare its list with the real one: models.py, a migration, schemas.py, seed, types.ts and the page.
topics.prove: Explain to a colleague, in two minutes, why an AI coding tool sometimes 'forgets' part of the project.
topics.interview: Why does an AI assistant work better on some repositories than others?

topics.title: Rules files: CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules
topics.summary: A rules file is a plain-text file in the repo that the AI tool reads at the start of every session: how to run the project, what the stack is, what must never happen. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md; Cursor reads rules in .cursor/rules (older projects use a single .cursorrules file) and also AGENTS.md.
topics.why: It is the cheapest quality lever you have. Writing down the team's rules once stops the AI repeating the same mistakes, and it doubles as onboarding documentation for humans.
concepts: What goes in: commands, stack, conventions, never-do rules
What stays out: secrets, long essays
Project vs personal vs team rules
topics.do_it: Open CLAUDE.md in this repo. Add one rule you learned the hard way (for example, 'Explain every change in plain English before committing') and commit it.
topics.prove: Write a CLAUDE.md for a project at work (without secrets) and get one engineer to review it.
topics.interview: How would you make AI coding assistants follow your team's standards?

topics.title: Skills: reusable AI workflows (SKILL.md)
topics.summary: A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file (a short name and description at the top, instructions below) plus any scripts or templates it needs. Claude reads only the name and description until a task matches, then loads the full instructions. It turns a workflow you repeat into something Claude does the same way every time.
topics.why: Skills are how you package your PM know-how: status-report format, risk-review checklist, release-notes style. Instead of re-explaining in every chat, you write it once and the whole team gets consistent output.
concepts: SKILL.md structure: frontmatter (name, description) and body
The description decides when it triggers
Skills vs rules files vs Projects
Only install Skills from sources you trust
topics.do_it: Write a SKILL.md for your weekly status report: inputs, sections, tone and one example. Ask Claude to use it on last week's notes.
topics.prove: Run the same Skill on two different weeks and check the output follows the same structure both times.
topics.interview: How would you standardise how your team uses AI for recurring documents?

topics.title: GitHub fundamentals for non-coders
topics.summary: GitHub hosts Git repositories online. A repository holds the project and its full history; a commit is a saved change with a message; a branch is a parallel line of work; a pull request asks for a branch to be reviewed and merged; Actions run checks automatically. Issues track work, and open-source projects share code publicly.
topics.why: Pull requests are where engineering decisions, reviews and quality gates actually happen. If you can read a PR, its checks and its discussion, you can follow delivery in real time instead of waiting for stand-up.
concepts: Open source: licences, stars, forks, trending
topics.do_it: Do the GitHub Hello World exercise in a new repo. Then open nitishnarayan01/study, click the latest commit and the Actions tab, and find the test count in the backend job log.
topics.prove: Open a pull request in your own repo that changes one lesson's text, and merge it yourself after the checks pass.
topics.interview: How do you use GitHub to track delivery without micromanaging engineers?

topics.title: Terminal, CLI and shell basics
topics.summary: The terminal is a text window where you type commands instead of clicking. The shell (PowerShell on Windows; bash or zsh on Mac and Linux) runs those commands. CLI tools such as git, npm, docker and claude are programs you control from there.
topics.why: Every setup guide, including this project's README, starts with terminal commands. You don't need to master it; you need to run commands, read the output and tell whether something failed.
topics.do_it: Open PowerShell, go to your study folder with cd, list files, then run 'git status' and 'git log --oneline -5'. Ask Claude to explain each line of output.
topics.prove: Start the project with docker compose from the README without help, and stop it cleanly.
topics.interview: An engineer says 'just run the migration locally'. What would you actually do?

topics.title: Project files: package managers, lock files, .env, .gitignore, README
topics.summary: Every project has a few standard files around the code. package.json or requirements.txt lists the libraries it needs; a package manager (npm, pip) installs them; a lock file pins exact versions; .env holds secrets and settings for one machine; .gitignore lists files Git must not track; README explains how to run it.
topics.why: These files explain many 'works on my machine' problems, security leaks and broken builds. Knowing them lets you review a repo's health in five minutes and ask the right question when a build breaks.
topics.do_it: In this repo open frontend/package.json, backend/requirements.txt, .env.example and .gitignore. Ask Claude why .env is ignored but .env.example is committed.
topics.prove: Write a five-point 'repo health check' you could run on any project at work.
topics.interview: A build that worked yesterday fails today with no code changes. What do you suspect?

topics.title: Postman for API testing
topics.summary: Postman is an app for calling APIs without writing code. You set the method, URL, headers and body, press Send and see the response. Requests can be saved into collections, use variables and environments (local vs production), and include small tests that check the response.
topics.why: It lets you verify a backend yourself: does the endpoint exist, what does it return, what happens with a bad token? You can reproduce a bug before filing it and confirm a fix without waiting for the UI.
topics.do_it: With the hub running locally, call POST /api/auth/login with your admin email and password, copy the token, then call GET /api/progress/me with an Authorization: Bearer header.
topics.prove: Build a collection that logs in, fetches the catalog and updates one topic's progress, with a status-200 test on each step.
topics.interview: How would you check whether a bug is in the front end or the back end?

topics.title: Vercel: deploy a web app in minutes
topics.summary: Vercel is a hosting platform for web front ends (it makes Next.js). You connect a GitHub repo and every push builds and deploys automatically: each branch or pull request gets its own preview URL, and the main branch goes to production. Settings such as environment variables and domains are managed per project.
topics.why: Preview links change how teams review work: product, design and QA click a real link on every pull request instead of reading screenshots. It is also the fastest route to putting this hub online.
concepts: Import a Git repo and deploy
Front end on Vercel, backend and database elsewhere
topics.do_it: Deploy a starter Next.js template to Vercel from GitHub. Make a change on a branch, open a pull request and open its preview link.
topics.prove: Write the steps (and the open questions, such as where the FastAPI backend and Postgres would run) to put this hub online.
topics.interview: What changes for QA and stakeholders when every pull request gets a preview deployment?

topics.title: Lovable and v0: AI app and UI prototyping
topics.summary: Lovable and v0 build web apps from a chat. You describe what you want, they generate the code, show a live preview and publish it. Lovable leans towards complete products with a built-in backend; v0, from Vercel, generates Next.js and React apps that deploy to Vercel and can open pull requests on an existing repo.
topics.why: They are the quickest way for a PM to turn an idea into something clickable for user tests or stakeholder alignment. The skill is knowing when a prototype is good enough and when it needs real engineering.
concepts: Backend, auth and data in generated apps
topics.do_it: Build the same small app (a team reading-list tracker) in both Lovable and v0 in under an hour each. Note where each one struggled.
topics.prove: Show one prototype to two real users and write down what you learned that a document would not have told you.
topics.interview: When would you prototype with an AI app builder, and when would you insist on engineering from the start?

topics.title: Google AI Studio deep dive
topics.summary: Google AI Studio is Google's free browser workspace for the Gemini models. You can try prompts, change model settings, upload files, compare outputs, create an API key and export the working prompt as code.
topics.why: It is the quickest way to test whether a model can do a task before anyone builds anything. A PM who can bring a working prompt and sample outputs to a kick-off saves the team a week of debate.
topics.do_it: Take 10 real support tickets (with personal data removed) and build a prompt in AI Studio that classifies them by product area. Note how many it gets right.
topics.prove: Share the prompt, settings and a results table with a colleague and agree whether it is good enough for a pilot.
topics.interview: How would you test whether an AI feature is feasible before committing engineering time?

topics.title: NotebookLM for research and learning
topics.summary: NotebookLM is Google's research notebook. You add sources (PDFs, Google Docs, websites, YouTube videos) and it answers questions grounded in those sources, with citations back to the exact passage. It can also create summaries, study guides and audio overviews.
topics.why: It is a ready-made RAG system you can use today, which makes it ideal for learning a new domain fast and for seeing what source-grounded AI feels like before you build one.
concepts: Limits: only as good as the sources
topics.do_it: Create a notebook with the Claude Code docs pages from this phase. Ask it for the five things a PM must know and click every citation.
topics.prove: Use a notebook to prepare for a real meeting and note one question it answered faster than search would have.
topics.interview: What's the difference between asking a chatbot and asking a source-grounded tool?

topics.title: Cloudflare for builders
topics.summary: Cloudflare sits in front of websites on a global network. It provides DNS, a CDN that caches content close to users, security (DDoS protection, firewall rules, bot control) and developer products such as Workers (small serverless functions that run at the network edge) and Pages (static site hosting).
topics.why: A large share of the web runs through Cloudflare, so it shows up in outages, security reviews and performance discussions. For builders, it is also a cheap place to host small tools and APIs.
concepts: When an outage is 'Cloudflare, not us'
topics.do_it: Read the CDN and WAF explainers, then follow the Workers get-started guide far enough to see a 'Hello World' running on a workers.dev URL.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder in three sentences what would and wouldn't keep working if Cloudflare had an outage.
topics.interview: Our site is slow for users in Asia. What could a CDN do, and what couldn't it?

topics.title: Code quality basics: linters, tests, design patterns, SOLID
topics.summary: Code quality has automatic and human parts. Linters flag likely mistakes and formatters fix layout; unit tests check small pieces of logic, integration and end-to-end tests check that pieces work together. Design patterns are named, proven solutions to common design problems, and SOLID is five principles for code that stays easy to change.
topics.why: With AI writing more of the code, automatic checks are your main quality gate. Knowing the vocabulary lets you ask 'Is there a test for that?' and understand answers like 'that breaks single responsibility'.
concepts: Common patterns: adapter, strategy, observer, factory
topics.do_it: Open backend/tests/test_api.py and ask Claude to explain, test by test, what each one proves about the app. Find one behaviour that has no test.
topics.prove: Ask Claude to add the missing test, run CI and see it pass.
topics.interview: How do you know AI-generated code is good enough to ship?

topics.title: Code review and technical debt
topics.summary: Code review is a second person (or AI) checking a change before it merges: its design, whether it works, complexity, tests, naming and documentation. Technical debt is the extra future cost of shortcuts in code: like a loan, it buys speed now and charges interest later as every change in that area takes longer.
topics.why: Review speed and debt levels quietly drive delivery dates. A TPM who can talk about both in business terms (risk, cost of delay, interest) gets debt work prioritised instead of endlessly postponed.
concepts: Small pull requests review faster and better
Approve when it improves the code, not when perfect
Deliberate vs accidental, prudent vs reckless debt
Making debt visible and budgeting for it
topics.do_it: Read Google's 'What to look for in a code review'. Then ask Claude to review the last commit in this repo against that list and tell you which points apply.
topics.prove: Write a one-page debt register for a project at work: three items, the interest each one charges, and a proposed fix.
topics.interview: Engineering wants a quarter to pay down tech debt. How do you evaluate the request?

topics.title: Starter kits, SDK wrappers and internal AI tools
topics.summary: Starter kits (templates, boilerplates) give you a working project skeleton so you don't start from an empty folder. SDKs are official libraries that wrap a raw API with types, retries and streaming; many teams add their own thin wrapper on top. Internal developer tools are the scripts, bots and consoles a company builds for its own teams.
topics.why: These are the build-vs-reuse decisions you'll make on every AI project: which starter, which SDK, whether to build an internal wrapper for logging and cost control. Each one saves weeks or creates lock-in.
concepts: Official SDKs vs raw HTTP calls
Internal wrapper: one place for keys, logging, cost, model switching
topics.do_it: Browse the Vercel Next.js templates and pick one AI starter. Read its README and list what it gives you and what you'd still need to build.
topics.prove: Write a half-page proposal for an internal AI wrapper at your company: what it centralises and who owns it.
topics.interview: Should every team call the model provider directly, or should we build a shared AI gateway?

topics.title: API keys, SDKs, requests and payloads
topics.summary: Every model provider works the same basic way: your software sends an HTTPS request with an API key, a model name, some settings and the conversation; the provider sends back JSON with the model's reply and how many tokens it used. SDKs are libraries that build those requests for you.
topics.why: Once you can read one request and one response, every provider's documentation, every cost report and every 'the AI is broken' incident becomes understandable. It is the single most reusable technical skill in AI delivery.
concepts: API key: a password for software
Payload fields: model, messages, max tokens
Keys in environment variables, never in code
topics.do_it: Create a Claude or Gemini API key, store it as an environment variable, and use Postman (or the quickstart code with Claude's help) to send one message. Find the input and output token counts in the response.
topics.prove: Annotate a real request and response line by line in plain English, and work out the cost of that call from the token counts and the price page.
topics.interview: Walk me through what happens, technically, when our app sends a question to an LLM.

topics.title: Anthropic Claude API: messages, tools, prompt caching
topics.summary: The Claude API centres on the Messages endpoint: you send a list of user and assistant turns (plus an optional system prompt) and receive the next assistant turn. Tool use lets Claude ask your code to run a function and use the result. Prompt caching lets repeated prompt prefixes be reused at a much lower price and latency.
topics.why: These three features cover most real product designs: conversation, actions (look up an order, create a ticket) and cost control at scale. Knowing how they work lets you challenge estimates and spot designs that will be slow or expensive.
concepts: Tool definitions and the tool-use loop
topics.do_it: Read the tool use overview and draw the round trip for 'What's the status of order 123?': which messages go back and forth, and where your code runs.
topics.prove: For a support assistant with a 20-page policy document in every request, estimate monthly cost with and without prompt caching for 10,000 conversations, using the current price page.
topics.interview: How would you keep the cost of an LLM feature under control as usage grows?

topics.title: OpenAI API: structured outputs and streaming
topics.summary: OpenAI's current API for new work is the Responses API. Two features matter most for products: structured outputs, which force the reply to match a JSON schema you define, and streaming, which sends the reply in pieces as it is generated so users see text immediately.
topics.why: Structured outputs turn a model from a text generator into a reliable component other software can consume. Streaming decides whether a feature feels instant or sluggish. Both shape design, testing and error handling.
concepts: Schemas defined with Pydantic or Zod
Partial output and error handling while streaming
topics.do_it: Write a JSON schema (in plain English first, then with Claude's help) for extracting a meeting summary: decisions, owners, due dates. Note which fields are required.
topics.prove: Explain to an engineer, in five bullet points, what could still go wrong even with schema-enforced output.
topics.interview: When would you use structured output instead of free text in an AI feature?

topics.title: Gemini API: multimodal and structured output (current models)
topics.summary: The Gemini API gives access to Google's Gemini models. They are multimodal: one request can include text, images, PDFs, audio or video. Like other providers, Gemini supports structured output against a JSON schema or a fixed list of values. Model generations change often (the 1.5 and 2.0 models listed in older material are retired), so always check the models page.
topics.why: Multimodal input opens use cases text-only models can't touch: reading invoices, checking photos, summarising recordings. And the retirement of older models is a lesson in itself: model choice is a dependency with an end-of-life date.
concepts: Text, image, document, audio and video input
Structured output: JSON schema and enums
Model families: fast vs most capable
Free tier vs paid tier terms
topics.do_it: In AI Studio, upload a photo of a receipt and ask for merchant, date, total and line items as JSON. Try three receipts and note any mistakes.
topics.prove: Write a one-page plan for a 'receipt to expense claim' feature: model choice, schema, error handling and what a human still checks.
topics.interview: What new risks come with multimodal input compared with text-only?
covers: Gemini API (sheet lists Gemini 1.5/2.0, now retired)

topics.title: Rate limits, quotas, retries, backoff and timeouts
topics.summary: Providers limit how much you can use: requests per minute, tokens per minute and monthly spend. Exceed a limit and you get an error (HTTP 429). Sometimes the service itself is overloaded or slow. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, sensible timeouts and fallbacks are how software stays reliable anyway.
topics.why: Rate limits are a launch risk that is easy to miss in testing and painful in production. TPMs who ask about limits, tiers and retry behaviour early avoid the classic 'it worked in the demo, it fell over at launch' story.
concepts: RPM, input and output tokens per minute
topics.do_it: Read the Claude rate limits page and estimate whether 200 users each sending 10 messages an hour (about 2,000 input tokens each) would fit in the lowest tier.
topics.prove: Write a launch checklist section on capacity: limits, expected peak, retry policy, fallback and who requests a limit increase and when.
topics.interview: Our AI feature works in testing but fails under load at launch. What happened and what would you do?

topics.title: Open model landscape: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, Phi
topics.summary: Open-weight models are models whose trained weights you can download and run yourself. The main families come from Meta (Llama), Mistral AI, Alibaba (Qwen), DeepSeek, Google (Gemma) and Microsoft (Phi). They come in many sizes, are often fine-tuned by others, and each has its own licence.
topics.why: Open models are the alternative whenever data can't leave your environment, costs at scale must drop, or you need full control. A TPM needs to know the families, the size trade-offs and the licence questions to frame build-vs-buy honestly.
concepts: Where to find them: Hugging Face, Ollama library
Reading model cards and leaderboards critically
topics.do_it: Pick two open models on Hugging Face, read their model cards and fill in a table: maker, sizes, licence, context length, intended use, known limits.
topics.prove: Write a half-page note for legal and security on what to check before using an open model in a product.
topics.interview: Why might we choose an open model over a commercial API, and what would worry you?

topics.title: Running models locally: Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp
topics.summary: You can run open models on your own laptop. Ollama is a simple command-line tool and local server; LM Studio is a desktop app with a model browser and chat window; llama.cpp is the open-source engine many of these tools are built on. All of them can expose an OpenAI-compatible API on your machine.
topics.why: Running a model yourself makes the abstract concrete: you feel the speed difference between sizes, see memory limits and learn what 'private, offline AI' really means. It is also a practical option for sensitive documents.
concepts: Model size vs your RAM and GPU
Local API server and OpenAI compatibility
Quality and speed vs hosted frontier models
Privacy: data stays on the machine
topics.do_it: Install Ollama or LM Studio and run a small model (around 1 to 4 billion parameters). Ask it the same three questions you ask Claude and compare quality and speed.
topics.prove: Write a short note: which internal tasks at your company could reasonably run on a local model, and which could not.
topics.interview: A team wants to use local models for confidential documents. What would you check?

topics.title: Weights, parameters, quantization and GGUF
topics.summary: A model's parameters (weights) are the billions of numbers it learned in training; a checkpoint is a saved copy of them. Quantization stores those numbers with fewer bits (for example 4-bit instead of 16-bit), making the model much smaller and faster with some loss of quality. GGUF is a popular file format for quantized models used by llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio.
topics.why: These ideas explain hardware costs, why a model fits on one GPU but not another, and what names like '7B Q4_K_M' mean. You'll hear them in every self-hosting or on-device discussion.
concepts: Memory rule of thumb: parameters times bytes per parameter
topics.do_it: Estimate the memory needed for a 7B and a 70B model at 16-bit and at 4-bit. Then check a GGUF model page on Hugging Face and compare with the listed file sizes.
topics.prove: Explain to a finance stakeholder, in one paragraph, why a 4-bit model is cheaper to run and what you give up.
topics.interview: What does '7B, 4-bit quantized' tell you about a model?

topics.title: Model serving: inference, GPUs, VRAM, batching, KV cache, vLLM
topics.summary: Inference is running a trained model to produce output; serving is doing that reliably for many users. GPUs do the maths and the model must fit in their memory (VRAM). Serving engines such as vLLM batch many requests together and manage the KV cache, the memory that stores context for each conversation, to get far more throughput from the same hardware.
topics.why: If your company self-hosts models, GPU cost and capacity become programme-level risks. Knowing the vocabulary (time to first token, throughput, batching, KV cache) lets you discuss capacity plans and performance targets with ML platform teams.
concepts: Time to first token vs tokens per second vs throughput
KV cache and why long contexts use memory
topics.do_it: Read the vLLM PagedAttention blog post and, with Claude's help, write a five-sentence explanation of why memory, not raw computing power, is often the bottleneck.
topics.prove: Draft the performance requirements section for a self-hosted chatbot: target time to first token, tokens per second, peak concurrent users and context length.
topics.interview: What drives the cost of self-hosting an LLM, and how would you size it?

topics.title: Choosing a model: build vs buy, API vs custom
topics.summary: Choosing a model is a product decision with technical inputs: quality on your task, speed, cost, data and privacy constraints, operational effort and vendor risk. The options range from calling a commercial API, to a cloud platform version of the same models, to self-hosting open models, to fine-tuning or training your own.
topics.why: This is one of the most consequential decisions in an AI programme and is often made on hype or habit. A TPM who runs a structured, evidence-based selection protects the budget, the timeline and the product.
concepts: Criteria: quality, latency, cost, privacy, operations, risk
Start with the strongest model, then optimise down
Evaluate on your own test set
API vs cloud platform vs self-hosted
Plan for model changes and retirement
topics.do_it: For one real use case at work, list your top five criteria and weight them. Score three options (two commercial APIs and one open model) on paper.
topics.prove: Write a one-page model decision record: options, evidence, decision, and what would make you revisit it.
topics.interview: How would you decide between a commercial LLM API and hosting an open-source model?
covers: Build vs. Buy AI (API vs custom models)

topics.title: AI competency rubric for TPMs
topics.summary: A rubric that describes what 'AI-enabled TPM' means in practice across five areas: AI literacy, building with AI, delivery of AI features, quality and risk, and leadership. Each area has four levels from aware to expert, with observable evidence for each.
topics.why: It turns a vague goal into something you can assess, plan against and show in an interview or performance review. It also helps you design learning plans and job descriptions for others.
concepts: Four levels: aware, practitioner, advanced, expert
Linking the rubric to this learning path
Using it for hiring and team growth
topics.do_it: Score yourself on each of the five areas today, with one piece of evidence each. Save it in your notes to compare at the end of the path.
topics.prove: Ask a technical colleague to review your self-assessment and challenge one score.
topics.interview: What makes a TPM 'AI-enabled', and how would you show it?

topics.title: What AI agents are and how they act
topics.summary: An AI agent is a model that works towards a goal by deciding its own next steps: it chooses tools, looks at the results and keeps going until the job is done. A workflow, by contrast, follows steps your code defines in advance, even if each step uses a model.
topics.why: 'Agent' is the most overused word in AI right now. Being able to say 'this is a workflow, not an agent' or 'this needs an agent because the steps can't be predicted' is how a TPM keeps scope, cost and risk realistic.
concepts: The augmented LLM: model + tools + retrieval + memory
Autonomy is a dial, not a switch
Start simple, add complexity only when needed
topics.do_it: List five AI features you've seen at work or in products. Label each as single call, workflow or agent, and write one sentence on why.
topics.prove: Write a one-page recommendation for one real use case: workflow or agent, and why.
topics.interview: When would you not use an AI agent?

topics.title: Tool and function calling with strict schemas
topics.summary: Tool calling is how a model asks your software to do something: you describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its inputs, the model replies with a request to call one, your code runs it and returns the result. Strict schemas make those requests reliably well-formed.
topics.why: Tools are where AI meets real systems: orders, tickets, payments, databases. Tool design decides whether an agent is accurate, safe and affordable, and it's a design decision a TPM can review without reading code.
concepts: Tool name, description and input schema
The model requests; your code executes
Good tool design: few, clear, non-overlapping tools
topics.do_it: Design three tools for an internal support agent (search_orders, get_order, create_refund_request) on paper: name, one-line description, inputs with types, and what each returns.
topics.prove: Mark which of your tools change data, and write the rule for each: automatic, needs approval, or not allowed.
topics.interview: How would you make sure an AI agent can't take a dangerous action?

topics.title: The agent loop, planning and reasoning (ReAct)
topics.summary: Agents run a loop: reason about the situation, take an action (usually a tool call), observe the result, and repeat. ReAct, a well-known 2022 research approach, showed that interleaving reasoning and actions works better than either alone. Planning means deciding the steps up front, revising them as results come in.
topics.why: The loop explains agent behaviour you'll see in demos and incidents: why it took 14 steps, why it got stuck repeating a search, why it gave up. It also tells you where to put limits and checkpoints.
concepts: Plan first vs plan as you go
topics.do_it: Watch Claude Code (or any agent) complete a small task and write down each thought, action and observation in a three-column table.
topics.prove: Identify one point in the run where a limit or a human check would have made sense, and explain why.
topics.interview: An agent keeps looping without finishing. How would you diagnose it?

topics.title: Agent memory and state management
topics.summary: Memory is what an agent knows beyond the current request. Short-term memory is the conversation and working state of one task; long-term memory is information kept across sessions, such as user preferences or past decisions. State management is how the system stores, updates and recovers that information.
topics.why: Memory decides whether an agent feels useful or forgetful, and it's also where privacy, cost and correctness problems hide. TPMs need to ask what is remembered, for how long, and who can see or delete it.
topics.do_it: Compare how Claude Projects, CLAUDE.md and a chat conversation each 'remember' things. Write one line on what each stores and when it's used.
topics.prove: Write the memory section of a requirements doc for a support agent: what's remembered, for how long, and how a user deletes it.
topics.interview: What could go wrong if an AI assistant remembers too much?

topics.title: Human-in-the-loop approval gates
topics.summary: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) means a person reviews, edits or approves an agent's work at defined points before it continues: approving a refund, editing a drafted email, confirming a deployment. The system pauses, waits for the human, then resumes.
topics.why: Approval gates are how organisations get value from agents without handing over full control. Deciding where the gates go is a risk and process design problem, which is squarely TPM territory.
concepts: Where to place gates: by risk and reversibility
Escalation when the agent is unsure
topics.do_it: Take a process you know (for example, invoice approval) and mark each step as 'agent alone', 'agent + human approval' or 'human only'.
topics.prove: Write the gate rules for one AI feature: thresholds, who approves, time limits and what happens if nobody responds.
topics.interview: How would you decide which AI actions need human approval?

topics.title: Multi-agent patterns: supervisor, sequential, parallel, handoffs
topics.summary: Multi-agent systems split work between several specialised agents or model calls. Common patterns: sequential (a pipeline), parallel (several work at once, results combined), supervisor or orchestrator-workers (one agent delegates to others), and handoffs (one agent passes the conversation to a specialist).
topics.why: Teams often reach for multiple agents too early. Knowing the patterns, and their costs, lets you push for the simplest design and recognise when splitting work genuinely helps.
topics.do_it: Draw a customer-support system three ways: one agent, a router plus specialists, and a supervisor with workers. List one pro and one con for each.
topics.prove: Recommend one design for your example with a short rationale covering cost, latency and testability.
topics.interview: When do multiple agents make sense, and what problems do they introduce?

topics.title: Agent error recovery, retries and checkpoints
topics.summary: Agents fail in more ways than normal software: tools time out, models return bad arguments, steps produce wrong results, runs get interrupted. Recovery design covers retries for temporary failures, feedback so the agent can correct itself, checkpoints so work isn't lost, and safe fallbacks when it can't continue.
topics.why: Unrecovered failures lead to duplicated actions (two refunds), lost work or silent wrong results. Recovery behaviour belongs in requirements and launch checklists, not only in code.
concepts: Retries with backoff for tools and models
Feeding errors back to the agent
topics.do_it: For the support-agent tools you designed earlier, write what should happen when each one fails: retry, ask the agent to fix the input, or escalate.
topics.prove: Write a failure-mode table (failure, detection, response, user message) for one agent workflow.
topics.interview: An agent issued the same refund twice. What went wrong and how would you prevent it?

topics.title: MCP basics and architecture
topics.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An AI application (the host) runs one MCP client per connection; each client talks to an MCP server that exposes tools, resources and prompts. Build a server once and any MCP-compatible app can use it.
topics.why: MCP has become the common way to plug AI assistants into company systems: GitHub, Slack, databases, internal APIs. TPMs will be asked to approve, prioritise and secure MCP integrations, so understanding the moving parts is essential.
concepts: Why a standard beats one-off integrations
topics.do_it: Look at which connectors or MCP servers your Claude account or Claude Code can use. For two of them, list the tools they expose and whether each reads or changes data.
topics.prove: Write a one-page proposal for an internal MCP server at your company: which system, which tools, who uses it and what's off-limits.
topics.interview: What problem does MCP solve, and what new risks does it bring?

topics.title: Advanced MCP patterns and security
