topics.summary: Once MCP servers reach real systems, the hard questions are about trust: who the server acts as, which permissions it has, how authorisation works for remote servers, and how to stop malicious tool descriptions or data from steering the model. The MCP specification includes a security best-practices document covering specific attacks and mitigations.
topics.why: An MCP server is effectively a new integration with access to company data and actions. TPMs need to make sure security review, least privilege and monitoring are part of rolling them out.
concepts: Tool poisoning and prompt injection through data
Logging, review and allow-lists of servers
topics.do_it: Read the 'token passthrough' and 'confused deputy' sections of the MCP security best practices and explain each in two sentences of plain English.
topics.prove: Write an MCP server approval checklist for your company (10 items or fewer).
topics.interview: How would you safely let an AI assistant access an internal system through MCP?

topics.title: Agent framework landscape
topics.summary: Agent frameworks are libraries that provide the loop, tool handling, memory, multi-agent patterns and tracing so teams don't build them from scratch. Major options include LangChain and LangGraph, CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK (which replaced the experimental Swarm), the Claude Agent SDK, Vercel's AI SDK, and Microsoft Agent Framework (the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen).
topics.why: Framework choice affects hiring, lock-in, debugging and how fast teams ship. TPMs should be able to ask the right questions rather than accept 'everyone uses X'.
concepts: Direct API calls as a valid option
topics.do_it: Make a comparison table of four frameworks: language, model support, key idea, maturity signal and one thing it's best at.
topics.prove: Write a recommendation for one team's use case, including the option of using no framework.
topics.interview: How would you choose an agent framework for a new product team?

topics.title: LangGraph and LlamaIndex deep dive
topics.summary: LangGraph models an agent or workflow as a graph: nodes are steps (model calls, tools, code), edges decide what runs next, and a shared state object flows through it. Checkpoints after each step give durable execution, human-in-the-loop pauses and debugging. LlamaIndex focuses on connecting models to your data: loading, indexing, retrieval, and agents and workflows built on top.
topics.why: These two are among the most widely used libraries for production agents and RAG. Knowing their core ideas helps you understand design documents, estimates and failure reports from teams using them.
concepts: Mixing fixed steps and model-driven steps
Agents with RAG as a tool
topics.do_it: Draw a LangGraph-style graph for 'triage a support ticket': nodes, edges, the state fields, and where an interrupt for human approval goes.
topics.prove: Explain to a colleague when you'd pick LangGraph, LlamaIndex, or both together.
topics.interview: How do you make a long-running agent resumable and auditable?

topics.title: Claude Agent SDK
topics.summary: The Claude Agent SDK gives developers the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, as a library for Python and TypeScript. Teams use it to build their own agents, such as a bug-fixing bot, a research assistant or an operations agent, with built-in file, search and command tools, plus hooks, subagents and permission controls.
topics.why: It's the shortest path from 'Claude Code does this well for me' to 'our product or internal workflow does this automatically'. Knowing what it provides helps you scope agent projects realistically.
concepts: Built-in tools and custom tools via MCP
Permissions: what runs automatically vs needs approval
Hooks at key points in the loop
When to use the SDK, the CLI or the plain API
topics.do_it: Read the Agent SDK overview and list which built-in capabilities you'd need for an agent that reviews pull requests and posts a summary.
topics.prove: Write a one-page spec for that agent: trigger, tools, permissions, approval points and success measure.
topics.interview: How would you turn a manual engineering task into an automated agent safely?

topics.title: No-code automation: Zapier, Make, n8n
topics.summary: No-code automation tools connect apps with visual workflows: a trigger (new form response, new email, a schedule) starts a sequence of actions (create a ticket, call an AI model, post to Slack). Zapier calls them Zaps, Make calls them scenarios, and n8n calls them workflows; n8n can also be self-hosted.
topics.why: These tools let a PM automate real work this week, without engineering time, and increasingly include AI steps and agents. They're also a fast way to prototype automations before engineering builds them properly.
topics.do_it: Build one automation: when a Google Form or Typeform is submitted, summarise the response with an AI step and post the summary to Slack or email.
topics.prove: Run it for a week and note failures, costs and time saved.
topics.interview: Tell me about an automation you built and what it saved.

topics.title: Custom API automation built with Claude
topics.summary: When no-code tools aren't enough, a small script can call APIs directly: fetch data from one system, process it with an AI model, and write results to another. With Claude Code you can describe the automation in plain English and have it write, test and explain the script, then run it on a schedule.
topics.why: This is the step from user of automation to builder. It unlocks automations that no-code tools can't do well, such as large data volumes, unusual APIs or complex logic, without needing to learn to code.
concepts: Describe inputs, steps and outputs precisely
API authentication with keys in environment variables
Scheduling: cron, GitHub Actions, cloud functions
topics.do_it: With Claude Code, build a script that reads your GitHub repo's merged pull requests from the past week and writes a plain-English summary to a Markdown file. Start in plan mode.
topics.prove: Schedule it with GitHub Actions to run every Friday, and check one week's output.
topics.interview: Describe something you automated yourself and how you made it reliable.

topics.title: Reliable automations: error handling, monitoring, security, scaling
topics.summary: An automation that people depend on needs the same care as a small product: it must handle errors, report its health, protect the data and credentials it uses, and cope as volumes grow. This lesson pulls together the practices that make automations trustworthy.
topics.why: Automations fail quietly: nobody notices until a customer, a report or an audit does. TPMs who build or approve automations need a reliability checklist.
topics.do_it: Take the automation you built earlier and add an error notification, a weekly success summary and a README describing its owner and purpose.
topics.prove: Write a reliability checklist for automations in your team and apply it to three existing ones.
topics.interview: How do you make sure an automation doesn't fail silently?

topics.title: Event-driven architecture and message queues
topics.summary: In an event-driven architecture, services communicate by publishing events ('order placed', 'payment failed') that other services react to, instead of calling each other directly. Message queues and event streaming platforms such as RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS and Apache Kafka carry those events reliably between producers and consumers.
topics.why: Many automations and agents are triggered by events, and most large systems are partly event-driven. Understanding events, queues and their trade-offs helps you follow architecture discussions and incident reports.
topics.do_it: Draw an e-commerce order flow event by event: which service publishes each event and which services react.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why an order confirmation email might arrive before the order shows in their account.
topics.interview: What are the benefits and the trade-offs of event-driven systems?

topics.title: Why evals matter and how to define quality
topics.summary: An eval is a repeatable test for an AI system: a set of inputs, the system's outputs, and a way to grade them. Defining quality means turning 'it should be good' into specific, measurable criteria such as accuracy on a task, tone, safety, latency and cost.
topics.why: Without evals, every prompt change, model upgrade or bug fix is a guess. Evals turn AI quality into something you can plan, report and gate releases on, which is exactly what a TPM needs.
concepts: Multiple dimensions: accuracy, tone, safety, latency, cost
Pass rate as a product decision
Look at the data: error analysis first
Evals as the shared language between product and engineering
topics.do_it: For one AI feature you know, write five success criteria with a number attached to each (for example, '95% of answers cite a source').
topics.prove: Turn those criteria into a one-page quality scorecard you could review weekly with the team.
topics.interview: How do you know if an AI feature is good enough to launch?

topics.title: Golden datasets and ground truth
topics.summary: A golden dataset is a curated set of test inputs with known correct answers (ground truth) or clear grading notes, used to evaluate an AI system the same way every time. It should represent real usage, including hard and unusual cases.
topics.why: The golden dataset is the foundation of every eval. If it's small, unrepresentative or wrong, every score built on it misleads. Building one is a practical task a TPM can lead with domain experts.
concepts: Ground truth labels and grading notes
topics.do_it: Build a 30-row golden dataset in a spreadsheet for one task (for example, classifying support tickets): input, expected answer, category, difficulty, notes.
topics.prove: Have a colleague label 10 rows independently and compare. Where you disagree, improve the labelling guidelines.
topics.interview: How would you build a test set for an AI feature with no production data yet?

topics.title: LLM-as-a-judge rubrics
topics.summary: LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to grade another model's output against a rubric, such as 'Did the answer resolve the customer's question? Pass or fail, with reasoning.' It scales evaluation to thousands of cases, but only after the judge has been checked against human expert judgement.
topics.why: Many qualities that matter (helpfulness, tone, faithfulness) can't be checked with simple code. A calibrated judge makes them measurable every day, which makes continuous quality management possible.
concepts: Binary pass/fail with a critique beats vague 1 to 5 scales
Domain expert defines what good means
Calibrate the judge against human labels
topics.do_it: Write a pass/fail rubric for 'good meeting summary' with three criteria and one example of a pass and a fail. Test it in Claude on five summaries.
topics.prove: Grade the same five summaries yourself and calculate how often you and the judge agree.
topics.interview: How can you trust an AI to grade another AI?

topics.title: Precision, recall, F1
topics.summary: Precision asks: of everything the system flagged, how much was right? Recall asks: of everything it should have flagged, how much did it find? F1 is a single score that balances the two. They're the standard metrics for classification tasks such as spam detection, fraud flags or ticket routing.
topics.why: These metrics expose trade-offs that accuracy hides. Choosing whether precision or recall matters more is a business decision, and TPMs are often the ones who should make it explicit.
concepts: True and false positives and negatives
F1 as the balance of both
Why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data
topics.do_it: From this example: the model flags 50 tickets as urgent, 40 really are urgent, and 20 urgent tickets were missed. Calculate precision, recall and F1.
topics.prove: For two features at work, decide whether precision or recall matters more and explain the business reason.
topics.interview: Our fraud model has 99% accuracy. Is that good?

topics.title: Retrieval metrics: Recall@K, MRR, NDCG
topics.summary: In RAG systems, retrieval quality is measured separately from answer quality. Recall@K: did the relevant documents appear in the top K results? Precision@K: how many of the top K were relevant? MRR: how high was the first relevant result? NDCG: how good was the whole ranking compared with the ideal order?
topics.why: Most bad RAG answers start with bad retrieval: the right document was never found. Measuring retrieval directly tells teams whether to fix search or fix the prompt, which saves weeks of guessing.
concepts: Choosing K to match what the model sees
topics.do_it: For 5 questions about your company's documents, list which documents are relevant. Then search with your tool of choice and calculate Recall@5 for each question.
topics.prove: Explain to an engineer, using your results, whether the RAG problem is in retrieval or in generation.
topics.interview: A RAG assistant gives wrong answers. How would you find out why?
covers: Retrieval Metrics: Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, NDCG

topics.title: Groundedness, hallucination detection and citation accuracy
topics.summary: Groundedness (or faithfulness) measures whether every claim in an answer is supported by the provided sources. Hallucination detection flags claims that aren't. Citation accuracy checks that each citation actually supports the sentence it's attached to.
topics.why: For assistants answering from company documents, an unsupported claim is the most damaging failure: it looks authoritative and is wrong. These checks are how you prove the assistant sticks to the sources.
concepts: Each claim checked against the context
Answering 'I don't know' when sources are silent
Automated checks plus human spot checks
topics.do_it: Take three RAG answers (from NotebookLM or your own tool). Split each into claims and mark each claim supported, partly supported or unsupported by the cited source.
topics.prove: Write a groundedness policy for an assistant: target score, what happens to unsupported claims, and when it should refuse.
topics.interview: How would you measure and reduce hallucinations in a document assistant?

topics.title: Answer relevance
topics.summary: Answer relevance measures whether a response actually addresses the question asked: complete, on-topic and without padding. An answer can be accurate and grounded yet still unhelpful if it answers a different question or buries the point.
topics.why: Users judge assistants on whether they got what they asked for. Relevance complements accuracy and groundedness to give a fuller picture of quality.
concepts: Does it answer the actual question?
topics.do_it: Write three questions with two parts each. Ask an assistant, and mark each answer for whether both parts were addressed.
topics.prove: Add a relevance criterion to your quality scorecard with a target and how it's measured.
topics.interview: An assistant's answers are accurate but users are unhappy. What might be wrong?

topics.title: Regression testing for prompts and models
topics.summary: Regression testing for AI means running the same eval suite whenever something changes (the prompt, the model, retrieval settings, tools) and comparing results with the previous version, so improvements in one place don't silently break another.
topics.why: AI systems change constantly: prompt tweaks, model upgrades, new documents. Without regression tests, every change is a gamble and quality drifts. This is the AI equivalent of the test suite engineers already rely on.
concepts: Fixed suite run on every change
topics.do_it: Write 10 test cases for a prompt (input plus what must or must not appear), run them against two prompt versions in Claude, and compare.
topics.prove: Define the release rule: which metrics must not drop, by how much, before a change can ship.
topics.interview: A model upgrade improved average quality but users complain. What might your evals have missed?

topics.title: Reproducibility: temperature, seeds, prompt drift
topics.summary: Reproducibility is getting the same (or acceptably similar) results when you rerun an AI system. Model outputs vary because of sampling settings like temperature, provider-side changes, and untracked changes to prompts, data or models. Managing those sources makes behaviour explainable.
topics.why: When a stakeholder asks 'why did it say that last Tuesday?', you need to know exactly which prompt, model and data produced the answer. Reproducibility underpins debugging, audits and fair evaluation.
topics.do_it: Ask the same question five times at default settings and five times with temperature 0 (in AI Studio or the API). Note how much the answers vary.
topics.prove: Write the list of things that must be logged with every AI response for full traceability.
topics.interview: How would you investigate a complaint about an AI answer from last week?

topics.title: RAG benchmarking with Ragas
topics.summary: Ragas is an open-source library for evaluating RAG systems with metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and context recall. Similar tools include DeepEval and TruLens. They let teams benchmark a RAG pipeline on a test set and compare versions.
topics.why: RAG has many moving parts (chunking, embeddings, retrieval, prompts, models). A standard benchmark shows which change actually helps, so teams stop debating and start measuring.
concepts: A RAG test set: question, reference answer, retrieved context
Limits: judge cost, calibration, small sets
topics.do_it: Read the Ragas metrics documentation and write a one-line plain-English definition for faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and context recall.
topics.prove: Design a benchmark plan for a RAG assistant: test set size, metrics, targets, and which pipeline variants to compare.
topics.interview: How would you decide whether a new chunking strategy improved your RAG system?

topics.title: Evaluating agents
topics.summary: Agents work over many steps, use tools and change things, so evaluating them means checking both the outcome (did the final state meet the goal?) and the path (sensible tool use, safe actions, reasonable cost). Agent evals run tasks in a controlled environment, often several times each, and grade with code, judges and humans.
topics.why: Agent failures are expensive and varied: wrong actions, loops, runaway costs. A clear eval approach is what lets an organisation trust agents with real work and adopt new models quickly.
concepts: Cost, steps and safety as metrics
topics.do_it: Design three eval tasks for a coding or support agent: the starting state, the goal, how success is checked automatically, and one thing the agent must never do.
topics.prove: Write an agent eval plan: tasks, trials per task, graders, metrics (success rate, steps, cost, safety violations) and release thresholds.
topics.interview: How would you evaluate an AI agent before giving it access to production systems?

topics.title: Public benchmarks and synthetic data
topics.summary: Public benchmarks such as MMLU (knowledge across 57 subjects), GSM8K (grade-school maths) and HumanEval (coding) compare models on standard tasks. Synthetic data is test or training data generated with models to fill gaps. Both are useful, and both have serious limits for judging your own product.
topics.why: Vendors quote benchmark scores constantly. A TPM needs to read them critically and know why your own evals, built partly with synthetic data, matter more for decisions.
concepts: Saturation: top models score near the maximum
Contamination: test data seen in training
Validating synthetic data against real usage
topics.do_it: Look up a recent model announcement and list which benchmarks it quotes. For each, write one line on how relevant it is to your use case.
topics.prove: Generate 20 synthetic test questions for a use case with Claude, then mark which ones resemble real user questions and which don't.
topics.interview: A vendor says their model tops the benchmarks. How do you respond?

topics.title: Tracing, telemetry and observability for LLM apps
topics.summary: Observability for an LLM app means being able to see, for any single request, every step it took: the prompt sent, the documents retrieved, the tools called, the model's answer, the tokens used, the time taken and the cost. A trace records those steps as a tree of spans.
topics.why: When a user says 'the bot gave a wrong answer', you can't fix it without the trace. Tracing is also how you measure cost, latency and quality over time, which is what a TPM reports on.
concepts: What to capture: prompt, context, tool calls, output, tokens, latency
Drift: inputs and quality changing over time
Sampling and privacy of logged prompts
topics.do_it: Sketch the trace for one request in an AI feature you know: list each span (retrieve, rerank, call model, call tool, format) and what you would record on each.
topics.prove: Write a one-page observability requirement for an AI feature: what is traced, which dashboards exist, who gets alerted and when.
topics.interview: A user reports a wrong answer from our AI assistant. How would you investigate it?

topics.title: Cost tracking, budgets and token monitoring
topics.summary: LLM costs are driven by tokens: input tokens sent and output tokens generated, priced per million by model. Cost tracking means measuring tokens and spend per feature, team and customer, setting budgets and alerts, and finding the biggest levers to reduce spend.
topics.why: AI features can have a variable cost per use that grows with adoption. A TPM who can forecast and control that cost protects margins and keeps the feature funded.
concepts: Input vs output tokens and price per million
Cost per request, per user, per feature
Levers: model choice, prompt length, caching, batching
topics.do_it: Estimate the monthly cost of one AI feature: requests per day × average input and output tokens × price. Then list three ways to cut it by a third.
topics.prove: Build a simple cost model spreadsheet with assumptions, a base case, a high-usage case and the effect of each saving lever.
topics.interview: Our AI feature's costs doubled last month. How would you find out why and what would you do?

topics.title: Latency optimisation and semantic caching
topics.summary: Latency is how long a user waits. For LLM apps the key measures are time to first token and total response time. Optimising it means choosing the right model, keeping prompts short, streaming output, running steps in parallel and caching. Semantic caching returns a stored answer when a new question means the same as a previous one.
topics.why: Slow AI features feel broken and get abandoned. Latency targets belong in the requirements, and the TPM has to weigh speed against quality and cost.
concepts: Time to first token vs total time
Parallel steps and fewer round trips
topics.do_it: Take one AI flow and list each step with an estimated time. Mark which steps could run in parallel, which could be cached and which could use a smaller model.
topics.prove: Write latency requirements (p50 and p95 for first token and full answer) for an AI feature and a plan to meet them.
topics.interview: Users say the AI assistant is too slow. What options would you consider, and what are the trade-offs?

topics.title: AI CI/CD with evaluation gates
topics.summary: AI CI/CD extends the normal build-test-deploy pipeline so that changes to prompts, models, retrieval settings or tools are automatically evaluated before release. An evaluation gate blocks the release if quality scores drop below agreed thresholds.
topics.why: Prompts and model versions change behaviour as much as code does. Without eval gates, a one-line prompt tweak can silently break answers in production.
concepts: Prompts and configs as versioned code
Regression comparison against the last release
Canary release and rollback for AI changes
topics.do_it: Write the pipeline stages for an AI feature change, from pull request to production, marking where evals run and what the pass thresholds are.
topics.prove: Draft a release checklist for prompt and model changes that your team could adopt.
topics.interview: How would you stop a prompt change from breaking production?

topics.title: Guardrails for inputs and outputs
topics.summary: Guardrails are checks placed around a model to keep it within safe and intended behaviour. Input guardrails screen what goes into the model; output guardrails check what comes out before the user sees it or before an action runs.
topics.why: The model alone can't guarantee safe, on-topic, correctly formatted output. Guardrails are how you turn policy ('never give medical diagnoses', 'never reveal account numbers') into enforced behaviour.
concepts: Input checks: topic, abuse, injection, PII
Output checks: safety, grounding, format, policy
topics.do_it: For one AI feature, list five input checks and five output checks, and for each say what happens when it fails.
topics.prove: Write a guardrail policy table: rule, where it runs, method (rule or model), action on failure, owner.
topics.interview: What guardrails would you put on a customer-facing AI chatbot for a bank?

topics.title: Prompt injection and jailbreak defence
topics.summary: Prompt injection is when text the model reads (from a user, a web page, an email or a document) contains instructions that override the intended behaviour. A jailbreak is a user deliberately crafting prompts to get around the model's safety rules. Indirect injection, hidden in content the model processes, is the most dangerous for agents.
topics.why: Once AI can read external content and take actions, injection can turn it against your users: leaking data, sending messages or changing records. It is ranked first in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications.
topics.do_it: Pick an AI agent that reads emails or web pages. Write three injection scenarios and, for each, what damage it could do and which control would stop it.
topics.prove: Write a threat model for one AI feature: assets, untrusted inputs, possible injections, impact and controls.
topics.interview: Our AI assistant can read customer emails and send replies. How do we protect against prompt injection?

topics.title: PII protection and data leakage
topics.summary: PII (personally identifiable information) is data that can identify a person, such as names, phone numbers, emails, ID numbers and addresses. In AI systems it can leak through prompts sent to vendors, logs and traces, training or fine-tuning data, retrieval that ignores permissions, and model outputs.
topics.why: Privacy breaches bring legal penalties and lost trust. India's DPDP Act and Europe's GDPR apply to AI features just as to any other system, and AI adds new leak paths that teams often miss.
concepts: Types of PII and sensitive data
Leak paths: prompts, logs, retrieval, outputs, training
Vendor data retention and training terms
topics.do_it: Map one AI feature's data flow and mark every place personal data could be stored, sent or exposed.
topics.prove: Write a privacy checklist for AI features covering vendor terms, masking, logging, retrieval permissions and retention.
topics.interview: How would you make sure an AI support assistant doesn't leak customer data?

topics.title: Sandboxing, access control and secrets
topics.summary: Sandboxing runs AI-generated code or agent actions in an isolated environment with limited access. Access control (often role-based, RBAC) decides who and what can use which data and tools. Secrets management keeps API keys and credentials out of code, prompts and logs.
topics.why: Agents that run code or call tools can do real damage if compromised. Strong isolation, permissions and secret handling limit the blast radius of mistakes and attacks.
concepts: Sandbox: isolated container, no network by default
topics.do_it: For an agent that reads a database and sends emails, list each permission it needs and reduce it to the minimum.
topics.prove: Write an access-control matrix for an AI feature: roles, tools, data, allowed actions.
topics.interview: An AI agent needs access to our CRM. How do you keep that safe?

topics.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and AI vulnerability assessment
topics.summary: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists the most important security risks in AI apps, such as prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain risks and excessive agency. Vulnerability assessment combines this with standard application testing: SAST (scanning source code), DAST (testing the running app) and SCA (checking third-party dependencies).
topics.why: Security reviews increasingly ask AI-specific questions. A TPM who knows the categories and the test types can plan security work, read reports and track fixes.
concepts: Where each scan runs in the pipeline
topics.do_it: Map one AI feature against the OWASP LLM Top 10: for each risk, write whether it applies and which control covers it.
topics.prove: Create a security test plan listing which scans run where (PR, nightly, pre-release) and who triages results.
topics.interview: What security testing would you plan before launching an AI feature?

topics.title: Audit logs for AI systems
topics.summary: An audit log is a tamper-resistant record of who did what, when and with what result. For AI systems it also records what the AI did on someone's behalf: which tools it called, which data it accessed, which actions were approved and by whom.
topics.why: When something goes wrong, or a regulator or customer asks, audit logs are the evidence. They are also required by many security standards and by AI regulations for higher-risk systems.
concepts: Not logging secrets or excess personal data
topics.do_it: List ten events an AI agent feature should write to the audit log, with the fields for each.
topics.prove: Write an audit logging requirement for an AI feature, including retention, access and review process.
topics.interview: What would you log for an AI agent that can update customer records?

topics.title: AI risk, data privacy and governance
topics.summary: AI governance is the set of policies, roles and processes an organisation uses to decide which AI uses are acceptable, assess their risks, approve them and monitor them. Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework give a structure: govern, map, measure and manage.
topics.why: Companies are setting up AI review boards and risk processes. TPMs often run the delivery side: getting features through review, producing evidence and tracking controls.
concepts: Risk categories: safety, bias, privacy, security, reliability
NIST AI RMF: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
topics.do_it: Write a one-page risk assessment for an AI feature: purpose, users, data, possible harms, likelihood, impact, controls and owner.
topics.prove: Draft a lightweight AI governance process for a team: intake form, risk tiers, approvals and review cadence.
topics.interview: How would you set up AI governance in a company that is starting to use AI widely?

topics.title: AI regulation: EU AI Act and India's approach
topics.summary: The EU AI Act is a law that regulates AI by risk level: some practices are banned, high-risk systems have strict requirements, some systems have transparency duties, and general-purpose AI models have their own obligations. India has chosen a different path: voluntary AI Governance Guidelines released in November 2025, relying on existing laws such as the DPDP Act rather than a dedicated AI law.
topics.why: If your product serves EU users, the AI Act can apply even if you are based in India. Regulations shape requirements, documentation and timelines, so TPMs need to know when legal review is needed.
concepts: Risk-based approach: prohibited, high-risk, transparency, minimal
Timeline and the 2026 Digital Omnibus changes
India's AI Governance Guidelines and seven sutras
DPDP Act and Rules for personal data
topics.do_it: Classify three AI features you know under the EU AI Act risk levels and note what each would need.
topics.prove: Write a one-page regulatory note for a product team: which rules may apply, key dates, and questions for legal.
topics.interview: We plan to launch an AI hiring tool in Europe and India. What regulatory questions should we ask?

topics.title: AI documentation: model cards and API contracts
topics.summary: AI documentation explains what an AI system is for, how it was tested, where it fails and how to use it safely. Model cards and system cards describe models; prompt registries track prompt versions; API contracts define exactly what an AI service accepts and returns.
topics.why: Good documentation lets other teams use AI safely, supports audits and regulation, and stops knowledge living only in one engineer's head.
concepts: Model cards: intended use, evaluation, limitations
Change logs for prompts and models
topics.do_it: Read the summary of one provider system card and note three limitations relevant to your product.
topics.prove: Write a one-page AI fact sheet for a feature: purpose, model and version, data, evaluation results, known limits, owner, escalation path.
topics.interview: What documentation would you require before an AI feature goes live?

topics.title: DevOps lifecycle and culture
topics.summary: DevOps is a way of working where development and operations share responsibility for building, releasing and running software, supported by automation. The lifecycle is usually drawn as a loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, and back to plan.
topics.why: Most delivery delays sit in hand-offs between teams. A TPM who understands DevOps can spot those bottlenecks and push for automation and shared ownership instead of more meetings.
concepts: Shared ownership: you build it, you run it
DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore
topics.do_it: Map how a change in your current project moves from idea to production. Mark each manual hand-off and how long it waits.
topics.prove: Propose three improvements to that flow, each with the delay it would remove.
topics.interview: What does DevOps mean to you, and how have you applied it as a programme manager?

topics.title: Git concepts: repos, branches, commits, merge, rebase, tags
topics.summary: Git is a version control system: it records every change to files as commits, lets people work in parallel on branches, and combines work through merge or rebase. GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket host Git repositories online and add reviews and automation.
topics.why: Every engineering conversation about releases, hotfixes and conflicts uses Git words. Knowing them lets you follow, question and plan without needing to code.
topics.do_it: Complete GitHub's Hello World guide: create a repository, a branch, a commit and a pull request, then merge it.
topics.prove: Explain in five sentences, using your own repo, how a hotfix would reach production while a feature branch is still in progress.
topics.interview: Two developers changed the same file and there's a merge conflict. What does that mean and how is it resolved?

topics.title: Pull requests and branching strategies
topics.summary: A pull request (GitHub) or merge request (GitLab) proposes merging a branch, so others can review the change and automated checks can run. A branching strategy is the team's agreed pattern for branches, such as GitHub flow, trunk-based development or Git flow.
topics.why: Pull requests are where quality, knowledge sharing and release readiness meet. The branching strategy shapes how fast and safely a team can ship.
topics.do_it: Open a recent pull request in any public repo and note: the description, linked issue, checks that ran, review comments and how long it took to merge.
topics.prove: Write a one-page PR guideline for a team: size limits, description template, required checks and review time targets.
topics.interview: Pull requests in our team wait days for review. What would you do?

topics.title: CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment
topics.summary: Continuous integration (CI) means developers merge small changes often and every change is automatically built and tested. Continuous delivery means every change that passes is automatically prepared and can be released at any time with a button press. Continuous deployment goes one step further: every passing change goes to production automatically.
topics.why: People use 'CI/CD' loosely. Knowing the difference lets you set realistic release plans and know which approvals and tests are needed.
concepts: Integrating often to avoid big-bang merges
Automated build and test on every change
Choosing the right level for your product
topics.do_it: For your current product, decide which of the three you have today, and list what's missing to reach the next level.
topics.prove: Write a short roadmap with milestones from today's process to continuous delivery.
topics.interview: Should we move to continuous deployment? What would need to be true first?

topics.title: Build and release pipelines and artifacts
topics.summary: A build pipeline turns source code into a tested, versioned artifact (a package, container image or app file). A release pipeline takes that same artifact and promotes it through environments such as dev, staging and production. Build once, deploy many times.
topics.why: Release problems often come from building different things for different environments. Understanding artifacts and promotion helps you ask the right questions in release reviews.
topics.do_it: List your product's environments and how a change moves through them. Note whether the same artifact is promoted or rebuilt each time.
topics.prove: Draw the build and release pipeline for your product, with gates and who approves each.
topics.interview: What's the difference between deploying and releasing?

topics.title: GitHub Actions hands-on (plus Jenkins and GitLab CI overview)
topics.summary: GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform built into GitHub. You describe workflows in YAML files in your repository; they run on triggers such as a push or pull request. Jenkins and GitLab CI do the same job: Jenkins is self-hosted and plugin-based, GitLab CI is built into GitLab.
topics.why: Reading and tweaking a pipeline file is a practical skill. You've already seen GitHub Actions run tests for this learning hub's repo; now you can understand and change one.
topics.do_it: Follow the GitHub Actions quickstart in a test repo, then ask Claude to add a job that runs a simple test on every pull request.
topics.prove: Open the CI workflow in this learning hub's repository and explain, step by step, what each job does.
topics.interview: Walk me through a CI pipeline you've worked with. What runs and when?

topics.title: Testing in the pipeline
topics.summary: Automated tests run in the pipeline so every change is checked before it moves on. The usual mix follows the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests.
topics.why: Test strategy decides how confidently and quickly a team can release. A TPM should know what is tested where, how long it takes and what flaky tests cost.
concepts: Where each runs: PR, merge, nightly, pre-release
Coverage as a signal, not a target
topics.do_it: List the automated tests in your product's pipeline, where each runs and how long it takes.
topics.prove: Write a one-page test strategy: what runs on PR, on merge, nightly and after deploy.
topics.interview: How would you balance test coverage and release speed?

topics.title: Servers, VMs, Linux and scripting basics
topics.summary: A server is a computer that provides a service over a network. It can be bare metal (a physical machine), a virtual machine (a software-defined computer sharing physical hardware) or a container. Most servers run Linux and are managed through a command-line shell such as Bash, often over SSH; Windows servers use PowerShell.
topics.why: Incident calls and infrastructure plans use these words constantly. Knowing them helps you understand what's being changed and what could break.
concepts: Bare metal vs VM vs container
Why servers are treated as replaceable
topics.do_it: Work through the first sections of the Ubuntu command-line tutorial (navigate folders, create files, list contents). On Windows you can use WSL.
topics.prove: Explain to a non-technical colleague what happens when an engineer 'SSHes into a box to check the logs'.
topics.interview: What's the difference between a VM and a container?

topics.title: Containers and Docker
topics.summary: A container packages an application with everything it needs (code, runtime, libraries, settings) so it runs the same anywhere. Docker builds images from a Dockerfile, runs them as containers and stores them in registries such as Docker Hub.
topics.why: Containers are the standard way to ship modern software, including this learning hub. Understanding them explains 'works on my machine' problems and how deployments happen.
topics.do_it: Open this project's docker-compose.yml and identify each service, its image or build folder, and its ports.
topics.prove: Explain to a teammate how docker compose up starts the database, backend and frontend for the learning hub.
topics.interview: Why do teams use containers, and what problems do they solve?

topics.title: Kubernetes at a high level
topics.summary: Kubernetes is an open-source platform that runs and manages containers across a cluster of machines. You declare what you want (for example, three copies of the backend), and Kubernetes keeps reality matching: placing containers, restarting failed ones, scaling and routing traffic.
topics.why: Many companies run production on Kubernetes. Knowing the vocabulary helps you follow capacity, deployment and incident discussions.
topics.do_it: Draw a simple cluster: two nodes, a backend deployment with three pods, a service in front, and an ingress for internet traffic.
topics.prove: Explain what Kubernetes does automatically when one node crashes.
topics.interview: Do we need Kubernetes for our product? How would you decide?

topics.title: Infrastructure as code and configuration management
topics.summary: Infrastructure as code (IaC) means defining servers, networks, databases and permissions in files that are versioned and reviewed, then applied by a tool such as Terraform. Configuration management tools such as Ansible keep the software and settings on servers consistent.
topics.why: IaC makes environments repeatable, reviewable and recoverable. It turns 'someone clicked something in the console' into a change you can see in a pull request.
topics.do_it: Read the Terraform intro and write, in plain English, the plan you'd expect for creating one storage bucket and one database.
topics.prove: Write a short policy: which infrastructure changes must go through IaC, and who reviews them.
topics.interview: Why would a team move from console changes to infrastructure as code?

topics.title: Cloud platforms: AWS, Azure, GCP core services
topics.summary: Cloud platforms rent computing resources on demand. AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud offer similar building blocks: virtual machines, storage, databases, serverless functions and networking, priced by usage.
topics.why: Cloud choices drive cost, speed and risk. TPMs often run migrations, cost reviews and vendor discussions, so the core services and pricing models need to be familiar.
concepts: Compute: EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine
Storage: S3, Blob Storage, Cloud Storage
Serverless: Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions
topics.do_it: Map your product's components to cloud services: where the app runs, where files are stored, which database, and what serverless functions exist.
topics.prove: Write a one-page cloud cost summary for a product: top five services by cost and one saving idea for each.
topics.interview: Explain cloud computing to a business stakeholder in two minutes.

topics.title: Cloud networking and security: VPC, security groups, IAM
topics.summary: A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private network inside the cloud, split into subnets. Security groups act as firewalls around resources. IAM (identity and access management) controls who and what can do which actions on which resources. Load balancers spread traffic across servers.
topics.why: Most cloud security incidents come from misconfigured networks and permissions. Understanding these pieces helps you review designs and ask about exposure.
topics.do_it: Draw a simple VPC: a public subnet with a load balancer, a private subnet with app servers, and a private subnet with the database. Mark which ports are open between them.
topics.prove: Write five questions you'd ask in a design review about network exposure and permissions.
topics.interview: How would you make sure our database isn't exposed to the internet?

topics.title: Auto scaling, storage types and managed services
topics.summary: Auto scaling adds or removes servers automatically based on demand. Cloud storage comes in three types: block (disks for servers), file (shared folders) and object (files with metadata in buckets, such as S3). Managed services let the provider run components such as databases, queues and caches for you.
topics.why: These choices affect cost, performance and team workload. TPMs weigh build-vs-buy and scale plans every quarter.
topics.do_it: For one product, list which storage type each kind of data uses (database disks, user uploads, logs, backups) and whether each service is managed.
topics.prove: Write a recommendation on moving one self-managed component to a managed service, with costs and risks.
topics.interview: Our traffic spikes every evening. How should our infrastructure handle that?

topics.title: Deployment strategies: blue-green, canary, rolling, zero downtime
topics.summary: Deployment strategies control how a new version replaces the old one. Rolling replaces servers a few at a time. Blue-green runs two identical environments and switches traffic at once. Canary sends a small share of users to the new version first. All aim for zero downtime and easy rollback.
topics.why: Choosing the strategy sets release risk, cost and rollback speed. TPMs plan releases and communicate risk, so this vocabulary is essential.
topics.do_it: For a feature in your product, choose a deployment strategy and write why, including how you'd roll back.
topics.prove: Write a release plan for a risky change using a canary: stages, percentages, metrics watched and go/no-go criteria.
topics.interview: How would you release a risky change to a payment flow with minimal impact?

topics.title: Environment variables and secrets management
topics.summary: Configuration that differs between environments (database addresses, feature switches, API keys) should live outside the code, usually in environment variables. Secrets, such as passwords and keys, need extra protection in a secrets manager with access control, auditing and rotation.
topics.why: Leaked secrets are one of the most common causes of breaches. Clean config handling also makes the same build run in every environment.
topics.do_it: Look at this project's .env.example and docker-compose.yml. List which values are config and which are secrets.
topics.prove: Write a secrets policy for a team: where secrets live, who can read them, how often they rotate and what to do after a leak.
topics.interview: A developer committed an API key to GitHub. What do you do?

topics.title: Web servers, hosting, domains and SSL renewal
topics.summary: Web servers such as Nginx and Apache receive HTTP requests and serve files or pass requests to applications (as a reverse proxy). Hosting is where the app runs. Domains are mapped to servers through DNS. SSL/TLS certificates enable HTTPS and must be renewed before they expire.
topics.why: Expired certificates and wrong DNS records cause embarrassing outages. Launches and migrations need someone to own these details.
topics.do_it: Check the certificate of a website you use (padlock icon): who issued it and when it expires.
topics.prove: Write a launch checklist for a new domain: DNS records, certificate, redirects from HTTP to HTTPS, monitoring for expiry.
topics.interview: Our site went down because the certificate expired. How do we stop that happening again?

topics.title: Observability: logs, metrics, traces and alerting
topics.summary: Observability is how well you can understand what a system is doing from its outputs. The three main signals are logs (event records), metrics (numbers over time) and traces (a request's path across services). Alerting notifies people when signals cross thresholds that matter to users.
topics.why: You can't manage reliability you can't see. TPMs use dashboards for status, incident calls and planning.
concepts: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
topics.do_it: Sketch a dashboard for one service with the four golden signals and one business metric.
topics.prove: Write alert rules for that service: condition, severity, who is paged and the first action.
topics.interview: How would you know our service is unhealthy before customers tell us?

topics.title: SLA, SLO, SLI and error budgets
topics.summary: An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement of service, such as the share of successful requests. An SLO (service level objective) is the target for it, such as 99.9% per month. An SLA (service level agreement) is a contract with customers, usually with penalties. The error budget is the allowed unreliability: 100% minus the SLO.
topics.why: SLOs turn reliability into a shared, numeric agreement between product and engineering. Error budgets help decide when to ship features and when to fix reliability.
topics.do_it: Define two SLIs and SLOs for a product you know, and calculate the monthly error budget for each.
topics.prove: Write an error budget policy: what happens when 50%, 75% and 100% of the budget is used.
topics.interview: Engineering wants to pause features to fix reliability; product wants to ship. How do you decide?

topics.title: Incident management, RCA, MTTR and MTBF
topics.summary: Incident management is the process for detecting, responding to and learning from service disruptions. Roles such as incident commander and communications lead keep response organised. After the incident, a root cause analysis (RCA) or blameless postmortem finds contributing causes and actions. MTTR and MTBF measure recovery speed and failure frequency.
topics.why: TPMs often coordinate incident communication and own the follow-up actions. A calm, structured process shortens outages and builds trust.
topics.do_it: Read one public postmortem from a well-known company and identify the timeline, impact, contributing causes and action items.
topics.prove: Write an incident process for your team: severity definitions, roles, update cadence and postmortem template.
topics.interview: Tell me about a production incident you managed. What did you do and what changed afterwards?

topics.title: Disaster recovery and backups
topics.summary: Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan for restoring service after a major event such as a region outage, data corruption or ransomware. It is defined by RTO (how quickly service must be back) and RPO (how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable). Backups are one part; tested restores are what matter.
topics.why: Leaders ask 'what if the data centre goes down?' The TPM needs clear RTO and RPO commitments, costs and tested evidence.
concepts: DR strategies: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active
topics.do_it: For one product, agree an RTO and RPO with a business owner and map them to one of the four DR strategies.
topics.prove: Write a DR test plan: scenario, steps, success criteria, who takes part and how results are recorded.
topics.interview: What is the difference between RTO and RPO, and how do they affect cost?

topics.title: DevSecOps and security scanning
topics.summary: DevSecOps builds security into every stage of delivery instead of checking at the end. Automated scans in the pipeline cover code (SAST), dependencies (SCA), secrets, containers, infrastructure code and the running app (DAST), with findings routed to the teams that own them.
topics.why: Late security reviews delay releases and miss issues. Shifting checks left makes security part of normal delivery.
topics.do_it: List the security checks in your product's pipeline today and mark gaps against SAST, SCA, secret scanning, container scanning and DAST.
topics.prove: Write a vulnerability management policy: severity levels, fix timelines and exception process.
topics.interview: How do you make security part of delivery without slowing teams down?

topics.title: Monolith vs microservices vs serverless
topics.summary: A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit. Microservices split the system into small services that are deployed independently and talk over the network. Serverless runs code as functions or managed services that scale automatically, with no servers for you to manage.
topics.why: Architecture style decides team structure, release speed, cost and failure modes. TPMs are often in the room when teams debate splitting a monolith.
concepts: Monolith strengths: simple to build, test and deploy
Microservices: independent deploys, team autonomy, network complexity
Serverless: pay per use, scale to zero, cold starts, limits
Modular monolith as a middle path
Conway's law: systems mirror team structure
topics.do_it: Classify three products you know as monolith, microservices or serverless, and note one benefit and one pain each team probably feels.
topics.prove: Write a one-page recommendation for a 10-person startup choosing an architecture, with trade-offs.
topics.interview: When would you advise against microservices?

topics.title: High-level design (HLD)
topics.summary: A high-level design shows the main parts of a system and how they connect: clients, APIs, services, databases, caches, queues and third parties. It explains how requirements will be met without going into code. The C4 model offers a simple way to draw it at different zoom levels.
topics.why: HLD reviews are where big risks get caught cheaply. TPMs often facilitate them and must be able to read, question and summarise the design.
concepts: C4 levels: context, containers, components, code
topics.do_it: Draw a C4 context and container diagram for a food delivery app: users, mobile app, API, order service, database, payment provider, notifications.
topics.prove: Write a two-page HLD for one feature: requirements, diagram, data flow, key decisions, risks.
topics.interview: Walk me through how you'd design a URL shortener at a high level.

topics.title: Low-level design (LLD)
topics.summary: Low-level design zooms into one component: its modules, data models, API contracts, database tables, error handling and important algorithms. It is detailed enough for engineers to build from.
topics.why: TPMs don't write LLDs, but reading them reveals hidden scope, edge cases and dependencies that affect estimates and plans.
concepts: API contracts: endpoints, requests, responses, errors
topics.do_it: For an 'apply coupon at checkout' feature, list the tables, API endpoints and error cases you'd expect in its LLD.
topics.prove: Review an LLD (or ask Claude to draft one) and write five questions that would change the estimate.
topics.interview: How do you use design documents to improve estimates?

topics.title: Scalability: horizontal vs vertical
topics.summary: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load. Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger (more CPU, memory). Horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer. Databases scale with read replicas, caching, partitioning and sharding.
topics.why: Growth plans, sales events and launches all raise 'will it hold?' questions. TPMs need to understand the options and their cost and complexity.
topics.do_it: For a product expecting 10 times more users next year, list which parts would hit limits first and one scaling option for each.
topics.prove: Explain scaling options for your product to a business stakeholder in five sentences, including cost implications.
topics.interview: Our app slows down during sales. How would you approach scaling it?

topics.title: Availability, fault tolerance and circuit breakers
topics.summary: Availability is the share of time a system works for users. Fault tolerance means continuing to work when parts fail, through redundancy, failover, timeouts, retries and graceful degradation. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while so failures don't cascade.
topics.why: Every dependency eventually fails. Designs that expect failure keep customers served; TPMs should check these patterns exist before launch.
concepts: Redundancy and no single points of failure
topics.do_it: List the external dependencies of a product you know and, for each, what users would see if it went down.
topics.prove: Write a failure-mode table: dependency, failure, user impact, current mitigation, gap.
topics.interview: Our payment provider has intermittent outages. How should our system handle that?

topics.title: Latency, throughput and load testing
topics.summary: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests the system handles per second. Load testing simulates traffic to measure both and find limits. Tools include JMeter, k6, Gatling and Locust.
topics.why: Performance problems found in production are expensive and public. TPMs plan load tests before launches and read the results.
concepts: Test types: smoke, load, stress, spike, soak, breakpoint
topics.do_it: Write a load test plan for a checkout API: target requests per second, test types, pass criteria and environment.
topics.prove: Summarise a load test result (real or Claude-generated sample) for executives: capacity, headroom and risks.
topics.interview: How would you make sure our system can handle Diwali sale traffic?

topics.title: Caching strategies and invalidation
topics.summary: Caching keeps copies of data closer or faster to reach: in the browser, at a CDN, in an in-memory store such as Redis or Memcached, or inside the app. Strategies differ in when data is loaded and how stale copies are removed (invalidation).
topics.why: Caching is the cheapest big performance win and a common source of 'why do users see old data?' bugs. TPMs should understand both sides.
concepts: Cache layers: browser, CDN, application, database
topics.do_it: For a product page, decide what to cache at the CDN, what in Redis and what never, and the TTL for each.
topics.prove: Write a caching decision table for a feature with staleness tolerance agreed with product.
topics.interview: Users sometimes see an old price after we change it. What might be happening?

topics.title: Reading a real architecture: review exercise
topics.summary: An architecture review walks through a system's design to check it meets requirements for function, scale, reliability, security and cost. This exercise uses this learning hub's own architecture as the case study.
topics.why: Reviews are where TPMs add most value technically: asking the right questions and making risks visible. Practising on a system you know makes it concrete.
concepts: Review checklist: requirements, data, scale, failure, security, cost, operations
topics.do_it: Draw this learning hub's container diagram: browser, Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL, and where Docker Compose fits.
topics.prove: Write a one-page review of the learning hub: strengths, risks, and three recommendations to make it production-ready, with rough monthly cost.
topics.interview: You're asked to review an architecture you didn't design. How do you approach it?

topics.title: iOS vs Android: platforms and design guidelines
topics.summary: iOS (Apple) and Android (Google and many device makers) are the two mobile platforms. They differ in devices, update patterns, app stores, design guidelines (Apple's Human Interface Guidelines vs Google's Material Design) and user behaviour.
topics.why: Mobile programmes ship to both platforms with different rules, timelines and expectations. TPMs plan for those differences.
concepts: Market share varies by region (Android dominates India)
Device variety and OS version spread
Navigation patterns: back button, tab bars
topics.do_it: Compare the same app on an iPhone and an Android phone (or screenshots) and list five design differences.
topics.prove: Write a one-page platform strategy for an app launching in India: priority platform, minimum OS versions, and design approach.
topics.interview: Should we launch on iOS or Android first in India? Why?

topics.title: Native vs hybrid vs cross-platform
topics.summary: Native apps are built separately for each platform with their own languages (Swift for iOS, Kotlin or Java for Android). Cross-platform frameworks (Flutter with Dart, React Native with JavaScript) share most code across both. Hybrid apps wrap web content in a native shell.
topics.why: This choice shapes team size, cost, speed and app quality for years. TPMs often frame the decision for leadership.
concepts: Performance and access to device features
topics.do_it: For an app idea, score native, Flutter and React Native on speed to market, performance, team skills and long-term cost.
topics.prove: Write a decision memo recommending an approach, with trade-offs and risks.
topics.interview: How would you decide between native and cross-platform for a new app?

topics.title: Flutter vs React Native
topics.summary: Flutter (Google, Dart) and React Native (Meta, JavaScript/TypeScript) are the two leading cross-platform frameworks. Both share most code across iOS and Android and support hot reload; they differ in how they render UI, language and ecosystem.
topics.why: If your organisation goes cross-platform, this is the next decision. Knowing the trade-offs helps you challenge or support the recommendation.
concepts: Rendering: own engine vs native components
topics.do_it: Look at the official getting-started pages for both and note the setup steps and first-app experience.
topics.prove: Write a comparison table for your organisation's context and a recommendation.
topics.interview: Our web team knows React. Would you choose React Native or Flutter for our app?

topics.title: Mobile app architecture and auth flows
topics.summary: Mobile app architecture separates the app into layers: the UI layer (screens and state holders), an optional domain layer (business rules), and the data layer (repositories that talk to local storage and remote APIs). Authentication on mobile usually uses OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and short-lived tokens stored securely.
topics.why: Clean architecture makes apps testable and resilient to the OS killing them at any time. Auth design affects security and user friction.
topics.do_it: Sketch the layers for a 'view my orders' screen: screen, state holder, repository, local database, API.
topics.prove: Draw the login flow for a mobile app using OAuth with PKCE, including where tokens are stored and how refresh works.
topics.interview: How should a mobile app handle login and keep users signed in securely?

topics.title: Screens, navigation and app lifecycle
topics.summary: Each platform has its own building blocks for screens: activities and fragments on Android, view controllers on iOS, or composables and SwiftUI views in newer apps. Apps move through lifecycle states (created, foreground, background, killed), and navigation keeps a stack of screens the user can go back through.
topics.why: Many mobile bugs (lost form data, wrong screen after returning, duplicate actions) come from lifecycle and navigation. Knowing the terms helps triage.
topics.do_it: Open any app, fill half a form, switch to another app for a few minutes, then return. Note what was kept and what was lost.
topics.prove: Write test cases for lifecycle scenarios: rotation, backgrounding, low memory, phone call, notification tap.
topics.interview: Users lose what they typed when they switch apps. What could be wrong?

topics.title: Mobile state management
topics.summary: State is the data that drives what the screen shows: the logged-in user, cart items, a loading flag. State management is how an app stores, updates and shares that data between screens. Common approaches include Provider and Bloc in Flutter and Redux or similar stores in React Native.
topics.why: Messy state causes bugs like stale carts and screens out of sync. Teams spend a lot of time debating approaches; TPMs should understand what's at stake.
concepts: React Native: hooks, Context, Redux, Zustand
topics.do_it: For a shopping app, list which state is local to a screen and which is shared app-wide.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why the team wants to adopt a state management library, with the benefit in user terms.
topics.interview: The cart count in the header doesn't match the cart page. What kind of problem is this?

topics.title: Local storage and offline-first design
topics.summary: Mobile apps store data on the device in key-value stores, files, or local databases such as SQLite (often via Room on Android or Core Data on iOS) and Realm. Offline-first design treats the local database as the source of truth for the screen and syncs with the server in the background.
topics.why: Users lose connectivity in lifts, trains and rural areas. Offline-first apps feel faster and more reliable, which matters for Indian networks.
concepts: Local database as source of truth
topics.do_it: Put your phone in airplane mode and try three apps you use. Note which still show data and allow actions.
topics.prove: Write offline requirements for a field-sales app: what works offline, how sync happens and how conflicts are resolved.
topics.interview: Our field agents often lose network. How would you design the app for them?

topics.title: Background tasks and device features
topics.summary: Background tasks run when the app isn't on screen: syncing data, uploading photos, tracking location. Both platforms restrict them to save battery. Device features such as camera, gallery and GPS need permissions and careful handling.
topics.why: Features like 'upload in background' or 'track delivery' often fail because of OS limits. TPMs need to know what's realistically possible.
concepts: Location: precise vs approximate, foreground vs background
topics.do_it: List three features in an app idea that need background work or device features, and what OS limits might affect each.
topics.prove: Write requirements for a background photo upload feature, including what happens if the app is killed or the network drops.
topics.interview: Product wants live location tracking all day. What constraints should we discuss?

topics.title: Deep links and universal links
topics.summary: Deep links open a specific screen inside an app from a link, such as an order page from an email. Verified web links (Android App Links and iOS Universal Links) use normal https URLs that open the app if installed, or the website if not, after the domain proves it owns the app.
topics.why: Deep links power marketing campaigns, notifications, sharing and re-engagement. Broken links waste campaign spend and frustrate users.
concepts: Custom scheme links vs verified web links
topics.do_it: Tap a product link from a shopping app in a messaging app on your phone. Note whether it opens the app or the browser.
topics.prove: Write a deep link specification for three campaign links: URL pattern, target screen, fallback and analytics tags.
topics.interview: Marketing says links in their emails open the website instead of the app. What would you check?

topics.title: Push notifications: FCM and APNs
topics.summary: Push notifications are messages sent from a server to a user's device even when the app isn't open. Apple devices receive them through APNs (Apple Push Notification service); Android devices through Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), which can also send to iOS via APNs.
topics.why: Notifications drive engagement and important alerts, but overuse makes users turn them off. TPMs coordinate permissions, content, timing and measurement.
concepts: Permission prompts, especially on iOS and Android 13+
topics.do_it: Review the notifications you got this week. Classify each as transactional or marketing and note which you found useful.
topics.prove: Write a notification strategy: types, triggers, frequency caps, opt-in prompt timing and success metrics.
topics.interview: Our notification opt-in rate is low. What would you do?

topics.title: Biometrics, permissions and privacy
topics.summary: Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face) lets users unlock an app or confirm actions using the device's secure hardware; the app never sees the biometric data. Runtime permissions control access to sensitive data and hardware. Store privacy labels and data safety forms disclose what the app collects.
topics.why: Privacy and security are review blockers and trust drivers, especially for fintech and health apps. TPMs coordinate permissions, disclosures and security reviews.
concepts: App Store privacy labels and Play data safety
topics.do_it: Check the permissions of three apps on your phone. Mark any that seem unnecessary.
topics.prove: Write a permissions and privacy plan for a fintech app: each permission, why, when asked, and what's disclosed.
topics.interview: How would you add fingerprint login to our banking app safely?

topics.title: Payments, analytics and third-party SDKs
topics.summary: Most apps embed third-party SDKs: payment gateways (Razorpay, Stripe, PhonePe, UPI intents), analytics (Mixpanel, Firebase Analytics, Amplitude), crash reporting, maps and chat. Each adds features quickly but also size, risk, privacy duties and upgrade work.
topics.why: SDK choices affect revenue, data quality, store compliance and security. TPMs often own vendor evaluation and integration plans.
concepts: App store rules for digital goods (in-app purchase)
SDK evaluation: size, privacy, support, cost
topics.do_it: Write a tracking plan for a checkout flow: 6 to 8 events with names, properties and when they fire.
topics.prove: Create an SDK evaluation scorecard and use it to compare two payment or analytics options.
topics.interview: How would you choose and integrate an analytics SDK like Mixpanel?

topics.title: Builds, signing and provisioning
topics.summary: Mobile apps are packaged as APK or AAB files (Android) and IPA files (iOS). Every build must be cryptographically signed so devices and stores trust it. Android uses keystores and Play App Signing; iOS uses certificates and provisioning profiles that tie an app to devices and capabilities.
topics.why: Lost keys, expired certificates and wrong profiles block releases at the last minute. TPMs should know who owns them and when they expire.
concepts: Play App Signing and upload keys
topics.do_it: Find out where your team's signing keys and Apple certificates are stored, who has access and when they expire.
topics.prove: Write a release-readiness checklist covering signing, versioning, certificates and build automation.
topics.interview: The iOS release is blocked because of a provisioning error. What does that mean?

topics.title: Mobile testing and device fragmentation
topics.summary: Mobile testing combines unit, integration, UI and regression tests with manual testing on emulators (Android), simulators (iOS) and real devices. Device fragmentation means many screen sizes, OS versions, manufacturers and hardware levels must be covered.
topics.why: Mobile bugs reach users quickly and fixes take days through store review. A sensible device and test strategy prevents most of the pain.
concepts: Unit, integration, UI and regression tests
topics.do_it: Build a device matrix for an Indian consumer app: 6 to 8 devices covering low, mid and high-end Android plus two iPhones.
topics.prove: Write a mobile test strategy: automated layers, device matrix, manual scenarios, and release regression checklist.
topics.interview: How would you decide which devices to test on?

topics.title: Releases: TestFlight, Play Console, store review
topics.summary: Mobile releases go through store pipelines. On iOS, builds are uploaded to App Store Connect, tested via TestFlight and submitted for App Review. On Android, builds go to Play Console testing tracks (internal, closed, open) and then production, often as a staged rollout.
topics.why: Release timing on mobile depends on review and rollout, not just engineering. TPMs plan buffers, coordinate store listings and manage phased rollouts.
concepts: App Store Connect and TestFlight internal/external testers
App Review and common rejection reasons
topics.do_it: Map your app's release timeline from code freeze to 100% rollout, including review time buffers on both stores.
topics.prove: Write a mobile release runbook: steps, owners, checks, rollout percentages, halt criteria.
topics.interview: We need a fix in users' hands by Friday. How do you plan the mobile release?

topics.title: OTA updates and crash reporting
topics.summary: Over-the-air (OTA) updates let cross-platform apps (notably React Native with tools like Expo EAS Update) push JavaScript and asset changes directly to installed apps without a store release, within store rules. Crash reporting tools such as Firebase Crashlytics collect crashes from users' devices so teams can find and fix them.
topics.why: OTA updates shorten fix times and crash reporting tells you what's broken. Together they shape mobile incident response.
concepts: What OTA can and can't change
Channels, rollouts and rollbacks for updates
Crash reports, stack traces and symbol files
topics.do_it: Look at a crash dashboard (or Crashlytics demo screenshots) and identify the top crash, affected users and app versions.
topics.prove: Write a mobile incident playbook: crash threshold alerts, triage, OTA fix vs store hotfix, communication.
topics.interview: A new release is crashing for 3% of users. Walk me through your response.

topics.title: AI PM tools: ClickUp/Asana AI, Notion AI, ChatPRD, Motion, tl;dv
topics.summary: AI is now built into the tools PMs use daily: task tools (ClickUp, Asana) summarise and draft tasks; Notion AI drafts and queries documents; ChatPRD helps write product requirements; Motion schedules work automatically; meeting assistants such as tl;dv record, transcribe and summarise meetings. General assistants such as Claude cover much of the same ground.
topics.why: These tools can save hours a week, but only if chosen carefully and used with good inputs and checks. Your organisation's data rules also decide which you may use.
concepts: Categories: tasks, documents, PRDs, scheduling, meetings
What to automate vs keep human
topics.do_it: Pick one weekly task (status report, meeting notes or backlog grooming) and do it with an AI tool for two weeks. Track time spent and errors found.
topics.prove: Write a one-page AI toolkit for your team: chosen tools, what each is for, data rules and review steps.
topics.interview: Which AI tools do you use as a PM, and how do you make sure their output is reliable?

topics.title: Writing PRDs and technical specs with AI
topics.summary: A PRD (product requirements document) explains the problem, users, goals, scope, requirements and success measures. A technical spec explains how engineering will build it. AI can draft, structure and critique both, but the thinking and facts must come from you.
topics.why: Good PRDs prevent rework. AI makes a strong first draft fast and is an excellent reviewer that spots gaps, contradictions and missing edge cases.
concepts: Using AI as a critic, not just a writer
topics.do_it: Write a half-page problem statement for a feature, give it to Claude with your template, and ask for a PRD draft. Then ask Claude to critique it as a sceptical engineer.
topics.prove: Produce a complete PRD for one AI feature including success metrics, risks and an eval plan.
topics.interview: Walk me through how you write a PRD and how AI fits into your process.

topics.title: Engineering-ready user stories and Gherkin acceptance criteria
topics.summary: A user story describes a need from the user's side: 'As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]'. Acceptance criteria define when it's done. Gherkin writes criteria as Given (context), When (action), Then (outcome) scenarios that engineers and testers can use directly.
topics.why: Clear stories and criteria cut back-and-forth, make estimates more accurate and turn straight into tests.
concepts: Gherkin: Given, When, Then, And, But
topics.do_it: Write one user story for 'save card for faster checkout' with four Gherkin scenarios: happy path, expired card, network failure, user removes the card.
topics.prove: Take an epic from your backlog, split it into stories, and give each Gherkin acceptance criteria. Ask an engineer to rate how build-ready they are.
topics.interview: How do you write acceptance criteria that engineers and QA can actually use?

topics.title: SDLC, agile and sprint lifecycle with AI
topics.summary: The software development lifecycle (SDLC) runs from idea through requirements, design, build, test, release and operate. Agile approaches such as Scrum deliver in short iterations (sprints) with planning, daily standups, reviews and retrospectives. AI now helps at every step.
topics.why: You already know agile; the opportunity is applying AI to cut overhead and improve quality in each ceremony without losing the human conversations.
concepts: Product goal, sprint goal, definition of done
AI in planning, standups, reviews and retros
topics.do_it: For your next sprint, use AI for one ceremony: summarise the backlog before planning, or cluster retro comments into themes.
topics.prove: Write a 'sprint with AI' playbook: what AI does in each event and what stays human.
topics.interview: How have you used AI to improve your team's agile process?

topics.title: QA, UAT and release sign-off
topics.summary: QA (quality assurance) checks the product works as specified. UAT (user acceptance testing) checks it meets real users' or business owners' needs before release. Release sign-off is the formal agreement that a release is ready, based on evidence.
topics.why: TPMs often own the release decision process. Clear entry and exit criteria prevent both risky launches and endless delays.
concepts: AI features: eval results as sign-off evidence
topics.do_it: Write UAT scenarios for a feature from the business owner's point of view, separate from QA test cases.
topics.prove: Create a release sign-off checklist with exit criteria, including AI eval thresholds and known issues.
topics.interview: QA found three medium bugs the day before launch. How do you decide whether to ship?

topics.title: Problem framing and user journeys
topics.summary: Problem framing defines the right problem before solutions: who has it, what they're trying to do, what gets in the way and how we'll know it's solved. A user journey map visualises the steps a person takes to reach a goal, with thoughts, feelings and pain points, which reveals edge cases.
topics.why: Teams often build the wrong thing well. Framing and journey mapping keep AI features focused on real needs rather than 'add AI'.
topics.do_it: Map the journey of a customer raising a refund request in a product you know. Mark the three worst pain points.
