sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Estimate tokens per request in every AI business case.
Ask engineers to log input and output tokens per feature.
Test with real languages your users use, not only English.
Different providers tokenize differently: compare cost per completed task, not price per token.

p: Every AI business case needs token estimates. Build them from real samples: take ten typical inputs and outputs, count tokens with a tokenizer, and use averages. Add the system prompt, conversation history and retrieved context, which often exceed the user's message many times over.

For Indian-language products, test token counts and quality in each target language early. Higher token counts mean higher cost and less room in the context window, which can change your choice of model.

mis: A token is a word.
Tokens are often word pieces; one word may be several tokens.
Only the user's message is billed.
System prompts, history and context are all billed as input.
Token prices are comparable across providers.
Tokenizers differ, so compare cost per task.

gloss: Chunk of text a model processes.

quiz: Roughly how many tokens is 750 English words?
About 1,000.
Why may Hindi cost more?
It typically splits into more tokens per word.
Which is usually more expensive: input or output tokens?
Output tokens.
Name two hidden token consumers.
System prompts and conversation history (also RAG context, tool definitions).
Why compare cost per task instead of per token?
Tokenizers differ, so the same text costs different token counts.

p: The context window is everything the model can 'see' in one go: the system instructions, the conversation so far, any documents or tool results, and the answer it is writing. Measured in tokens, windows range from tens of thousands to around a million tokens in current frontier models. Anything not in the window does not exist for the model.

Models have no memory between separate requests. A chat 'remembers' only because the app resends the history each time. When history grows too long, apps drop or summarise older parts, which is why a long chat can 'forget' early details.

A 120-page contract is about 60,000 tokens. It fits in a large window, so you can send the whole thing and ask questions. But each question resends 60,000 tokens: slower and costlier. And models can pay less attention to details buried in the middle of very long inputs.
For one-off deep review, long context is great. For an assistant answering many questions across thousands of contracts, retrieval (RAG) is better: send only the relevant clauses.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Explain 'it forgot' issues as context limits and ask how history is managed (summaries, memory).
Decide long-context vs retrieval per use case using cost per question.
For agents, ask how context is compacted during long tasks.

p: When users complain that an assistant 'forgot' something, check how the app manages history: is it sending full history, a sliding window, or summaries? For long-running agent tasks, ask how context is compacted and what gets kept. These design choices directly shape user experience.

For document-heavy features, decide per use case between stuffing documents into context and retrieval. A useful rule: if users ask many questions across many documents, use retrieval; if they deeply analyse one document at a time, long context can be simpler.

mis: A bigger context window means the model remembers past chats.
Each request is independent; memory requires the app to store and resend information.
If it fits in the window, the model will use it well.
Quality can drop for details buried in very long inputs.
Context windows only limit input.
Output shares the same budget.

gloss: Max tokens a model considers at once.

quiz: Does an LLM remember previous API calls?
No, apps resend history each time.
Why might a long chat forget early details?
Older history is truncated or summarised to fit the window.
Does the answer count toward the window?
Yes.
When is RAG better than long context?
Many questions across a large document set.
One risk with very long inputs?
Details in the middle may get less attention.

p: A prompt is a brief to a very capable colleague who has zero context about you, your project or your audience. The quality of the output mostly reflects the quality of the brief. The good news for you: writing clear briefs is a PM skill you already have.

steps: Role and goal
What you want and why it matters. 'Draft a status update for the steering committee so they can decide whether to approve extra budget.'
Context
Audience, background, constraints. Paste the relevant notes or data.
Instructions
Specific asks, in order. Say what to do rather than only what to avoid.
Examples
One to five examples of the desired output: the most reliable way to control format and tone.
Output format
Length, structure, headings, table, JSON.
Criteria
How you'll judge it. 'Under 200 words, risks first, plain English.'

table: Write a status update for my project.

You're helping me write a weekly status update for executives who read it in 2 minutes. Use BLUF: first line is overall status (green/amber/red) and why. Then 3 bullets: progress, risks with owner, decisions needed. Plain English, under 150 words. Notes: [paste].
p: Run it three times, score each output against your criteria, tweak, and keep the version that scores best. That's prompt engineering: brief, test, improve.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Build a personal prompt library for recurring tasks (status, RAID log, PRD review, stakeholder email).
For product prompts, insist on written success criteria and a test set before tuning.
Version prompts like code; small wording changes alter behaviour.

p: Start a prompt library this week: status reports, RAID log updates, meeting summaries, stakeholder emails, PRD reviews, estimation challenges. For each, keep the prompt, an example input, a good output and notes on what improved it. That library becomes your personal productivity system and, later, a set of team templates.

For prompts inside products, push for discipline: written success criteria, a test set of realistic inputs, scored comparisons before and after changes, and version history. Without these, prompt changes become opinion battles and silent regressions.

mis: Prompt engineering is about magic words.
It's about clear goals, context, examples and testing.
Longer prompts are always better.
Clarity matters more than length; irrelevant detail can distract.
A prompt that worked once is done.
It should be tested across many inputs and re-tested when models change.

gloss: Instructions and context given to a model.
Standing instructions for a conversation or app.

quiz: Most reliable way to control output format?
Give examples of the desired output.
Why state the audience?
It changes tone, depth and length appropriately.
Why test several runs?
Outputs vary; one good run may be luck.
Rewrite 'Don't be long'.
'Keep it under 150 words.'
What two things should exist before tuning a product prompt?
Clear success criteria and a test set.

p: Basic prompting gets good one-off answers. Advanced techniques make outputs reliable and repeatable enough to run inside products and automations.

steps: System prompts and roles
Standing instructions that set behaviour, tone and boundaries for every turn, e.g. 'You are a support assistant for Acme payroll. Only answer from the provided policy.'
Structure with XML tags
Separate parts clearly: <notes>…</notes>, <instructions>…</instructions>. Models handle clearly delimited inputs better, and you can refer to sections by name.
Let it think
Ask the model to reason step by step, or use models with built-in extended thinking, for analysis, maths and multi-step decisions.
Prompt chaining
Split a complex job into steps where each output feeds the next; each step is easier to test and fix.
Structured output
Ask for JSON matching a schema so software can use the result; many APIs can enforce the schema.
Templates with variables
Reusable prompts with placeholders like {{meeting_notes}}, stored and versioned.

sections.h: Worked example: notes to user stories
p: Step 1 output: a numbered list of requirements with open questions. Step 2 turns each into 'As a…, I want…, so that…'. Step 3 adds acceptance criteria in Gherkin. If stories are weak, you can see whether extraction or writing failed, and fix just that step.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask how product prompts are versioned, reviewed and tested.
Prefer chains of simple steps over one complex prompt for anything important.
Store your best personal chains as reusable templates or Claude skills.

p: Once you have a reliable chain for a recurring task, package it: as a saved template, a Claude Project with instructions and reference files, or a skill. That turns a clever prompt into a repeatable workflow you and your team can reuse.

In product reviews, ask engineering how prompts are structured: is there a system prompt with clear rules, are user inputs separated from instructions (which also helps against prompt injection), is output validated against a schema? These questions signal real technical understanding.

mis: One master prompt can handle everything.
Complex tasks are more reliable as chains of focused steps.
Asking the model to think step by step always helps.
It helps for reasoning tasks but adds cost and latency to simple ones.
Structured output guarantees correct data.
It guarantees format, not truth; validate content too.

quiz: Why use XML tags?
To clearly separate inputs and instructions so the model doesn't mix them up.
Advantage of chaining?
Each step is simpler and can be tested and fixed separately.
When do you need structured output?
When software consumes the result.
What belongs in a system prompt?
Persistent role, rules, tone and boundaries.
How should product prompts be managed?
Versioned, reviewed and tested like code.

p: A hallucination is an output that sounds right but is false or unsupported: a made-up statistic, a non-existent policy clause, a fake citation. It happens because a model generates the most plausible continuation, not a verified fact. When it lacks the information, a plausible-sounding answer is still the most likely text.

steps: Allow 'I don't know'
Explicitly permit and encourage the model to say when information isn't available. This alone reduces false answers a lot.
Ground in sources
Provide the documents and instruct: answer only from these.
Quote first
For long documents, ask the model to extract exact quotes first, then answer from the quotes.
Require citations
Each claim must point to a source; claims without one are removed.
Verify
Run the same prompt several times (inconsistency signals hallucination), or have a second step check claims against sources.
Human review
For high-stakes outputs (legal, medical, financial), a person approves before use.

p: Without controls, a customer asks about refunds for damaged goods and the bot invents a 60-day window. The real policy is 30 days. That's a promise the company may have to honour.

With controls: the bot retrieves the refund policy, answers only from it, cites section 3.2, and if the question isn't covered says 'I can't find that in our policy; let me connect you to an agent'. A weekly sample of conversations is reviewed for accuracy.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Never promise 'zero hallucinations'; promise measured rates and controls.
Define the fallback behaviour when the answer isn't known.
Track groundedness and user-reported errors as product metrics.

p: Hallucination risk is the top concern in AI steering committees. Bring a structured answer: risk level by use case, controls in place (grounding, citations, refusal when unknown, human review), how you measure (sampled audits, automated groundedness scoring, user feedback) and the escalation path when errors are found.

Design the 'I don't know' experience deliberately. A good fallback (hand off to a human, link to the source, ask a clarifying question) keeps trust high. A bot that always answers confidently loses trust after the first visible mistake.

mis: Newer models don't hallucinate.
They hallucinate less but still do.
Hallucinations are random bugs that can be fully fixed.
They're inherent to how models generate text; you manage the rate.
Citations prove correctness.
Citations can be wrong or misread; check them.

gloss: Plausible but false or unsupported output.
Comparing several runs to detect inconsistency.
What happens when the AI can't answer.

quiz: Why do hallucinations happen?
Models generate plausible text, not verified facts.
Simplest high-impact mitigation?
Explicitly allow the model to say it doesn't know.
What does 'quote first' do?
Forces answers to rest on exact text from the source.
How can multiple runs help?
Inconsistent answers flag likely hallucinations.
What should you promise legal instead of 'no hallucinations'?
Measured error rates with grounding, citations, fallbacks and human review where needed.

p: Grounding means making the model answer from specific trusted sources (your documents, a database, live search results) instead of from its general training memory. It turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one, and ideally the student also shows which page they used.

table: Your files via RAG or upload

p: NotebookLM only answers from the sources you upload and shows numbered citations you can click to see the exact passage. Upload three project documents and ask ten questions; check each citation. You'll notice it says when something isn't in the sources, and that answer quality depends on what you uploaded. That's grounding in action.

Faithfulness or groundedness is the share of claims in an answer that are supported by the provided sources. Evaluation tools can score it automatically by checking each claim against the retrieved text. It's distinct from correctness: an answer can be faithful to an outdated document and still be wrong, which is why source quality matters.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Make 'answers must cite approved sources' a requirement for enterprise assistants.
Assign owners for source documents; grounding is only as good as the sources.
Track groundedness alongside user satisfaction.

p: For enterprise assistants, grounding is also a governance question: which sources are approved, who owns each, how often are they reviewed, and how are outdated documents removed? A content governance plan is often the missing piece in AI assistant projects.
When demoing grounded assistants to stakeholders, show the citations and click through them. It builds trust faster than any accuracy statistic, and shows exactly where quality depends on content.

mis: Grounding guarantees accuracy.
It ties answers to sources; the sources must be right.
Uploading documents means the model learned them.
It reads them in context; nothing is permanently learned.
Search grounding is always current.
It depends on what the search returns and how it's filtered.

gloss: Degree to which claims are supported by sources.
Link from a claim to its source.

quiz: Grounding analogy?
An open-book exam with page references.
Can a grounded answer still be wrong?
Yes, if the source is outdated or wrong.
What does faithfulness measure?
How much of the answer is supported by the given sources.
Example of tool grounding?
Using a calculator or code tool for exact maths.
Why do source documents need owners?
Someone must keep them correct and current.

p: An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector), often hundreds or thousands long, so that texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. 'Cheap flights to Goa' and 'low-cost airfare to Goa' share few words but land close together. 'Python programming' and 'python snake' land far apart despite sharing a word.

steps: Embed content
Run each document chunk through an embedding model; store the vectors.
Embed the query
Turn the user's question into a vector with the same model.
Compare
Measure closeness, usually cosine similarity. Closest vectors = most similar meaning.
Return results
The best matches feed search results, RAG, recommendations or duplicate detection.

p: Imagine a map with only two dimensions: one for 'royalty' and one for 'fruitiness'. King and queen sit together high on royalty; apple and banana sit together high on fruitiness. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions capturing many aspects of meaning at once, which can't be named so neatly, but the principle is the same: nearness means similarity.

table: Legal, medical or code text may need specialised models
More dimensions can mean better quality but more storage

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Treat the embedding model as an architectural decision: changing it later means re-processing all documents.
Test candidate models on real queries from your users.
Budget for re-embedding when documents or models change.

p: Embedding choices are rarely discussed by stakeholders but have long-term consequences. In design reviews ask: which embedding model, tested on what queries, in which languages, and what's the plan if we switch? Re-embedding a large corpus costs time and money and needs a migration plan.

Embeddings power more than RAG: duplicate ticket detection, similar-case recommendations, clustering customer feedback into themes. Once a team has embeddings, these quick wins become cheap, which is a useful roadmap insight.

mis: Embeddings store the text.
They store numbers representing meaning; the text is stored separately.
Any embedding model works for any language.
Quality varies a lot by language and domain.
Embeddings understand exact codes.
They're weak on exact identifiers; add keyword search.

gloss: Measure of how aligned two vectors are.

quiz: Why do 'cheap flights' and 'low-cost airfare' match?
Their embeddings are close because their meanings are similar.
What must be the same for query and documents?
The embedding model.
Cost of switching embedding models?
Re-embedding every document.
Name two uses of embeddings.
Semantic search and recommendations (also RAG, duplicate detection).
What does cosine similarity measure?
How similar two vectors' directions are.

p: Once you have millions of embeddings, you need a fast way to find the ones nearest a query. A vector database stores vectors with their original text and metadata, and uses approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes to search millions in milliseconds, trading a tiny bit of accuracy for huge speed.

steps: Metadata filtering
Search only documents from 2025, or only this customer's documents.
Access control
Ensure users only retrieve what they're allowed to see.
Hybrid search
Combine keyword and vector search.
Updates and deletes
Keep the index in sync when documents change.
Backup and scaling
Operational maturity for production.

p: For an internal knowledge base of 10,000 documents (maybe 200,000 chunks) at a company already running PostgreSQL, pgvector is often the pragmatic choice: no new system, existing backups and access control, good enough performance at that scale.
At hundreds of millions of vectors, heavy traffic, or with no database team, a managed vector database becomes attractive.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask 'can our existing database do this?' before adding a new system.
Make permission filtering a launch requirement for enterprise data.
Include re-indexing and deletion (e.g. data deletion requests) in the design.

p: Vector database vendor evaluations should include: performance at your scale, metadata filtering, access-control support, hybrid search, operational burden, cost at projected volume, data residency and exit path. Run a small proof of concept with real data instead of relying on benchmarks.

Deletion is a frequently missed requirement. When a document is removed, or a customer requests data deletion, its chunks and embeddings must be removed too. Ask how deletes propagate through the pipeline.

mis: You must have a dedicated vector database for RAG.
Existing databases with vector support often suffice.
Vector search returns exact matches.
It returns approximately nearest results.
Vector databases handle permissions automatically.
You must design permission filtering.

gloss: Extra fields like date, owner, permissions.

quiz: What does ANN trade?
A little accuracy for much faster search.
Is FAISS a database?
No, it's a library.
When is pgvector a good choice?
When you already run PostgreSQL at moderate scale.
Why is metadata filtering important?
To limit results by date, customer or permissions.
Enterprise must-have for vector search?
Access control on retrieval.

p: Keyword (lexical) search finds documents containing the exact words you typed; BM25 is the standard ranking method. Semantic search finds documents with similar meaning using embeddings. Each fails where the other shines.

Hybrid search runs both and merges the ranked lists (commonly with reciprocal rank fusion). Query 'refund policy for SKU-4471': keyword search nails the product code; semantic search finds 'returns and exchanges' sections that never use the word refund. Together they return both. Many production RAG systems add a reranker afterwards to order the combined results.

sections.h: Worked example: 'it can't find documents I know exist'
steps: Check the query type
Is it an exact code or name? Pure semantic search may miss it: add keyword search.
Check indexing
Was the document actually ingested and chunked correctly?
Check filters
Are permissions or date filters excluding it?
Check chunking
Is the answer split across chunks?
Measure
Build a set of queries with known correct documents and track how often they're found (recall@k).

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Default to asking for hybrid search in enterprise search and RAG.
Collect real failed queries from users as test cases.
Treat search quality as measurable, not anecdotal.

p: Collect failed searches from real users: those are your best test cases. Each week, review a sample of queries with poor results, categorise them (exact code missed, synonym missed, document missing, permission issue), and prioritise fixes by category.
When vendors claim 'semantic search', ask whether they support hybrid search and reranking, and how they handle exact identifiers. It's a quick way to separate mature products from demos.

mis: Semantic search makes keyword search obsolete.
They complement each other.
Search quality is subjective.
It can be measured with test queries and expected results.
More results means better recall for users.
Too many results bury the right one.

gloss: Model that re-orders results by relevance.

quiz: Why might semantic search miss 'SKU-4471'?
Embeddings capture meaning, not exact identifiers.
What is hybrid search?
Combining keyword and semantic search results.
Where is keyword search weak?
Synonyms and paraphrasing.
First check when a known document isn't found?
Whether it was indexed, and whether the query needs exact matching.
How do you make search quality measurable?
A test set of queries with known correct documents.

p: There are three main ways to make a general model work for your use case. Prompting changes the instructions. RAG changes what knowledge the model sees at question time. Fine-tuning changes the model itself by further training it on your examples. They solve different problems, and most teams use the first two long before the third.

table: Model doesn't follow the task well
Consistent style, format or narrow skill at scale
Classify 1M tickets in our taxonomy cheaply

steps: Full fine-tuning
Updates all weights. Most powerful, most expensive.
LoRA
Trains small add-on matrices instead of all weights: far cheaper, and you can swap adapters.
QLoRA
LoRA on a compressed (quantised) model, so it fits on smaller GPUs.
Hosted fine-tuning
Providers let you upload examples and fine-tune via API without managing GPUs.

p: An engineer proposes fine-tuning a model on the company wiki so it 'knows everything'. Problems: the wiki changes weekly, so the model goes stale; the model may blend facts and still hallucinate; you can't easily cite sources or enforce permissions; and every update means retraining.
Better: RAG over the wiki with citations and permission filtering. If answers then need a specific tone or format that prompting can't deliver, consider a small fine-tune on top.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask 'is this a knowledge gap or a behaviour gap?' in every adaptation discussion.
Require a prompting + RAG baseline with evaluation before approving fine-tuning.
Count the full cost of fine-tuning: data preparation, training, evaluation, hosting and retraining.

p: Use a one-page decision record whenever fine-tuning is proposed: problem statement, knowledge vs behaviour gap, baseline results with prompting and RAG, expected improvement, data available, total cost (including retraining), and how success will be measured. This keeps decisions evidence-based.

Fine-tuning has a valid place: high-volume classification or extraction where a small fine-tuned model replaces a large general one, cutting cost and latency. Recognise those cases instead of rejecting fine-tuning outright.

mis: Fine-tuning teaches the model new facts reliably.
It's better at teaching behaviour and format; facts are better served by retrieval.
Fine-tuning is a one-time effort.
Data, models and requirements change, so it needs maintenance.
You need millions of examples.
Some tasks improve with hundreds to a few thousand quality examples.

gloss: Further training a model on specific examples.
Small trained add-on to a base model.

quiz: Best lever for frequently changing private knowledge?
RAG.
When does fine-tuning make sense?
Consistent behaviour, format or narrow skill at scale that prompting can't achieve.
What does LoRA change?
Small add-on parameters instead of all weights.
Why is fine-tuning on a wiki weak?
Goes stale, can't cite or enforce permissions, still hallucinates.
What should precede approving fine-tuning?
A prompting + RAG baseline with evaluation results.

p: Classical machine learning learns patterns from data to make predictions, and it still powers fraud detection, demand forecasting, recommendations and churn prediction. For narrow, repetitive, high-volume tasks, a classic model can be cheaper, faster and more accurate than an LLM.

sections.h: How a supervised model is built
steps: Collect labelled data
Thousands of past tickets with the team that resolved them.
Split
Training data (learn), validation (tune), test (final honest score).
Train
Algorithms like logistic regression, decision trees or random forests learn the patterns.
Evaluate
Accuracy, precision, recall on the test set.
Deploy and monitor
Watch for drift: the world changes and accuracy decays.

table: Often better on a stable taxonomy
p: A common path: start with an LLM to launch fast and collect labelled data, then train a classifier once volume and data justify it.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask 'do we need generation, or just a prediction?' before choosing an LLM.
Check whether labelled historical data exists; it's often the deciding factor.
Plan monitoring for drift on any model in production.

p: When a team jumps to an LLM for a prediction task (churn risk, fraud flags, ticket routing), ask about existing data science capabilities and labelled data. A mature data science team might deliver a cheaper, more accurate classic model; the LLM might be best as a quick start while data is collected.
Model monitoring applies to classic ML and LLMs alike. Ask how accuracy is tracked after launch and what triggers retraining. Drift is a slow, silent failure.

mis: AI and machine learning mean LLMs.
LLMs are one branch of a much broader field.
More data always beats better data.
Label quality often matters more than volume.
Unsupervised means no human involvement.
Humans still interpret and validate results.

gloss: Model accuracy decaying as data changes.

quiz: Predicting delivery time is which task?
Regression.
Customer segmentation without labels?
Clustering (unsupervised).
Why keep a separate test set?
For an honest measure of performance on unseen data.
When might a classifier beat an LLM?
High-volume, stable, narrow tasks with labelled data.
What is drift?
Accuracy decaying as real-world data changes.

p: A neural network is layers of simple units connected by weights. Each unit takes numbers in, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, and passes the result on through an activation function. Stack many layers and the network can represent very complex patterns: recognising faces, translating languages, predicting the next word. 'Deep learning' just means many layers.

steps: Guess
Feed in an example; the network produces an output.
Measure the error
A loss function scores how wrong the guess was.
Assign blame
Backpropagation works out how much each weight contributed to the error.
Adjust
Gradient descent nudges every weight slightly to reduce the error.
Repeat
Millions or billions of times across the training data.

p: Imagine a sound engineer with a desk of a billion dials, trying to make every song sound right. After each song, a meter shows how far off it was, and an assistant tells them which way to nudge each dial. After enough songs, the dials settle into a configuration that works for most music. Training is that, with maths doing the nudging.

sections.h: Why it matters to a TPM
table: Data quality and quantity drive quality
Retraining is a project, not a button

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Use the intuition to explain AI cost and 'black box' concerns to stakeholders.
Ask about training data quality before trusting any custom model.
No maths required; focus on consequences.

p: Executives sometimes ask why AI can't explain its decisions. The honest, simple answer: the knowledge is spread across billions of learned numbers, not written rules. Explainability tools and design choices (citations, showing sources, simple models where explanations are legally required) help.

When teams talk about training or fine-tuning, the dials analogy helps you ask about data: where do the examples come from, how are they labelled, how is quality checked? Training data quality is the biggest driver of model quality.

mis: Neural networks work like the human brain.
They're loosely inspired by neurons but work very differently.
Training happens once.
Models are retrained or fine-tuned as needs change.
Bigger networks always generalise better.
Without good data, bigger models can just memorise.

gloss: Computing each weight's contribution to error.

quiz: What does 'deep' mean in deep learning?
Many layers.
What does the loss function do?
Measures how wrong the output is.
Role of backpropagation?
Works out how each weight contributed to the error.
Why are neural networks hard to explain?
Knowledge is spread across billions of weights.
Why does data quality matter so much?
The network learns whatever patterns are in the examples.

p: Traditional software costs little per extra user. AI features cost money on every request, priced per token, and usage grows in ways that are easy to underestimate: longer conversations, more documents in context, agents that call the model many times per task. A feature that costs a few rupees in a demo can cost lakhs a month at scale.

steps: Per request
(input tokens × input price) + (output tokens × output price), with prices quoted per million tokens.
Per user per month
Cost per request × requests per user per day × 30.
Total
× number of active users.
Multipliers
Conversation history, RAG context, retries, agent loops, reasoning tokens.

table: $3 per million input, $15 per million output
p: Per request: 3,000 × $3/1M = $0.009, plus 500 × $15/1M = $0.0075, total ≈ $0.0165. Per user per month: × 10 × 30 ≈ $4.95. For 10,000 users ≈ $49,500 a month. Switching to a smaller model priced 3–5× lower, caching the repeated prompt, or trimming context can cut this dramatically. Always use the provider's current price list; prices change often.

table: Repeated prompt prefix billed at a fraction of normal price
Better perceived speed (time to first token)

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Put a token cost model in every AI business case, with low/expected/high scenarios.
Ask for per-feature token and cost dashboards from day one.
Set spending limits and alerts at the provider and in the app.

p: Build a reusable AI cost model spreadsheet: inputs for users, requests per user, tokens in and out, model prices, cache hit rate and batch share; outputs for monthly cost per scenario. Bring it to every AI initiative's business case and update it with real usage after launch.

Ask for cost observability from day one: tokens and cost per feature, per customer and per request type. It's how you catch runaway agents, unexpectedly long prompts or a single customer driving most of the spend.

mis: AI cost is mostly the model price.
Context size, call volume and agent loops often matter more.
Prices only go down.
Prices change both ways, and new models can cost more.
Latency is all network.
Model size and output length dominate.

gloss: Discounted reuse of repeated prompt content.

quiz: What drives per-request cost?
Input and output tokens times their prices.
Name three cost levers.
Smaller models, prompt caching, trimming context (also batch, output limits).
Why do agents cost more?
They call the model many times per task.
What improves perceived speed most?
Streaming the response.
Why use scenarios in cost models?
Usage is uncertain; ranges show risk.

p: When your product 'uses AI', a model is running on GPUs somewhere. Most products don't host models themselves; they call a provider's API. The choice of where the model runs affects data privacy, cost, speed, reliability and lock-in.

table: Best models, no ops, fast to start
Data leaves your environment (under contract), vendor dependence
AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure AI
Inside your cloud account, enterprise controls, regional hosting, consolidated billing
Model availability and features can lag direct APIs
Llama, Gemma, Qwen on your GPUs
GPU cost, ops skills, usually weaker than frontier models

p: Your backend should sit in the middle: it holds the API key securely, adds context, enforces permissions, logs usage, and can switch providers. Never call model APIs directly from a browser or mobile app with your key.

A bank asks where their data goes. A good answer covers: which provider and region processes the data; whether data is stored or used for training (enterprise API terms usually say no training and limited retention); encryption in transit and at rest; logging and who can access logs; and options like running through their preferred cloud region. Have this written up before the question comes.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Create a one-page AI data-flow and data-handling summary for security reviews.
Design for multiple models behind your own backend to reduce lock-in.
Track provider uptime and have a fallback model for critical features.

p: Prepare an AI data-handling summary before customers ask: which providers and models, regions, retention, training use, encryption, subprocessors, logging and human access. Security and legal teams will thank you, and sales cycles speed up.

Architect for change: route every model call through your own service layer, so you can switch models for cost or quality, add a fallback during outages, and log consistently. Providers change models and prices frequently; your product shouldn't be hard-wired to one.

mis: Using an API means our data trains their models.
Enterprise API terms typically exclude training; check the specific agreement.
Self-hosting is always cheaper.
GPU and operational costs often exceed API costs at moderate volume.
Cloud platforms always have the newest models first.
Availability and features can differ from direct APIs.

gloss: Running a model to produce output.
Model accessed directly from its maker.
Models offered inside a cloud provider.
Where data is processed and stored.
Alternative used if the primary fails.

quiz: Why route AI calls through your backend?
To protect keys, add context, enforce permissions, log and switch providers.
One advantage of cloud platforms like Bedrock?
Enterprise controls and staying inside your cloud account and region.
Main cost of self-hosting?
GPU infrastructure and operational skills.
What should an AI data-handling summary cover?
Provider, region, retention, training use, encryption, access.
How do you reduce vendor lock-in?
Abstract model calls behind your backend and support multiple models.

sections.h: Four ways to work with Claude
table: A workspace with its own files, instructions and chat history
Ongoing work: a programme, a product area, your learning
A page, document or small app produced in the conversation
Something to keep, share or click: a dashboard, a one-pager, a prototype
An agent that works inside a codebase
Real changes to software: reading files, running commands, editing code
p: The same model sits behind all four. What changes is what Claude can see and what it is allowed to do. In a chat it sees only the conversation. In a Project it also sees the files and instructions you added. In Claude Code it can open any file in the repository and, with your permission, run commands and change things.

A Project bundles knowledge (uploaded documents) with instructions (how Claude should behave in every chat inside it). Upload the programme charter, architecture notes and last quarter's decisions, add an instruction such as 'Answer as our TPM; flag risks first', and every new chat starts informed.

When the knowledge gets large, Claude retrieves the relevant parts rather than reading everything each time (the RAG idea from the AI Fundamentals lesson). Good file names and clean documents improve what it finds.

When the output is something you'll come back to, ask for it as an artifact: a status page, a decision log, a calculator, a clickable mock-up. Artifacts can be revised in place and shared by link. The first version of this learning hub was an artifact, built entirely by describing what was needed.

sections.flowLabel: Claude Code loop: you describe, it explores, plans, acts and checks, you review
p: Claude Code repeats a loop: gather context, take an action, check the result, decide the next step. Plan mode lets it explore and propose without changing anything, which is the safest way to start any task. Permission prompts ask before risky actions such as running commands, and a CLAUDE.md file in the repository gives it the project's rules every time.

sections.h: Worked example: how this hub was built
steps: Plan in chat
Agree the scope, stack and structure in plain English before any code
Prototype as an artifact
A single-page dashboard to test the idea with real content
Move to a repository
Claude Code generates the FastAPI back end, Next.js front end and tests
Let CI judge
GitHub Actions runs the tests on every push; red means stop
Iterate in small steps
One feature per change, each explained in plain English

p: Use Projects to give yourself a programme memory: charter, architecture, decision log and stakeholder map in one place, with instructions like 'flag risks before answering'. Before any steering meeting, ask the Project for open decisions and contradictions between documents.

When a team starts using Claude Code, agree three norms upfront: start in plan mode, one change per pull request, and CI must be green before merge. These turn a powerful tool into a predictable one, and they map directly onto the controls you already run.

mis: Claude Code just writes code faster.
It also explores, runs commands and checks results in a loop; the bigger win is that non-engineers can drive real changes safely.
Artifacts are only for demos.
Many are durable working tools: trackers, calculators and dashboards that people keep using.
A Project means Claude reads every file every time.
For large knowledge it retrieves the relevant parts, so clear, well-named documents matter.

gloss: Files attached to a Project that Claude can draw on in every chat
Standing guidance applied to every chat in the Project
A standalone output (page, document, app) produced by Claude
Able to take actions in a loop towards a goal, not just answer
Claude Code explores and proposes without editing
A file Claude Code reads at the start of each session

quiz: You need Claude to remember your programme's architecture across many chats. Which mode?
A Project: add the architecture docs as knowledge and set instructions.
What's the safest first step when asking Claude Code to change a codebase?
Use plan mode so it explores and proposes before editing anything.
Why build a quick artifact before a full app?
To test the idea and content cheaply before investing in a real codebase.
What makes Claude Code different from chat?
It can read the whole repository, run commands and edit files in a loop, with your permission.

p: AI-generated code is usually reasonable and occasionally wrong in ways that look right. Experienced engineers catch some of those mistakes by reading; you mostly can't, yet. So you rely on what engineering teams rely on anyway: small changes, automatic checks, save points and independent review.
Think of it like approving a supplier's work. You don't inspect every weld; you insist on test certificates, a sign-off process and the ability to roll back.

steps: Plan before building
Ask for a plan in plain English: which files change, what could break. Approve or correct it.
One small change at a time
A change you can describe in one sentence is a change you can check.
Commit after every working step
A commit is a save point. If the next step goes wrong you can return to it.
Let tests and CI decide
Ask for a test with every behaviour change. Never merge on a red CI run.
Ask what could go wrong
Have Claude list risks, edge cases and anything it is unsure about.
Get a second opinion
A fresh session, a different tool or a human engineer reviews before real users see it.

bullets: API keys, passwords and tokens go in a .env file that .gitignore excludes, never in code, screenshots or chat.
Commit a .env.example with the names but not the values.
If a secret is ever committed, treat it as leaked: rotate it, even if you delete the commit.
Turn on GitHub secret scanning and push protection where available.
Don't paste customer personal data into AI tools your company hasn't approved.

p: AI tools sometimes suggest a library that doesn't exist or has a name close to a popular one; attackers register such names. Before adding a dependency, check it is real, widely used and maintained.

If your product itself uses an LLM, a second set of risks applies, such as prompt injection, sensitive data disclosure and excessive agency. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is the standard checklist; you'll study it in Phase 4.
Before you merge anything an AI wrote, ask three questions: what changed, what could break, and which test proves it works? If nobody, human or AI, can answer the third, the change isn't finished.

Agree a 'two keys' rule for anything touching auth, payments or personal data: an engineer reviews it even if everything else is AI-driven. Being explicit about where human review is mandatory is what makes AI-assisted delivery acceptable to security and leadership.

mis: If it runs, it's correct.
Code can run and still be wrong, insecure or fragile; tests and review catch what a quick click-through can't.
Deleting a leaked key from the code fixes the leak.
It stays in Git history and may already be copied; rotate it.
Non-coders can't review code.
You can review intent, scope, tests and risk, which is where many serious problems show up.

gloss: A saved snapshot of changes with a message
Continuous integration: checks that run automatically on every push
Any credential that grants access: keys, passwords, tokens
Replace a credential with a new one and disable the old
Blocks a push that contains a detected secret
The exact lines added and removed by a change

quiz: You accidentally committed an API key and deleted it in the next commit. Are you safe?
No. It remains in Git history; rotate the key immediately.
Why commit after every working step?
Each commit is a save point you can return to if the next change breaks something.
CI is red but the app looks fine locally. Merge?
No. Find out why it fails; red means a check that should pass doesn't.
What should you check before adding a library the AI suggested?
That it exists, is widely used, maintained and is the package you think it is.

table: Predicts the next lines as you type

Review the diff, approve commands, accept or reject
p: Cursor is a fork of VS Code, so it looks like the editor many engineers already know, with AI added at each level. VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Windsurf and others offer similar tiers; the concepts transfer.

The AI answers well only about what it can see. In Cursor you add context by @-mentioning files, folders, documentation or the web. Cursor also indexes the codebase so the Agent can search by meaning, not only by exact words.
Files listed in .gitignore or a .cursorignore are left out of the index. That keeps searches accurate and keeps generated or sensitive files out of view.

sections.h: Rules: team standards for the AI
p: Cursor reads rules from the .cursor/rules folder in the project, from your personal settings, from team settings and from an AGENTS.md file. Older projects use a single .cursorrules file. Rules carry things like 'use our logging helper' or 'never edit generated files'. The next lesson but two covers rules files in depth.

steps: Ask first
Ask the chat where something lives and how it works before changing it
Scope the task
One clear outcome per request, with the relevant files mentioned
Read the plan
Check which files it intends to touch
Review the diff
Red lines removed, green lines added; ask about anything surprising
Run the checks
Lint and tests locally or in CI before committing

p: When teams adopt AI editors, the risky period is the first month: big unreviewed diffs, inconsistent styles and secrets pasted into chat. A short shared rules file, a 'small PRs' norm and an agreed list of what can be sent to the AI prevent most of it.
Measure adoption by outcomes (cycle time, review time, defects) rather than lines of AI-generated code. More code is not the goal.

mis: The Agent understands the whole codebase.
It sees what it retrieves; on large repos it can miss related code unless guided.
AI editors replace code review.
They make producing changes faster, which makes review more important.
Rules files are optional extras.
They're the cheapest way to make output consistent across the team.

Pointing the AI at a specific file, folder or doc
A searchable map of the code built from embeddings
AI that edits files and runs commands to complete a task
Side-by-side or inline view of proposed changes

quiz: The Agent changed the wrong file. What's the most likely cause?
It lacked context; point it at the right files or improve the rules and README.
Where does Cursor look for project rules today?
The .cursor/rules folder, plus user and team rules and AGENTS.md; .cursorrules is the older single-file form.
Why exclude build folders from indexing?
Generated files add noise, slow indexing and reduce search accuracy.
Tab, chat or Agent: which suits renaming a field across 12 files?

p: Because Copilot is part of GitHub, it works with things your organisation already manages: repositories, issues, pull requests and access permissions. Administrators control which features are enabled and for whom.

When an AI agent can take an issue and come back with a pull request, the bottleneck moves from writing code to specifying and reviewing it. Well-written issues with clear acceptance criteria become far more valuable, and review capacity becomes a planning constraint.
Treat agent work like work from a new team member: scope it tightly, review it fully, and don't let it merge without the same checks as human code.

bullets: Which features are enabled for our organisation, and who has seats?
Which repositories may the coding agent work on?
Who reviews and approves agent pull requests?
How do we measure impact: cycle time, review time, defects?
What is our policy on code suggestions that match public code?

p: If your company buys Copilot, ask for the admin policy settings and the usage reports: they tell you which features are on, who uses them and how often. That data turns 'is AI helping?' into a fact-based discussion.

Treat AI-assignable issues as a ticket type: clear acceptance criteria, small scope, and a named human reviewer. Agents return the most value on well-defined, repetitive tasks such as test additions, small bug fixes and dependency updates.

mis: Copilot is just autocomplete.
It also includes chat, pull request review and a coding agent.
The agent's PR passed checks, so merge it.
Checks only test what they test; a human still reviews intent and design.
More AI seats means faster delivery.
Without good specs and review capacity, it often means more work waiting in review.

An AI that works on a task independently and returns a pull request
Conditions a change must meet to be accepted
An admin setting that enables or restricts a feature

quiz: What's the biggest planning change when AI agents can implement issues?
Specification quality and review capacity become the main constraints.
Can agent-written pull requests skip review?
No. They need the same review and checks as any other change.
Name four Copilot capabilities.
Code completion, chat, pull request code review and the coding agent.
Why do companies often prefer Copilot?
It lives inside GitHub, where code, issues and permissions are already managed.

sections.h: The problem: big code, limited context
p: A model's context window holds a lot, but a real product may have thousands of files. The AI can't read everything for every question, so the tool must decide what to show it. Whatever it doesn't find, the AI effectively doesn't know, and it may fill the gap with a confident guess.

p: Cursor builds an index of your codebase and combines semantic search with exact-text search. Claude Code mainly explores on demand: it lists, searches and reads files as it goes. Both are forms of retrieval, the same idea as RAG applied to code.

p: When an engineer says 'the AI keeps getting this wrong', the fix is often context, not a better model: add a README section, rename confusing files, or record the convention in the rules file. That's a cheap, high-leverage improvement a TPM can sponsor.
On large codebases, ask teams how their tools see the code: indexed, searched on demand, or both, and what's excluded. It affects both answer quality and what data is sent to vendors.

mis: The AI has read the entire repository.
It has seen only what it retrieved for this task.
Bigger context windows solve everything.
Quality drops as context fills with irrelevant detail; focused context still wins.
Indexing means the code is used to train the model.
Indexing is for search; training use depends on the vendor's terms, which you should check.

A tool that finds exact text across files
Finding the relevant material to put in front of the model

quiz: Why might an AI invent a function that doesn't exist?
It never retrieved the real code, so it generated something plausible.
Indexing vs agentic search: which is always current?
Agentic search, because it reads the files as they are now.
A long session is getting worse. What do you do?
Start a fresh session with a short summary of the goal and key files.
Name two cheap ways to make a repo easier for AI.
A clear README and a rules file; also good names, ignore files and tests.

p: A rules file is a plain text (usually Markdown) file in the repository that the AI tool loads automatically. It gives every session the same starting knowledge: what the project is, how to run it, how the team works and what must never happen. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md; Cursor reads its rules folder and AGENTS.md; other tools have similar files.

table: Shared with everyone working on the repo

Project rules, can target specific files
A cross-tool convention for agent instructions

sections.h: What to put in, and what to leave out
table: Never-do rules: no edits to migrations, no secrets
How to explain changes to you
p: Keep it short and specific. The rules are read every session, so every line costs a little context and attention. If a rule must never be broken, also enforce it with a test, a linter or CI; a rules file guides, it does not guarantee.

This project's CLAUDE.md lists the stack, says every schema change needs an Alembic migration, says permissions are enforced in the back end, requires tests for every API change, defines the lesson JSON format and forbids committing .env. Each rule exists because breaking it would cause a real problem: data loss, a security hole or broken content.
Treat the rules file as living documentation: whenever the AI repeats a mistake, add a one-line rule and commit it. Review it at retrospectives the same way you review the definition of done.
For teams using several tools, keep one source of truth (for example AGENTS.md) and point the tool-specific files at it, so rules don't drift apart.

mis: Rules files are enforced.
They're instructions the model usually follows; enforce critical rules with tests and CI.
More rules give better results.
Long rules files dilute the important lines and waste context.
Rules files are only for AI.
They're excellent onboarding notes for new humans too.

p: A Skill is a folder that teaches Claude one repeatable job. At minimum it contains SKILL.md: a small header (YAML frontmatter) with a name and a description, then the instructions in Markdown. It can also include templates, examples, reference files and scripts.

Claude doesn't read every Skill all the time. It sees the names and descriptions, and loads the full instructions only when your task matches. That's why you can have many Skills without crowding the context.

Start with the documents you produce every week or month: status reports, release notes, risk reviews, meeting summaries. Each is a natural Skill, and consistency across a programme is valuable to stakeholders.
Version your Skills like any other asset. When a stakeholder asks for a format change, update the Skill once instead of telling ten people.

p: Git is the version-control tool: it records every change to a project as a history of snapshots. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration: pull requests, reviews, issues, automation and permissions. Your study repository lives on GitHub; Claude pushes Git commits to it.

Use GitHub as your delivery dashboard: open PRs per team, PR age, failing checks and linked issues tell you more about real progress than a status meeting. Ask for read access to the repos you manage.
When a release slips, look at the PRs: are they huge, waiting on review, or failing checks? Each points to a different fix: smaller slices, review capacity or test stability.

mis: GitHub is only for engineers.
Issues, PRs and Actions are core delivery signals a TPM should read.

It's the agreed source of truth; protect it with required reviews and checks.
Open source means free to use any way you like.
The licence sets the rules, and some carry obligations.

p: Public repositories let anyone read the code. Stars show interest, forks show reuse, and GitHub Trending lists repositories gaining attention, which is a good way to spot new AI tools early. Always check the licence before using open-source code in a product: some licences place obligations on how you distribute your own software.

Git tracks versions; GitHub hosts Git repos and adds collaboration and automation.
A PR has a red cross next to it. What does it mean?
A check, such as tests or lint, failed. It shouldn't merge yet.
Why prefer small pull requests?
They're reviewed faster and more thoroughly, and are easier to roll back.
What should you check before using an open-source library in a product?
Its licence, plus whether it's maintained and widely used.

sections.h: The handful of commands you need

p: Most commands follow the pattern: program, subcommand, options, arguments. In 'git log --oneline -5', git is the program, log is the subcommand, and --oneline and -5 are options that change the output. 'docker compose up --build' reads the same way.
Paths can be relative (cd backend, from where you are) or absolute (the full path from the drive). Most 'file not found' errors come from running a command in the wrong folder; check with pwd.

bullets: Errors usually say 'error' and stop the command; warnings let it continue.
The useful line is often the last one, or the first line mentioning your own file.
A long red block is often one problem repeated; copy the whole thing to Claude and ask for the cause in one sentence.
Never paste a command you don't understand from a random website; ask Claude to explain it first, especially anything with sudo, rm or curl piped to a shell.

p: Keep a small personal command cheat sheet for your projects: start, stop, test, check status. Most of your terminal use will be those few commands.
When asking engineers for help, paste the exact command and the full output rather than 'it doesn't work'. You'll get answers in minutes instead of hours.

mis: The terminal is dangerous.
Most commands are harmless; be careful with deletion, admin rights and scripts piped from the internet.
You need to memorise commands.
You need to recognise patterns and know how to ask; help flags and AI do the rest.

Whether you're in the right folder (pwd), since paths are relative to it.

Press Ctrl+C.

An option that changes behaviour: rebuild images before starting.

Ask Claude to explain exactly what it does.

p: Projects reuse libraries other people wrote. A package manager (npm for JavaScript, pip for Python) downloads them from a registry and installs them. The project declares what it accepts (for example 'version 2.x'), and the lock file records exactly what was installed, so every machine and every build gets the same versions.
Without a lock file, two installs a week apart can pull different versions, which is a classic cause of 'it worked yesterday'. Commit the lock file.

Settings that differ between machines or must stay secret (database address, JWT secret, API keys) are read from environment variables instead of being written in code. Locally they live in .env; in production they're set in the hosting platform's settings.
The rule: .env is ignored by Git and never shared; .env.example is committed so a new person knows which variables to set.

bullets: Secrets: .env files
Huge downloaded folders: node_modules, virtual environments
Build output: .next, dist, __pycache__
Personal editor and OS files
Note: .gitignore only affects files not yet tracked. A file already committed must be removed from tracking first.

p: A five-minute repo health check: is there a README that explains how to run it, a lock file, a .env.example, a sensible .gitignore, and CI that runs tests? Missing pieces predict onboarding pain and fragile releases.
When a vendor or contractor hands over code, check these files first. Secrets committed in history or no lock file are red flags worth raising before acceptance.

mis: Lock files are clutter and can be deleted.
They're what make installs repeatable; commit them.
.gitignore removes files from the repository.
It only stops untracked files being added; tracked files stay.
Environment variables are only for secrets.
They hold any per-environment setting, such as URLs and feature flags.

gloss: A library your project needs to run

A record of exact installed versions

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering; a major bump can break things

quiz: Why commit package-lock.json?
So every install uses the same exact versions.
Why is .env.example committed but .env isn't?
The example lists variable names safely; .env holds real secrets.
You add a secret file to .gitignore after committing it. Is it now safe?
No. It's still tracked and in history; stop tracking it and rotate the secret.
A build broke with no code change. One likely cause?
A dependency updated to a new version, often because there was no lock file or it wasn't used.

p: Postman is an API client: a tool for building a request, sending it and inspecting the response, with no code. In the earlier API lessons you learned the theory of methods, status codes and JSON. Postman is where you see them for real.
Postman acts as the client, just like the browser or the mobile app would. That lets you test the back end on its own and see exactly what it returns.

p: A collection is a saved, ordered set of requests: perfect for 'can a user log in, load the catalog and save progress?' Environments hold variables such as the base URL, so the same collection runs against local, staging or production by switching one dropdown.
Store tokens and passwords as secret variables or in Postman's Vault, and never share a collection export that still contains real credentials.

Before filing a bug, reproduce it in Postman. If the API returns the wrong data, it's a back-end bug; if the API is right but the screen is wrong, it's front end. That one step routes the ticket correctly and saves a day of back-and-forth.
Keep a smoke-test collection for each product you manage: log in, fetch the main data, perform the key action. Running it after a release takes two minutes and catches the obvious breaks.

mis: Postman is a testing tool only for QA.
Anyone who needs to see what an API really does can use it.
If the UI hides a button, the action is protected.
Only the back end protects data; check by calling the API directly.
A 200 status means the answer is correct.

quiz: You remove the Authorization header and still get data back. What does that tell you?
The endpoint isn't protected on the back end, which is a security bug.
Why use environments?
To run the same requests against local, staging and production by switching variables.
The login request returns 422. What's the likely cause?
The request body is malformed or missing fields.
How do you keep tokens safe in Postman?
Use secret variables or the Vault, and don't export collections with real credentials.

p: Vercel takes your code from GitHub, builds it and serves it on a global network. It is built by the company behind Next.js, so Next.js apps deploy with almost no configuration, though it supports many other frameworks too.
The key idea is that deployment is tied to Git: you don't 'release' by hand, you merge, and the platform deploys.

sections.flowLabel: Pushing a branch creates a preview deployment; merging to main creates the production deployment
p: Every push to a branch or pull request gets its own preview URL. Reviewers, designers and stakeholders click a real working version instead of reading screenshots. Merging into main deploys to production.

p: This project has three parts: the Next.js front end, the FastAPI back end and a Postgres database. The front end is a natural fit for Vercel. The back end and database could run on Vercel or on another provider, and that choice involves cost, region and operations trade-offs. Deciding this is exactly the kind of question a TPM frames for engineering, so it's part of the prove exercise.
Push for preview deployments in your teams' workflow: attach the preview link to the ticket, and make 'stakeholder clicked it' part of the definition of done for UI changes.
Check who can see preview URLs. Previews of unreleased features may need protection, especially for regulated or confidential work.

Why are preview deployments valuable to non-engineers?
Everyone can click and test a real version of each change before it ships.
A deploy fails. Where do you look first?
The build log.
Should production and preview share the same secrets?
Usually not; set environment variables per environment.

p: Lovable and v0 are AI app builders. You describe an app in plain language, they generate a working web app, show it in a live preview, and let you refine it through conversation or visual edits. When you're happy, you publish it to a public URL.

Lovable aims at complete products, with integrations for a database, user login and payments. v0, made by Vercel, generates Next.js and React code, deploys to Vercel, and can connect to a GitHub repository and open pull requests for review.

p: A generated app can look finished long before it's safe. Before real users or real data: check who can see what (row-level security, auth), where secrets are stored, what happens on errors, and who will maintain it. Lovable's own docs include a security best-practices page; read it before publishing anything with personal data.
Used well, these tools change the PM role: you can test an idea with users on day two instead of week six, and hand engineering a working reference instead of a document.

Use app builders to answer one question at a time: will users understand this flow, will they use this feature, does this layout work? Then throw the prototype away or hand it to engineering as a reference.
Set a team rule: prototypes built with app builders never get real customer data or production credentials without an engineering and security review.

A security review: auth, data access rules and secret handling.

Smaller steps are easier to check and fix, and earlier choices shape later ones.
You want generated UI to go into an existing Next.js repo via review. Which fits better?
v0, which can work with a GitHub repo and open pull requests.
What's the main PM benefit of these tools?
Testing ideas with users quickly using something clickable.

p: AI Studio is for prototyping. For production, companies typically use the Gemini API with proper key management, or Google Cloud's Vertex AI for enterprise controls. Free-tier usage may be used to improve Google's products, so check your company's data policy before using real customer data.
Bring evidence, not opinions, to AI feature discussions: a scored test set run in AI Studio (accuracy, typical errors, cost per call) ends most debates about feasibility.
Save the exact prompt, model and settings with your results. Results change when any of those change, and engineering needs them to reproduce your test.

mis: A great demo means the feature works.
A few hand-picked examples prove little; test on 20 or more real cases.
AI Studio is the production platform.
It's for prototyping; production uses the API or an enterprise platform.
The most powerful model is always best.
Smaller models are often good enough, faster and much cheaper.

A small, scored experiment to see if AI can do the task

Low, for consistent answers.
Why include 'unknown' as an allowed answer?
So the model doesn't force a wrong category when unsure.
What do you hand engineering after a successful test?
The exported code, settings, test set and results.
Can you paste customer data into a free AI tool?
Only if your company's data policy allows it; anonymise by default.

p: A general chatbot answers from what it learned in training plus whatever you paste. NotebookLM answers from the sources you add to a notebook, and every claim links back to the passage it came from. That's retrieval-augmented generation packaged as a product.

sections.flowLabel: Requests go from the user to Cloudflare's edge (DNS, security, cache, Workers) and then to your origin servers
p: When a site uses Cloudflare, users connect to Cloudflare's nearest data centre first. Cloudflare answers what it can (cached files, blocked attacks) and forwards the rest to your own servers, called the origin.

table: Caches static content close to users
Absorbs floods of traffic, blocks malicious requests
Runs small pieces of code on Cloudflare's network, close to users
Hosts static and front-end sites from Git

p: A Worker is a small function that runs on Cloudflare's network for each request, without you managing a server. Typical uses: redirect rules, adding headers, a small API, A/B routing, or calling an AI model and returning the result. They start fast and you pay for usage, which makes them a cheap home for small tools.
Cloudflare also offers storage and AI products around Workers. For a TPM the important point is architectural: some logic can live at the edge, which changes where bugs, logs and costs appear.

Because so much of the internet runs through a few providers, an outage at one can take down many unrelated sites at once. In incident reviews, ask which parts of the user journey depend on each provider, and what the fallback is.
During incidents, check provider status pages (Cloudflare, your cloud, your CDN) early. Many 'our site is down' events are upstream, and knowing quickly changes the communication plan.
In architecture reviews, ask which requests go through the CDN, what is cached and for how long. Stale caches cause confusing bugs: users see old content after a release.

mis: A CDN makes everything faster.
It speeds up cacheable content; slow APIs and databases stay slow.
Cloudflare is only for big companies.
Its free and low-cost tiers are widely used by small sites and side projects.
Edge code replaces the back end.
It's suited to small, fast tasks; core logic and data usually stay at the origin.

gloss: Servers close to users, at the network's edge
Your own servers behind the CDN

A request served from the CDN without reaching the origin
Code that runs on demand without servers you manage

quiz: What is the 'origin'?
Your own servers that Cloudflare forwards requests to.
Will a CDN speed up a slow database query?
Not for dynamic, uncached responses; it mainly speeds up cacheable content.
Name two uses for Cloudflare Workers.
Redirects, header changes, small APIs, A/B routing, calling AI models.
Why does a Cloudflare outage break many sites at once?
Many sites route their traffic through Cloudflare's network.

Test coverage measures how much code ran during tests, not whether the tests check the right things. A test that calls a function but checks nothing raises coverage and proves nothing. Ask 'which behaviour does this test prove?' rather than 'what's the coverage percentage?'

Track flaky tests as a delivery risk. A suite that randomly fails trains people to ignore red builds, which defeats the point of CI.

Coverage counts executed lines, not meaningful checks.
Design patterns should be used everywhere.

The linter passes. Does that mean the feature works?
No. Linters catch suspicious code patterns, not wrong behaviour; that's what tests are for.

p: Code review means someone other than the author examines a change before it merges. The goal is to keep the codebase healthy over time, not to make each change perfect. Google's published guidance says to approve a change once it clearly improves the overall health of the code, even if it isn't perfect.

table: Does this belong here and fit the system?
Does it do what's intended, for users and other developers?

Are there sensible tests that would fail if it broke?
Do they explain why, not what?
Does it follow the style guide; are docs updated?

bullets: Small pull requests get faster and better reviews; large ones get rubber-stamped or stall.
Review turnaround time is a real constraint, and it grows with AI-generated code.
AI reviewers catch many issues fast; a human still owns design and risk decisions.
Watch for PRs waiting days: ask whether the change is too big, unclear or blocked on a decision.

p: Ward Cunningham's metaphor: taking a shortcut is like borrowing money. You get speed now (the principal), and then every future change in that area costs extra effort (the interest) until you pay it back by cleaning up.

Martin Fowler adds a useful split: debt can be deliberate or inadvertent, and prudent or reckless. 'We must ship now and will fix it next sprint' is deliberate and prudent. 'What's layering?' is inadvertent and reckless.
table: 'Now we know how we should have done it'

Budget continuously
Reserve a share of each sprint rather than waiting for a 'debt quarter'
Record deliberate debt when taken

p: Add review turnaround to your delivery metrics alongside cycle time. If PRs wait two days for review, adding more AI-generated code makes the queue worse, not better.
When engineering asks for debt work, ask for the interest: which features are slowed, by how much, and what breaks more often. Then you can trade it against roadmap items honestly.

mis: Reviews should block until the code is perfect.
Approve when it clearly improves code health; perfect is the enemy of shipped.
All technical debt is bad.
Deliberate, prudent debt can be a smart trade if it's recorded and repaid.

Continuous budgeting works better; big clean-up projects often get cancelled.

p: A starter kit (also called a template or boilerplate) is a working project skeleton: folder structure, configuration, login, styling and deployment already wired up. Vercel's template gallery, for example, has starters for AI chatbots, SaaS apps and RAG chat with a vector database.
They save days, but you inherit every choice the author made. Check the licence, how actively it's maintained and whether its stack matches what your team can support.

table: POST to the Messages API endpoint

Your company's thin layer on top of one or more SDKs
An ai_client module or an AI gateway service
p: An internal wrapper is often worth building once more than one team calls AI models. It's the one place to manage keys, log every call, track cost per team, enforce safety checks and switch models or providers. This is the adapter pattern from the code-quality lesson.

Companies build tools for their own engineers: command-line scripts, Slack bots that answer 'what's deployed?', admin consoles, project templates. Larger companies have a platform team that owns these. AI makes such tools cheap to build, so the real question becomes ownership: who maintains it when the person who built it moves on?

bullets: Does a maintained official option already exist?

Does it centralise something we must control: keys, cost, logging, safety?

p: When several teams start building AI features, propose a shared AI gateway or wrapper early. Retro-fitting cost tracking, logging and key management across ten codebases is much harder than starting with one.
For any internal tool someone builds in a weekend with AI, ask who owns it, where it's documented and what happens if it breaks. Unowned tools become hidden operational risk.

sections.h: The shape of every model API call
sections.flowLabel: Your app builds a request with an API key, the provider checks it and runs the model, your app reads the response and logs usage
p: Whether it's Claude, Gemini or OpenAI, a model API is an ordinary web API: an HTTPS POST request with JSON in and JSON out. The differences between providers are mostly field names.

p: An API key is a password for software. Anyone who has it can spend your money and read whatever your account can reach. Keep it in an environment variable (the SDKs read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY automatically), in a .env file locally and in the hosting platform's secret settings in production. Use separate keys per environment and per service so one leak can be revoked without breaking everything.

An SDK builds the request for you and adds retries, types and streaming helpers. The underlying call is identical, so anything you learn with raw requests in Postman applies when engineers use the SDK.

p: Ask for a sample request and response early in any AI project and keep it in the project docs. It settles arguments about what the model sees, and it's the first thing you'll need in an incident.
Insist on logging token usage and the response ID for every call from day one. Without it you can't explain cost, trace a bad answer or give the provider's support team what they need.

Where should an API key live in production?
In the hosting platform's secret or environment settings, never in code.
Which costs more per token, input or output?
Usually output; check the provider's price page.
Does using an SDK change what's sent to the provider?
No. It builds the same HTTPS request and adds conveniences like retries.

p: You send the whole conversation every time: a list of turns alternating between user and assistant, plus an optional system prompt with standing instructions. The API is stateless; it doesn't remember previous calls, so your application stores the conversation and sends it again. That is why long conversations cost more: every turn resends everything before it.

sections.flowLabel: Tool use loop: app sends tools, Claude asks for a tool, app runs it and returns the result, Claude answers
p: You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its inputs. When Claude decides a tool would help, it replies with a tool_use block instead of a final answer. Your code runs the function and sends the result back in a tool_result block; Claude then answers using it.

Client tools run in your code, so you control exactly what happens. Server tools, such as web search, are run by Anthropic and return results in the same response. Either way, your code decides what a tool is allowed to do, which is where safety lives.

sections.h: Prompt caching: pay once for the repeated part
p: Many products send the same large prefix with every request: tool definitions, a long system prompt, a policy document. Prompt caching lets the API reuse the processed prefix. You mark the end of the reusable part with cache_control, keeping the stable content at the start (tools, then system, then messages).

Reading from the cache is billed at a small fraction of the normal input price, and writing to it costs a little more than normal. Entries expire after a few minutes by default, with a longer, more expensive option. Cached reads also don't count towards input-token rate limits on most models, which raises your effective capacity.

table: Long, stable system prompts or documents

p: When reviewing a design that uses tools, ask what each tool can do in the worst case. A tool that can issue refunds needs limits, logging and possibly human approval, whatever the model decides.
Put prompt caching and batch processing on the cost checklist for every feature. Teams often discover them after the first large bill, when they could have been in the original estimate.

mis: Claude runs the tools itself.
For client tools, your code runs them; Claude only asks.
Caching changes the answer.
It reuses processing of an identical prefix; it doesn't cache replies.
Longer system prompts are free.
Every token is billed each call unless cached.

The API keeps no memory between calls
