Runs the workflow for each pull request.
Which tool is self-hosted and plugin-based?
Jenkins.
Where should API keys for pipelines go?
Encrypted secrets, not the YAML file.

table: Components working together, such as API and database
A full user journey through the UI
p: Martin Fowler's practical test pyramid explains why: higher-level tests are slower and more brittle, so most checks should sit lower down.

table: Smoke tests on the live environment

p: A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change. They waste time and teach people to ignore red builds. Track them, quarantine them, and fix or delete them quickly.

bullets: Coverage shows which lines tests execute, not whether behaviour is right.
Useful for spotting untested risky areas.
Harmful as a hard target; teams write shallow tests to hit the number.

p: Report flaky test count in sprint reviews; it's a hidden tax on every developer.
Make sure release sign-off includes post-deploy smoke tests, not only pre-release tests.

mis: More end-to-end tests mean more safety.
They're slow and brittle; balance the pyramid.
100% coverage means no bugs.
Coverage measures execution, not correctness.
QA tests at the end.
Testing runs throughout the pipeline.

gloss: Tests a small piece of code in isolation
A quick check that the basics work after deploy

quiz: Why have more unit tests than end-to-end tests?
They are faster and less brittle.
What is a flaky test?
One that passes or fails without code changes.
What do smoke tests check?
That the basics work right after deployment.
Is high coverage proof of quality?
No; it shows code was run, not that behaviour is correct.

table: A software computer with its own OS on shared hardware
An isolated process sharing the host's OS kernel
Very light and fast, less isolation

p: Ubuntu's tutorial describes the command line as a text interface to the computer, also called the shell, terminal or console. Engineers use it because it is precise, scriptable and works the same on remote servers.

SSH (Secure Shell) opens an encrypted terminal on a remote server. Access is usually by key pairs rather than passwords. In mature setups, direct SSH into production is rare and audited; changes go through pipelines instead.

Old practice treated servers like pets: named, hand-configured and nursed when sick. Modern practice treats them like cattle: identical, created from code, and replaced rather than repaired. This makes scaling and recovery predictable.
Ask how often engineers SSH into production; frequent manual access is a reliability and audit risk.
Learn five commands; it makes incident calls much easier to follow.

mis: The cloud means no servers.
Servers still exist; the provider manages the hardware.
Command line is only for experts.
Basic commands are learnable in an hour.
VMs and containers are the same.
They isolate at different levels.

gloss: A computer providing a service over a network
A program that runs typed commands
A file of commands run together

A VM has its own OS; a container shares the host OS kernel.
What is SSH?
Encrypted remote terminal access to a server.
What does 'tail -f' do?
Follows a log file as it updates.
Why treat servers as cattle?
Replaceable servers built from code make scaling and recovery predictable.

table: Read-only package built from a Dockerfile
A dish made from the recipe
A running instance of an image

p: Docker's overview describes an image as a read-only template with instructions for creating a container, and a container as a runnable instance of an image.

bullets: Same environment from laptop to production: fewer 'works on my machine' bugs.
Fast start-up, so scaling up is quick.
Isolation: apps don't conflict over library versions.
Clear artifacts: the image is the thing that's tested and deployed.

p: Docker Compose starts several containers together from one file. This project's docker-compose.yml runs three services: a PostgreSQL database, the FastAPI backend and the Next.js frontend, wired together on a private network.
A container's own files disappear when it is removed. Databases and uploads need volumes, storage that lives outside the container, or a managed database service.
Ask for image tags in release notes; 'latest' isn't a version you can roll back to.
When onboarding takes days, a Compose setup can cut it to an hour.

mis: Containers are lightweight VMs.
They share the host kernel; isolation is lighter.
Containers store data safely.
Use volumes or external databases for persistence.
Docker and Kubernetes compete.
Docker builds and runs containers; Kubernetes orchestrates many of them.

gloss: A running instance of an image
A place to store and share images

quiz: What is the difference between an image and a container?
An image is the template; a container is a running instance.
What builds an image?
A Dockerfile.
Why use volumes?
To keep data when containers are replaced.
What does Docker Compose do?
Runs several containers together from one file.

Keeps a set number of identical pods running and handles updates
A stable address that load-balances across pods

p: You write YAML describing what should run. Kubernetes constantly compares that with reality and fixes differences: if a pod dies, it starts a new one. The Kubernetes docs list service discovery and load balancing, self-healing and automated rollouts among its features.

table: Many services, multiple teams, need for portability
A single app or small team
Usually simpler options: a managed app platform or serverless
p: Kubernetes adds operational complexity. Managed versions from AWS (EKS), Azure (AKS) and Google (GKE) reduce, but don't remove, that burden.
When Kubernetes is proposed, ask who will run it and what it replaces; operational cost is the hidden line item.
Learn to read a deployment's replica count and image tag; they answer many incident questions.

mis: Kubernetes makes apps scalable automatically.
Apps must be designed to run as many copies.
Kubernetes is a container runtime.
It orchestrates containers run by a runtime.
Managed Kubernetes needs no expertise.
Teams still own configuration, upgrades and security.

gloss: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes
A stable network endpoint for pods

quiz: What is a pod?
The smallest deployable unit, one or more containers.
What happens when a pod crashes?
Kubernetes starts a replacement to match the desired state.
What gives pods a stable address?
A service.
Is Kubernetes right for every product?
No; small apps often do better with simpler platforms.

steps: Write: describe the desired resources in configuration files.
Plan: Terraform shows what it will create, change or destroy.
Review: the plan is checked, often in a pull request.
Apply: Terraform makes the changes and records them in a state file.
p: HashiCorp describes Terraform as declarative: files describe the end state, and Terraform works out the steps. It keeps a state file as the source of truth about real infrastructure.

bullets: Repeatable: create identical dev, staging and production.
Reviewable: changes go through pull requests.
Recoverable: rebuild an environment from code after a disaster.
Auditable: history shows who changed what and when.

table: Sets up software and settings on servers

p: Drift happens when someone changes infrastructure manually so it no longer matches the code. The next apply may undo the manual fix, or fail. Teams detect drift regularly and restrict console access for changes.
Ask for the Terraform plan output in change reviews for production infrastructure; it shows impact in plain terms.
Treat manual console changes in production as incidents to learn from.

mis: IaC is only for big companies.
Even small teams benefit from repeatable environments.
Writing IaC once is enough.
Code and reality drift; check regularly.
Terraform configures apps.
It provisions infrastructure; app config is separate.

gloss: Describing the end state, not the steps
A preview of changes before applying
Difference between code and real infrastructure

quiz: What does 'terraform plan' show?
What will be created, changed or destroyed.
What is drift?
Real infrastructure no longer matching the code.
Name a configuration management tool.
Ansible, Chef or Puppet.
Why is IaC good for disaster recovery?
Environments can be rebuilt from code.

p: The AWS overview whitepaper describes cloud computing as on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

A region is a geographic area, such as Mumbai. Each region has several availability zones, separate data centres with independent power and networking. Running across zones protects against one data centre failing; choosing the region affects latency and data residency.

bullets: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, flexible but priciest.
Reserved or savings plans: commit for one to three years for discounts.
Spot or preemptible: cheap spare capacity that can be taken back.
Data transfer out of the cloud often costs more than expected.
Tag resources by team and product so costs can be allocated.

p: Insist on cost allocation tags from day one; untagged spend is impossible to manage later.
Ask for the region choice to be documented with the data residency reason.

mis: Cloud is always cheaper.
Without management, it can cost more than on-premises.
One provider is clearly best.
They're broadly equivalent; fit, skills and contracts decide.
Serverless has no servers.
Servers exist; the provider manages them.

gloss: An isolated data centre within a region
Data leaving the cloud, often charged

quiz: What is the AWS equivalent of Azure Blob Storage?
Why use multiple availability zones?
To survive the failure of one data centre.
Name three pricing options.
On-demand, reserved or savings plans, spot (any three).
What is egress?
Data leaving the cloud, often charged.

table: Your isolated network in the cloud
Reachable from the internet, for load balancers
Not directly reachable, for apps and databases
Allow-list of traffic to a resource
Spreads traffic and checks server health
Lets private servers reach out without being reachable

p: AWS's IAM guide explains that an account starts with a root user with full access and strongly recommends not using it for everyday tasks. Instead, people and applications get identities with policies granting only the actions they need.
bullets: Users: people or long-lived identities (prefer federated sign-in).
Roles: temporary permissions assumed by services or people.
Policies: JSON rules allowing or denying actions on resources.
Least privilege: start with nothing and add what's needed.
Is the database in a private subnet with no public IP?
Which security group rules allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 (anywhere)?
Is multi-factor authentication on for the root and admin accounts?
Do apps use roles instead of stored access keys?

p: Ask for a network diagram in every architecture review; exposure problems are visible at a glance.
Track 'resources open to 0.0.0.0/0' as a security metric.

mis: Cloud resources are private by default everywhere.
Misconfiguration can expose them publicly.
IAM is only for people.
Applications and services need identities too.
A firewall at the edge is enough.
Defence in depth means rules around each tier.

gloss: A private network in the cloud

quiz: Where should a database usually sit?
In a private subnet.
What is a security group?
A virtual firewall listing allowed traffic.
Why avoid the root account for daily work?
It has full access; misuse or theft is catastrophic.
What does 0.0.0.0/0 in a rule mean?
Traffic from anywhere on the internet.

bullets: Set a minimum (always running), desired, and maximum (cost cap) number of instances.
Scale on a metric such as CPU, requests per server or queue length.
Scheduled scaling handles predictable peaks like evenings or sales.
Apps must be stateless so any instance can serve any request.

table: A hard disk attached to one server
p: AWS's comparison explains that the three types differ in how data is organised and accessed; object storage scales almost without limit and suits unstructured data.

table: Install and patch PostgreSQL on a VM
Use a managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL)
p: Managed services cost more per unit but save engineering time on patching, backups and failover. Under the shared responsibility model the provider secures the platform; you still own data, access and configuration.
Ask for scaling limits and the cost at maximum scale; finance should never be surprised by a traffic spike.
Review storage lifecycle rules; old logs and backups often cost more than expected.

mis: Auto scaling fixes all performance problems.
Databases and slow code still bottleneck.
Managed means no responsibility.
You still own data and access.
Object storage is a disk.
It's accessed over APIs, not mounted like a drive.

gloss: An app that keeps no user state on the server itself
Storage of files as objects in buckets
A component operated by the provider
Split of security duties between provider and customer

quiz: Which storage type suits user uploads?
Object storage.
Why must apps be stateless to scale out?
So any instance can handle any request.
What does a maximum instance count protect?
Cost.
What do you still own with a managed database?
Data, access control and configuration.

Prepare new environment, switch all traffic
p: Martin Fowler describes blue-green as two production environments, one live, so the cut-over and rollback are quick. His canary release article describes rolling out to a small subset of users first before everyone.

steps: Deploy the new version alongside the old.
Route 1% of traffic; watch errors, latency and business metrics for 30 minutes.
Increase to 10%, then 50%, checking the same signals.
Go to 100% when metrics stay within thresholds.
Roll back immediately if any threshold is breached.

p: Zero-downtime releases break if a database change isn't compatible with both versions running at once. The common pattern is expand and contract: add new columns first, deploy code that uses them, then remove old columns in a later release.

Flags separate deploying code from releasing features. You can deploy everything, then turn a feature on for staff, then 5% of users, without redeploying. They need cleanup, or old flags pile up as technical debt.
Write go/no-go thresholds before the release, not during it; decisions under pressure are worse.
Add 'database compatible with old version?' to the release checklist.

mis: Zero downtime is automatic in the cloud.
It needs the right strategy and compatible changes.
Canary means beta testers.
It's a share of real production traffic.
Rollback is always possible.
Irreversible data changes can block it; plan ahead.

gloss: Releasing to a small group first
Making database changes in compatible steps

quiz: Which strategy gives the fastest rollback?
Blue-green, by switching traffic back.
What does a canary release need most?
Good monitoring to compare versions.
Why can database changes break zero-downtime releases?
Old and new code run at the same time against one database.
How do feature flags differ from deployment strategies?
Flags control who sees a feature without redeploying.

p: The Twelve-Factor App says config, meaning anything that varies between deploys, should be stored in environment variables and kept strictly separate from code. That's why this project ships a .env.example with placeholders and keeps the real .env out of Git.

bullets: Examples: AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GitHub Actions secrets.
Encrypted storage, fine-grained access, audit logs.
Support rotation without code changes.

steps: Revoke or rotate the key immediately; deleting the commit is not enough.
Check logs for misuse.
Remove it from the code and history if needed.
Find why it happened and add secret scanning to prevent repeats.
p: GitHub's secret scanning detects many known credential formats in repositories and can alert or block pushes.
Run a 'leaked key' drill once; teams that have practised rotate in minutes, not days.
Ask for secret scanning on every repository as a default.

mis: Deleting the commit removes the leak.
It remains in history and copies; rotate the key.
Private repos don't need secret hygiene.
Access widens over time; treat all repos as exposable.
Environment variables are fully secure.
They can leak through logs and debugging; use managers for secrets.

gloss: A setting provided by the running environment
A local file of environment variables, not committed

quiz: Where should config that varies by environment live?
In environment variables, outside the code.
What's the first step after a key leak?
Revoke or rotate the key.
Why commit a .env.example but not .env?
The example documents settings; the real file holds secrets.

AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, Vault, GitHub secrets (any two).

p: Nginx's beginner's guide covers serving static content and setting up a simple proxy server. In most stacks, Nginx sits in front of the application, handling HTTPS, compression and routing, and forwards requests to the app.

p: DNS changes can take time to spread because of caching (TTL). Lower the TTL before a migration.

Let's Encrypt issues free certificates through the ACME protocol: a client on your server proves you control the domain and gets a certificate. Renewing means repeating that process. Its certificates are short-lived, so renewal must be automated and monitored.
bullets: Automate renewal with a client such as Certbot or your platform's built-in support.
Monitor expiry dates and alert well in advance.
Keep an inventory of all domains and certificates, including old marketing sites.

p: Keep a domain and certificate register with owners and expiry dates; forgotten domains cause outages.
Add expiry monitoring to the same alerting used for uptime.

mis: Certificates renew themselves.
Only if automation is set up and working.
DNS changes are instant.
Caches can hold old answers for the TTL period.
Nginx is the app.
It usually fronts the app.

An entry mapping names to destinations
How long DNS answers are cached

quiz: What does a reverse proxy do?
Receives requests and forwards them to backend apps.
Which DNS record points a name to another name?
CNAME.

Automate renewal and monitor expiry dates.
Why lower TTL before a migration?
So DNS changes take effect faster.

p: Prometheus, an open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit originally built at SoundCloud, collects metrics as time series. Grafana visualises them in dashboards. OpenTelemetry is the common standard for collecting traces, metrics and logs across vendors.

table: How full resources are: CPU, memory, connections
p: These come from Google's SRE practice and are a good default for any service dashboard.

bullets: Alert on user-visible symptoms (errors, slowness), not every internal cause.
Each alert needs an owner and a runbook link.
Too many alerts cause fatigue; people start ignoring them.
Review alerts after incidents: did the right one fire, early enough?

Count alerts per on-call shift; more than a handful usually means noise.

mis: More dashboards mean better observability.
Focused dashboards answer questions faster.
Logs are enough.
Metrics show trends; traces show where time goes.
Alert on everything.
Noise hides the alerts that matter.

A record of a request's path
Ignoring alerts because there are too many

quiz: Name the three main observability signals.
Logs, metrics, traces.

Latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
Why alert on symptoms?
They reflect user impact and cut noise.

Visualises metrics in dashboards.

99.5% monthly, with service credits if missed
p: Google's SRE book defines an SLO as a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI.
Each extra nine costs much more to achieve. Pick the level users actually need.

If the SLO is 99.9%, the error budget is 0.1%: in a month of 1 million requests, 1,000 can fail. While budget remains, the team can take risks and ship. When it's spent, priority shifts to reliability until it recovers.
Set the internal SLO tighter than the external SLA, so you get a warning and act before contractual penalties apply.
Put SLO status in the sprint review; it makes the reliability-vs-features trade-off explicit and data-driven.
Agree the error budget policy before you need it.

mis: 100% availability is the goal.
It's impossibly expensive; users don't need it.
SLA and SLO are the same.
The SLA is a contract; the SLO is an internal target.
Uptime is the only SLI.
Latency and correctness matter too.

quiz: What is the error budget for a 99.9% SLO?
0.1% of requests or time.

About 43 minutes.
Why keep the SLO stricter than the SLA?
To act before contractual penalties.
What happens when the error budget is spent?
Priority shifts to reliability work.

Assign roles.
Mitigate first: restore service, then find root cause.
Update stakeholders every 30 minutes, even if nothing changed.
Declare resolved and schedule the postmortem.

p: Google's SRE book describes blameless postmortems as focusing on contributing causes without blaming individuals or teams, because people hide information if they fear punishment. Good postmortems include a timeline, impact, causes, what went well and owned action items with dates.

Note each step, check and approval.
Ask what would trigger a rollback and who decides.
Write down what was manual and could be automated.

p: Track postmortem action items like any other backlog; unfinished actions are why incidents repeat.
Volunteer as communications lead; it's where TPMs add the most value in incidents.

mis: RCA finds the single root cause.
Incidents usually have several contributing factors.
Blameless means no accountability.
Teams are accountable for fixing systems and completing actions.
MTTR alone shows reliability.
Pair it with incident frequency and impact.

gloss: A written review after an incident

quiz: What comes first during an incident: root cause or mitigation?
Mitigation.
What does a communications lead do?
Gives stakeholders regular updates.
Why are postmortems blameless?
So people share information openly.

MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR).

Use infrastructure as code so environments can be rebuilt quickly.

steps: Choose a scenario, such as primary database lost.

Time each step against the RTO.

Fix gaps in the runbook and repeat.

p: Every website, from a small blog to a bank, goes through the same journey. Code is written on a developer's laptop, checked by others, tested, packaged, sent to servers, connected to a web address and then watched once real users arrive.

Engineers often call this the software delivery lifecycle (SDLC) or the 'path to production'. Knowing the stages in order is the single most useful thing for a TPM, because every status update, risk and delay belongs to one of them.

When you hear a new term at work, add it here with where it fits in the journey.

mis: Knowing definitions is enough.
Tests often ask where a term fits and why it matters; practise both.

quiz: Deploy vs release?
Deploy puts code on servers; release makes features available to users.
DNS vs CDN?
DNS finds the server's address; a CDN serves cached content from locations near users.
What is an artifact?
The packaged build output that gets deployed.
What is a provisioning profile?
An iOS file linking the app, signing certificate and distribution method.
SLO vs SLA?
SLO is an internal reliability target; SLA is a promise to customers.

steps: Set a timer
30 minutes for 30 questions.
Answer aloud or on paper
Don't open the answers until you've tried.
Score
One point each; half a point if partly right.
Review
For each miss, note the topic and reread it.
Retake
Retake in a few days; aim for 25 or more.

p: Before the questions, put these in order from memory: deploy, code review, set up repo, build in CI, monitor, write code, DNS and certificate, UAT on staging, launch, automated tests.

Answer: set up repo, write code, code review, automated tests, build in CI, UAT on staging, deploy, DNS and certificate, launch, monitor. (DNS and certificates are often prepared earlier but confirmed at go-live.)
Do the test twice: once now, once the day before your manager's test.
For scenario questions, structure answers as: check facts, contain impact, communicate, fix, learn.

mis: Memorising answers is enough.
Managers rephrase questions; understand the why behind each answer.

quiz: 1. What is the difference between a Git branch and a pull request?
A branch is a separate line of work; a pull request asks to merge that branch into main with review and checks.
2. Why use a lock file?
To make every install use exactly the same dependency versions.
3. What is the purpose of a staging environment?
Final testing in a production-like setup before release.
4. A bug appears only in production. Name three possible reasons.
Different data, configuration or secrets, scale or traffic, third-party live services, or caching.
5. What does a CI pipeline usually include?
Install dependencies, lint, run tests, security scans, build and publish an artifact.
6. What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
Delivery keeps every change deployable with a manual trigger; deployment releases automatically.
7. Explain blue-green deployment in one sentence.
Run the new version alongside the old one and switch traffic over, so you can switch back instantly.
8. When would you choose a canary release?
When a change is risky and you want a small share of users first while you watch metrics.
9. Why might a rollback be impossible?
A database or data change isn't backward compatible.
10. What is a feature flag and why is it useful at launch?
A switch to turn features on or off without deploying; it lets you launch gradually and turn off quickly.
11. What DNS record would you use to point www to a hosting provider's name?
A CNAME record.
12. Why lower the TTL before moving a domain?
So the change reaches users quickly instead of waiting for long-cached answers.
13. What happens if an SSL certificate expires?
Browsers show security warnings and block or scare away users.
14. Name the three Core Web Vitals and good values.
LCP 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less.
15. What does a CDN improve?
Speed and load on servers, by serving cached content from locations near users.
16. What is the difference between SAST and DAST?
SAST scans source code; DAST tests the running application.
17. Define RPO and RTO.
Maximum acceptable data loss and maximum acceptable downtime.
18. What happens in a go/no-go meeting?
Owners confirm readiness against the checklist and decide whether to release.
19. Name the three pillars of observability.
Logs, metrics and traces.
20. What is hypercare?
A period of extra monitoring and support right after launch.
21. Why is mobile rollback different from web rollback?
Installed versions stay on phones; you can halt a rollout or ship a new version but not pull it back.
22. What must increase with every Android upload?
The versionCode.
23. What is code signing for?
Proving the app comes from you and hasn't been tampered with.
24. What is TestFlight?
Apple's service for distributing beta builds to testers.
25. Describe Apple's phased release.
Updates go to users with automatic updates over 7 days: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100%; you can pause.
26. Describe Google Play's staged rollout.
You release an update to a chosen percentage of users and raise it manually; you can halt it.
27. Name two common App Store rejection reasons.
Crashes, no demo account, privacy mismatch, unclear permissions or incomplete content.
28. Why keep backend APIs compatible with older app versions?
Many users don't update straight away.
29. Scenario: launch is tomorrow and a high-severity security issue is found. What do you do?
Assess with security, decide fix vs delay with the risk owner, communicate, and don't launch with an unaccepted high risk.
30. Scenario: after a release, error rates jump. Your first three actions?
Confirm the impact on dashboards, decide rollback or halt using agreed triggers, and start incident communication with an owner.

steps: Setup
'Code lives in a Git repository. Developers run the app locally, work on feature branches and keep secrets out of the code using environment variables.'
Code
'A feature usually touches the frontend in the browser, an API, the backend logic and the database, sometimes with a migration.'
Review
'Developers open a pull request. CI runs linting and tests, and a colleague reviews before merging to main.'
Build
'The CI pipeline builds an artifact, often a Docker image, with a version number.'
Test
'The same artifact goes to QA and staging for regression and UAT.'
Deploy
'We deploy to production with a safe strategy, such as blue-green or canary, often behind a feature flag, with a tested rollback plan.'
Reachable
'DNS points our domain to the hosting platform, and a TLS certificate gives us HTTPS.'
Fast and safe
'A CDN and caching keep it fast; we track Core Web Vitals. Security checks include OWASP risks, scans and backups.'
Launch and run
'A go/no-go meeting, smoke tests, then monitoring with logs, metrics and traces, alerts, on-call and hypercare.'

bullets: Builds must be signed: certificates and provisioning profiles on iOS, a keystore and Play App Signing on Android.
Every upload needs a higher build number.
Beta testing via TestFlight and Play testing tracks.
Store listing, privacy labels and app review are a release gate.
Release gradually: Apple's 7-day phased release, Google Play's staged rollout. You can halt but not pull back installed versions.
Backend must support older app versions; feature flags and forced updates help manage this.

p: Draw one line left to right: Laptop → Git → CI → Artifact → Staging → Production → Users. Above Production, draw DNS and CDN. Below the line, write Monitoring with arrows back to the team. For mobile, draw a branch after CI: Sign → TestFlight/Play testing → Store review → Phased rollout → Phones.

table: How do you know a release is ready?
Agreed exit criteria: tests green, no critical bugs, UAT signed off, rollback ready, monitoring in place
Name one specific risk (for example a database migration), its impact and mitigation
How do you roll back on mobile?
Halt rollout, ship a fixed version, use feature flags or remote config, force update if critical
Measure first (Core Web Vitals, TTFB), then check CDN, images, JavaScript, API speed and region
Who do you involve for a domain change?
DevOps for DNS and certificates, security, marketing for any URL changes, SEO owner for redirects

steps: Clarify
Ask one question to understand impact.
Contain
Limit user impact: rollback, halt, feature flag.
Communicate
Who needs to know, and how often.
Fix
Owner, plan and timeline.
Learn
Post-mortem and prevention.

p: Use your own product's names and tools in the talk track; real examples are more convincing.
Keep a single-page cheat sheet of the journey for the day of the test.

mis: Using lots of jargon sounds expert.
Clear order and simple explanations with the right terms impress more.

quiz: What line do you draw for the whiteboard sketch?
Laptop → Git → CI → Artifact → Staging → Production → Users, with DNS/CDN above and monitoring below.
Name three mobile-specific steps.
Code signing, beta via TestFlight or Play tracks, store review, phased or staged rollout.
What five steps structure a scenario answer?
Clarify, contain, communicate, fix, learn.
